GERD — the 8-week rule and what counts as "objective" reflux

ACG Clinical Guideline, Katz et al., Am J Gastroenterol 2022;117:27–56 · Lyon Consensus 2.0, Gut 2024

InsideAlarm features that buy an EGD up frontAfter the 8 weeksWhat counts as objective GERD (matters before you ever discuss surgery)Lifestyle changes that actually have dataRefractory symptoms

Reflux of stomach contents causing troublesome symptoms or damage to the oesophageal lining. Enormously common — and the clinical difficulty is not making the diagnosis but working out when the symptoms are actually acid, because most “refractory reflux” turns out not to be reflux at all.

Must know
  • Eight-week empiric PPI trial, dosed 30–60 minutes before a meal.
  • Objective GERD = LA grade B, C or D (grade B was promoted to conclusive by Lyon 2.0 in 2024), long-segment Barrett's, peptic stricture, or acid exposure time >6%.
  • Indefinite PPI only for LA C/D, Barrett's, or stricture — otherwise attempt to taper.

AbbreviationsAET acid exposure time · CKD chronic kidney disease · GERD gastro-oesophageal reflux disease · H2RA histamine-2 receptor antagonist · PPI proton pump inhibitor

Full detail

Classic heartburn and regurgitation without alarm features gets an 8-week empiric trial of once-daily PPI taken 30–60 minutes before a meal. That timing detail is the single most common thing residents get wrong and attendings notice — PPIs are acid-activated prodrugs and need a stimulated parietal cell.

Alarm features that buy an EGD up front
  • Dysphagia, odynophagia, unintentional weight loss
  • GI bleeding, iron-deficiency anemia, recurrent vomiting
  • Family history of upper GI malignancy; new dyspepsia age ≥60
After the 8 weeks
  • Responded? Attempt taper or discontinuation — unless the patient has LA grade C/D esophagitis, Barrett's, or a peptic stricture, all of which are indications for indefinite maintenance PPI.
  • Didn't respond? Optimize first (adherence, dosing before meals, twice-daily trial), then EGD off PPI for 2–4 weeks. If the EGD is unrevealing, go to pH monitoring off therapy to establish whether reflux exists at all.
What counts as objective GERD (matters before you ever discuss surgery)
  • LA grade B, C or D erosive esophagitis — Lyon 2.0 (2024) moved grade B from "borderline" to conclusive; the 2018 consensus and the 2022 ACG guideline still say C/D
  • Long-segment Barrett's esophagus
  • Peptic stricture
  • Acid exposure time (AET) >6% on pH testing off PPI

LA grade A esophagitis is not conclusive evidence of GERD — it's seen in asymptomatic controls. Grade B was "borderline" under the original 2018 Lyon consensus but is conclusive under Lyon 2.0 (Gut 2024). On pH testing, AET >6% is conclusive, <4% is physiological, and 4–6% is inconclusive and needs adjunctive evidence (reflux episodes, mean nocturnal baseline impedance). A hiatal hernia is supportive, never conclusive. Knowing these distinctions is a fast way to sound like you've read Lyon.

Lifestyle changes that actually have data
  • Weight loss in the overweight or those with recent weight gain
  • Avoid meals within 2–3 hours of lying down
  • Head-of-bed elevation for nocturnal symptoms
  • Tobacco and alcohol cessation. Blanket "avoid chocolate, coffee, citrus, spicy food" is not recommended — target only the patient's own identified triggers.
Refractory symptoms
  • Confirm the diagnosis before escalating — most "refractory GERD" is functional heartburn or reflux hypersensitivity.
  • Nocturnal breakthrough: add an H2RA at bedtime (tachyphylaxis develops; use on-demand).
  • Baclofen reduces transient LES relaxations — reasonable adjunct in documented refractory reflux.
  • A large hiatal hernia is the commonest reason regurgitation-predominant symptoms persist on a PPI — acid suppression does not stop volume reflux. Document hernia size and Hill grade (see the hiatal hernia topic below); TIF is designed for hernias ≤2 cm, and fundoplication and magnetic sphincter augmentation include a crural repair.
  • Antireflux surgery, magnetic sphincter augmentation, or transoral incisionless fundoplication require objective GERD documentation first, and manometry to exclude achalasia or absent contractility before any wrap.
PitfallDon't reflexively deprescribe a PPI because of headlines about dementia, CKD, or fractures. The guideline states the evidence for these associations is low quality and confounded, and that PPIs should not be withheld when there is a clear indication. The right move is to reassess the indication, not to fear the drug.
On rounds, sayShe's had a full 8 weeks of pre-meal dosing without response, so before we escalate I'd rather establish whether this is actually reflux — EGD off PPI for 2–4 weeks, and if that's clean, pH monitoring off therapy looking for an acid exposure time above 6%.

Hiatal hernia — the four types, the Hill flap valve, and when the hernia is the problem

Hill LD, et al. Gastrointest Endosc 1996;44:541–547 · SAGES Guidelines for the Management of Hiatal Hernia, Kohn et al., Surg Endosc 2013 · SAGES update, Daly et al., Surg Endosc 2024 · Chicago Classification v4.0 · Lyon Consensus 2.0

InsideLandmarks and how to measureThe four typesHill classification of the flap valveComplications: Cameron lesions and volvulusManagement by typeWhat the hernia means for antireflux procedures

Part of the stomach sitting above the diaphragm. It is one of the commonest findings on any upper endoscopy and one of the most over-blamed — a small sliding hernia is a finding, not a disease. The job is to say which type it is, grade the valve, and recognise the minority of hernias that are themselves the problem.

Must know
  • Type I (sliding) is >95% of hiatal hernias, is treated only through the reflux it causes, and needs no repair on its own.
  • Hill grade I–II = intact flap valve; III–IV = defective valve and, in practice, a hernia. It belongs in every EGD report next to the hernia size.
  • Paraoesophageal hernias (types II–IV): repair when symptomatic. Obstruction, volvulus or strangulation is a surgical emergency.
  • Cameron lesions in a large hernia are a classic cause of unexplained iron-deficiency anaemia.

AbbreviationsGEJ gastro-oesophageal junction · HRM high-resolution manometry · LES lower oesophageal sphincter · MSA magnetic sphincter augmentation · PEH paraoesophageal hernia · SCJ squamocolumnar junction · TIF transoral incisionless fundoplication

Full detail
Landmarks and how to measure

Three landmarks on withdrawal, each recorded as a distance from the incisors: the squamocolumnar junction (Z-line), the gastro-oesophageal junction (the proximal margin of the gastric folds with the stomach minimally insufflated), and the diaphragmatic pinch (the extrinsic crural impression, easier to see if the patient sniffs). A sliding hiatal hernia is called when the GEJ sits ≥2 cm above the pinch; the hernia length is the distance between the two.

  • The endoscopic measurement drifts with insufflation, respiration and retching, so it is reproducible only to the nearest centimetre. Barium swallow and HRM are the alternatives — on manometry, Chicago v4.0 calls a separation of the LES and crural diaphragm of more than 3 cm a type 3 EGJ morphology.
  • Retroflex in the fundus and look at the hiatus from below: this is where the flap valve is graded and where the sac of a paraoesophageal hernia is seen alongside the scope.
  • The GEJ, not the pinch, is the zero point for Prague C&M in Barrett's. Measuring from the diaphragm adds the hernia to the segment.
The four types
TypeAnatomyHow commonWhat it causes
I — slidingGEJ migrates above the diaphragm; the fundus follows in line behind it. The phreno-oesophageal ligament is stretched, not torn.>95% of all hiatal herniasReflux — by removing the crural component of the sphincter and creating an acid pocket above the diaphragm
II — true paraoesophagealGEJ stays in place below the diaphragm; the fundus herniates alongside the oesophagus through a defect in the ligament.RareObstruction, volvulus; reflux less typical
III — mixedBoth the GEJ and the fundus are above the diaphragm; the fundus lies alongside or above the GEJ.The commonest paraoesophageal hernia (roughly 90% of them)Reflux and obstructive symptoms, Cameron lesions, volvulus
IVAnother organ in the sac — colon, spleen, pancreas, small bowel — with a large defect. The "upside-down stomach" is the giant end of this spectrum.RareObstruction, respiratory compromise, strangulation

Types II, III and IV are grouped together as paraoesophageal hernias because the management question is the same: does part of the stomach lie beside the oesophagus in a position where it can twist or obstruct?

Hill classification of the flap valve

Hill and colleagues graded what the endoscopist sees on retroflexion: how tightly the gastric folds hug the scope at the cardia. The fold is the endoscopic face of the angle of His and the crural sling, and its loss tracks with reflux far better than hernia length alone.

Hill gradeWhat you see on retroflexionImplication
IA prominent fold of tissue closely apposed to the scope, extending 3–4 cm along the lesser curveNormal valve
IIThe fold is present but less prominent; it opens with respiration and closes again promptly around the scopeUsually competent; reflux possible
IIIThe fold is not prominent and the scope is not gripped tightly; the hiatus is often patulousDefective valve; a hiatal hernia is usually present
IVNo fold at all; the hiatus is wide open and squamous epithelium can be seen from belowA hiatal hernia is always present; reflux is nearly universal
Complications: Cameron lesions and volvulus
  • Cameron lesions — linear erosions or ulcers on the crests of the gastric folds at the level of the diaphragmatic pinch, from mechanical trauma with each breath plus acid. Found in roughly 5% of hiatal hernias at endoscopy, more often in large ones. They bleed slowly and present as unexplained iron-deficiency anaemia or occult positive stool, and they are missed when the hernia sac is not examined carefully on withdrawal and in retroflexion. Treat with a PPI and iron; repair the hernia when bleeding is refractory or transfusion-dependent.
  • Gastric volvulus — the stomach twists on its long axis (organoaxial, the common form, associated with paraoesophageal hernias and diaphragmatic defects) or on its short axis (mesenteroaxial). Borchardt's triad: severe epigastric pain, retching without vomiting, and inability to pass a nasogastric tube. This is an emergency — decompress if a tube will pass, endoscopic or surgical detorsion, then repair — because ischaemia and perforation follow.
  • Obstruction, strangulation, bleeding and anaemia are the other paraoesophageal complications. Giant hernias also cause post-prandial fullness, early satiety, chest pain and breathlessness — a symptom set that is easily mistaken for cardiac disease.
Management by type
SituationApproach
Type I, asymptomaticNothing — no treatment, no surveillance, and no need to mention it to the patient as a diagnosis
Type I with refluxThe GERD algorithm. The hernia is repaired only as part of antireflux surgery, never on its own
Paraoesophageal, symptomatic (obstructive symptoms, anaemia, bleeding, volvulus history)Elective laparoscopic repair: reduce the stomach, excise the sac, close the crura, add a fundoplication (a gastropexy alone is acceptable in frail patients). Mesh reinforcement reduces early recurrence in some series but has no proven long-term benefit, so it is used selectively
Paraoesophageal, asymptomatic or minimally symptomaticWatchful waiting is acceptable, especially over 65 — the annual risk of needing emergency surgery is about 1%, and emergency repair carries several times the mortality of an elective one. Repair is reasonable in younger, fit patients
Acute volvulus, strangulation, perforationEmergency: decompression, resuscitation, surgery
What the hernia means for antireflux procedures
  • Fundoplication (Nissen or Toupet) always includes a crural repair — the hernia is fixed as part of the operation.
  • Magnetic sphincter augmentation (LINX): hernias over 3 cm were excluded from the original trials; the hernia is now repaired at the same time.
  • Transoral incisionless fundoplication is designed for hernias of ≤2 cm with a Hill I–II valve; larger hernias need a laparoscopic crural repair first (concomitant TIF).
  • Before any of these: HRM to exclude achalasia or absent contractility, a pH study when there is no LA grade B–D oesophagitis or Barrett's, and a barium study if the anatomy is unclear.
Numbers to know
  • Type I sliding hernia: >95% of hiatal hernias · type III: ~90% of paraoesophageal hernias
  • Endoscopic definition of a sliding hernia: GEJ ≥2 cm above the diaphragmatic pinch
  • Asymptomatic paraoesophageal hernia: about 1% per year risk of needing emergency surgery
  • Cameron lesions in roughly 5% of hiatal hernias at endoscopy
  • After paraoesophageal repair, radiological recurrence is common (roughly half at 5 years in the mesh trial) but symptomatic reoperation is uncommon (~3%)
PitfallA 2 cm sliding hernia explains heartburn. It does not explain dysphagia, chest pain, dyspnoea or anaemia on its own — keep looking. The reverse error is just as common: a giant paraoesophageal hernia in an older patient with "atypical chest pain", early satiety and iron deficiency that nobody has connected to the stomach on the chest film.
On rounds, sayHe has a 4 cm sliding hernia with a Hill grade III valve and LA grade B oesophagitis, so under Lyon 2.0 that's conclusive GERD without a pH study. Regurgitation is the dominant symptom and he's failed twice-daily PPI, which is what a big hernia does — so I'd get manometry and refer him for a fundoplication with crural repair rather than a TIF, which is really for hernias of 2 cm or less.

Barrett's Esophagus — screening, Seattle protocol, surveillance intervals

ACG Clinical Guideline, Shaheen et al., Am J Gastroenterol 2022;117:559–587

InsideWho to screen (once)Describing the segment: Prague C&MSampling: the Seattle protocolSurveillance and management by grade

The normal squamous lining of the lower oesophagus is replaced by intestinal-type columnar epithelium after years of reflux. It matters for one reason: it is the only known precursor of oesophageal adenocarcinoma. So the entire topic is about who to screen, how to sample, and how often to look again.

Must know
  • Definition: ≥1 cm salmon mucosa above the GEJ with intestinal metaplasia on biopsy.
  • Non-dysplastic surveillance: <3 cm → 5 years, ≥3 cm → 3 years.
  • Low- and high-grade dysplasia both go to endoscopic eradication therapy.
  • Seattle protocol: four-quadrant biopsies every 2 cm (every 1 cm if dysplasia suspected).
  • Report the segment as Prague C&M — C is the circumferential length, M the maximal extent; M is the length that sets the surveillance interval.

AbbreviationsCE-IM complete eradication of intestinal metaplasia · EAC oesophageal adenocarcinoma · EMR endoscopic mucosal resection · GEJ gastro-oesophageal junction · GERD gastro-oesophageal reflux disease · HGD high-grade dysplasia · LGD low-grade dysplasia · NDBE non-dysplastic Barrett's oesophagus · PPI proton pump inhibitor

Full detail

Definition: ≥1 cm of salmon-colored columnar mucosa extending proximal to the gastroesophageal junction, with intestinal metaplasia confirmed on biopsy. Under 1 cm is "irregular Z-line" — do not biopsy it and do not label the patient.

Who to screen (once)

A single screening endoscopy in patients with chronic GERD symptoms (weekly symptoms for 5 or more years) plus ≥3 additional risk factors: male sex, age >50, white race, tobacco smoking, central obesity, and family history of Barrett's or esophageal adenocarcinoma in a first-degree relative. Note that male sex is itself one of the counted risk factors, so women reach the threshold less often.

A swallowable non-endoscopic capsule sponge device with a biomarker is an acceptable alternative to EGD for screening — this is the newer recommendation people forget.

Describing the segment: Prague C&M

The Prague classification (Sharma P, et al. Gastroenterology 2006;131:1392–1399) is how the segment is written down so the next endoscopist can find the same thing. Two measurements, both taken from the gastro-oesophageal junction — the proximal margin of the gastric folds with the stomach minimally insufflated, not from the diaphragmatic pinch:

  • C — the length of circumferential columnar mucosa above the GEJ, in cm
  • M — the maximal extent, to the tip of the longest tongue, in cm
  • Islands of columnar mucosa above the tongues are not included in C or M — describe them separately
  • Write it as, for example, C2M5: circumferential for 2 cm, longest tongue reaching 5 cm. The M value is the segment length that decides short (<3 cm) versus long (≥3 cm) and therefore the 5-year versus 3-year interval
  • Record the distance from the incisors to the GEJ and to the diaphragmatic pinch as well — that documents any hiatal hernia separately and stops it being added to the Barrett's length

Prague was validated for segments ≥1 cm; its reliability below 1 cm is poor, which is one reason the ≥1 cm definition exists and irregular Z-lines are not labelled. It does not describe visible lesions — those are reported by Paris morphology, distance from the incisors and clock position, and go to EMR.

Sampling: the Seattle protocol
  • Both white light endoscopy and chromoendoscopy are recommended during surveillance; inspect carefully, with roughly a minute per cm of Barrett's segment as a commonly cited quality target
  • At least 8 biopsies at a screening exam when the appearance is consistent with possible Barrett's
  • Four-quadrant biopsies every 2 cm for non-dysplastic Barrett's
  • Four-quadrant biopsies every 1 cm when dysplasia is known or suspected
  • Target and separately label any visible lesion — visible lesions go to EMR, which is both staging and therapy
  • All dysplasia requires confirmation by a second expert GI pathologist
Surveillance and management by grade
FindingAction
NDBE, <3 cmSurveillance EGD every 5 years
NDBE, ≥3 cmSurveillance EGD every 3 years
Indefinite for dysplasiaOptimize acid suppression, repeat EGD in 3–6 months
Low-grade dysplasiaEndoscopic eradication therapy preferred; surveillance q12 months is an acceptable alternative after shared decision-makingTrialSURF — Phoa KN, et al. JAMA 2014;311:1209–1217 — ablation reduced progression from LGD
High-grade dysplasiaEndoscopic eradication therapy (EMR of visible lesion + ablation of remaining segment)TrialAIM Dysplasia — Shaheen NJ, et al. NEJM 2009;360:2277–2288 — radiofrequency ablation in dysplastic Barrett's
T1a intramucosal adenocarcinomaEndoscopic eradication therapy rather than esophagectomy
T1bMultidisciplinary — surgical/oncologic evaluation
Numbers to know
  • Annual progression NDBE → EAC: ~0.2–0.5%/yr
  • Annual progression LGD → HGD/EAC: ~0.5–1.5%/yr
  • Annual progression HGD → EAC: ~6–7%/yr
  • Barrett's prevalence in chronic GERD: ~5–15%
PitfallThe goal endpoint of ablation is complete eradication of intestinal metaplasia (CE-IM), not just eradication of dysplasia. Surveillance continues after CE-IM — recurrence runs roughly 8–10% per year.
On rounds, sayThis is a 4 cm segment with confirmed non-dysplastic intestinal metaplasia, so he's on a 3-year interval rather than 5, once-daily PPI, and I'd want the next exam done with a proper Seattle protocol — four-quadrant every 2 cm, with any visible lesion sent separately for EMR.

Eosinophilic Esophagitis — the PPI-responder concept is gone

ACG Clinical Guideline (update), Dellon et al., Am J Gastroenterol 2025;120(1):31–59

InsideBiopsy techniqueThe four therapeutic levers

A chronic immune-mediated disease in which eosinophils infiltrate the oesophagus, causing dysphagia and food impaction — classically in a young, atopic man. Untreated, it slowly remodels a distensible tube into a rigid narrow one.

Must know
  • Symptoms + ≥15 eos/hpf + exclusion of other causes. A PPI trial is no longer required.
  • Take at least 6 biopsies from two levels, even if the mucosa looks normal.
  • Judge response histologically — patients adapt their eating and will tell you they're fine.

AbbreviationsEREFS Edema, Rings, Exudates, Furrows, Stricture — the endoscopic scoring system in EoE · EoE eosinophilic oesophagitis · PPI proton pump inhibitor

Full detail

Diagnosis: symptoms of esophageal dysfunction + ≥15 eosinophils per high-power field on esophageal biopsy + exclusion of other causes of esophageal eosinophilia. A PPI trial is no longer required and PPI response no longer excludes EoE — "PPI-responsive esophageal eosinophilia" is a retired entity, and PPIs are now simply one treatment option.

Biopsy technique
  • At least 6 biopsies total, from at least two levels (proximal and distal esophagus), targeting areas of visible inflammation
  • Document the EREFS score — Edema, Rings, Exudates, Furrows, Stricture
  • Take gastric and duodenal biopsies if there's any concern for eosinophilic gastroenteritis or other cause
The four therapeutic levers
OptionNotes
PPITwice daily; ~40–50% histologic remission. Cheap, easy — reasonable first step.
Topical steroidBudesonide oral suspension (FDA-approved formulation) or swallowed fluticasone. Don't rinse/eat for 30 min. Watch for esophageal candidiasis.
DietEmpiric food elimination, starting with a 1-food (dairy) or 2-food elimination diet rather than jumping to six-food — comparable outcomes, far fewer endoscopies. Allergy testing should not be used to direct the diet — EoE is a delayed hypersensitivity, so skin prick and serum IgE testing predict triggers poorly.
DupilumabAnti-IL-4Rα. The 2025 guideline suggests dupilumab specifically for patients non-responsive to PPI therapy — in those aged 12 and over, and separately in children aged 1–11. This is the big change since your syllabus was written. No recommendation was made for or against cendakimab, benralizumab, mepolizumab, reslizumab, or lirentelimab; omalizumab is advised against.TrialLIBERTY-EoE-TREET — Dellon ES, et al. NEJM 2022;387:2317–2330
DilationTreats the stricture, not the inflammation. Always combine with anti-inflammatory therapy. Gradual, low-target dilation; perforation risk is lower than historically feared.
PitfallAssess response histologically, not symptomatically. EoE patients unconsciously adapt — chewing excessively, drinking with every bite, avoiding meat and bread — and will report they're "fine" with an esophagus full of eosinophils. Ask specifically about food modification behaviors.
On rounds, sayTwenty-eight-year-old with a food impaction — I'd take at least six biopsies from two levels even if the mucosa looks normal, score the EREFS, and note that under the 2025 guideline we no longer need a PPI trial to call this EoE.

Dysphagia — the branch point that organizes the whole workup

Jansson-Knodell, Mayo Clin Proc 2017 · ACG Achalasia Guideline 2020 · Chicago Classification v4.0, Neurogastroenterol Motil 2021

InsideWithin esophageal dysphagiaChicago Classification v4.0 — what changedAchalasia subtypes drive therapy

Difficulty swallowing. It is a symptom rather than a diagnosis, and almost all the value lies in sorting it into the right compartment at the bedside before you order a single test.

Must know
  • Oropharyngeal → video swallow study. Esophageal → EGD first.
  • Solids and liquids together from the outset means motility — go to high-resolution manometry.
  • Achalasia subtype changes therapy: type III → POEM. Always exclude pseudoachalasia.

AbbreviationsEGJ oesophagogastric junction · EoE eosinophilic oesophagitis · FLIP functional lumen imaging probe · GERD gastro-oesophageal reflux disease · IRP integrated relaxation pressure · POEM peroral endoscopic myotomy · PPI proton pump inhibitor

Full detail

Split it at the bedside before ordering anything:

OropharyngealEsophageal
ComplaintTrouble initiating a swallow, coughing/choking, nasal regurgitation, droolingFood "sticks" seconds after swallowing, points to the chest
CausesStroke, Parkinson's, ALS, myasthenia, Zenker's, post-radiationStructural or motility
First testVideofluoroscopic swallow study (modified barium swallow)EGD
Within esophageal dysphagia
  • Solids only, progressive, with weight loss → think malignancy or peptic stricture. EGD.
  • Solids only, intermittent, non-progressive → ring or web (Schatzki). EGD.
  • Solids and liquids from the start → motility disorder. EGD first to exclude mechanical cause, then high-resolution manometry.
  • Young man, food impaction, atopic history → EoE until proven otherwise.
Chicago Classification v4.0 — what changed
  • Manometry protocol now requires both supine and upright swallows, plus multiple rapid swallows and a rapid drink challenge.
  • Elevated median IRP in both positions is needed to call disordered EGJ outflow.
  • EGJ outflow obstruction is now a "manometric pattern," not a diagnosis — it requires conclusive supportive evidence (timed barium esophagram or FLIP) plus clinically relevant symptoms before you treat it.
  • "Ineffective esophageal motility" requires >70% ineffective or ≥50% failed swallows — a tighter definition than v3.0.
Achalasia subtypes drive therapy
TypeManometryPreferred treatment
IElevated IRP, 100% failed peristalsis, no pressurizationPneumatic dilation, Heller myotomy, or POEM
IIElevated IRP, ≥20% panesophageal pressurizationAny of the three — best treatment response of the three types
IIIElevated IRP, ≥20% premature/spastic contractionsPOEM — the myotomy length can be tailored to the spastic segmentTrialPonds FA, et al. JAMA 2019;322:134–144 (POEM vs pneumatic dilation); Werner YB, et al. NEJM 2019;381:2219–2229 (POEM vs Heller myotomy)
  • Always EGD first to exclude pseudoachalasia (GE junction malignancy) — suspect in age >60, symptoms <6 months, marked weight loss.
  • Botulinum toxin is for patients who are poor candidates for definitive therapy; effect wanes in 6–12 months and it scars the plane for later myotomy.
  • Eckardt score (dysphagia, regurgitation, chest pain, weight loss; 0–12) tracks response; ≤3 is treatment success.
  • Post-POEM GERD is common (roughly half) — those patients need PPI and often surveillance endoscopy.
On rounds, saySolids and liquids together from the outset points at motility, so EGD first to rule out pseudoachalasia, then high-resolution manometry — and the subtype matters, because if this is type III I'd steer toward POEM rather than pneumatic dilation.

Chest pain, odynophagia, and the esophagus you'll be consulted on overnight

Practice synthesis · ACG Esophageal Physiologic Testing Guideline 2020

InsideRule out cardiac firstPill esophagitisInfectious esophagitisEsophageal food impactionButton battery or sharp objectBoerhaave

The oesophageal problems you get called about after hours — pill injury, infection, food impaction, and the two kinds of tear. Mostly a question of recognising which of them needs a scope tonight rather than tomorrow.

Must know
  • Food impaction is an urgent scope within 24 hours — emergent if secretions can't be managed.
  • Biopsy for EoE after clearing an impaction regardless of how the mucosa looks.
  • Boerhaave (full-thickness, pneumomediastinum, surgical) vs Mallory-Weiss (mucosal, usually self-limited).

AbbreviationsCMV cytomegalovirus · EoE eosinophilic oesophagitis · GEJ gastro-oesophageal junction

Full detail
  • Rule out cardiac first. Every time. The GI consult for "non-cardiac chest pain" presumes someone has actually excluded ACS.
  • Pill esophagitis: doxycycline, tetracycline, NSAIDs, bisphosphonates, potassium chloride, iron. Classic story is a pill swallowed with little water at bedtime. Discrete mid-esophageal ulcer at the level of the aortic arch or left atrium.
  • Infectious esophagitis: Candida (linear white plaques, often on inhaled/systemic steroids or immunosuppression); HSV (small, well-circumscribed "volcano" ulcers); CMV (large, deep, solitary ulcers — biopsy the ulcer base for CMV, the edge for HSV).
  • Esophageal food impaction is an urgent endoscopy — within 24 hours, and emergent — preferably within 2 hours and at the latest within 6 — if the patient can't handle secretions or the obstruction is complete (ASGE/ESGE). Push or pull, then look hard for the underlying cause. Do not send glucagon and hope.
  • Button battery or sharp object in the esophagus: emergent removal, no exceptions.
  • Boerhaave vs Mallory-Weiss: full-thickness rupture after retching (pneumomediastinum, Hamman's crunch, surgical emergency) vs mucosal tear at the GEJ (usually self-limited, endoscopic therapy if actively bleeding).
On rounds, sayHe can't manage his secretions, so this is an emergent scope rather than an urgent one — I'd like to get him to the unit within a few hours, and once the bolus is cleared I want biopsies for EoE regardless of how the mucosa looks.

Caustic ingestion — nothing down the tube, CT decides surgery, endoscopy grades the rest

Chirica M, et al. Caustic ingestion. Lancet 2017;389:2041–2052 · Bonavina L, et al. Foregut caustic injuries: WSES consensus, World J Emerg Surg 2015;10:44 · Chirica M, et al. Esophageal emergencies: WSES guidelines, World J Emerg Surg 2019;14:26 · Chirica M, et al. Ann Surg 2016;264:107–113 · Zargar SA, et al. Gastrointest Endosc 1991;37:165–169 · Anderson KD, et al. N Engl J Med 1990;323:637–640 · Usta M, et al. Pediatrics 2014;133:e1518–e1524 · Thomson M, et al. ESPGHAN/ESGE paediatric endoscopy guideline, J Pediatr Gastroenterol Nutr 2017;64:133–153 · Birk M, et al. ESGE foreign-body guideline, Endoscopy 2016;48:489–496 · Mubarak A, et al. InsideAlkali versus acid, and the agents you will meetThe first hour: airway, resuscitation, what not to doCT decides surgery, endoscopy grades the restZargar grades and management by gradeStrictures, dilation and the late cancer riskButton batteries — the two-hour emergencyIntentional ingestion: before they leave

A strong alkali or acid swallowed by accident — young children, small volumes, usually mild — or on purpose — adults, large volumes, often severe. The injury declares itself over days rather than minutes. The questions in the first hours are whether the airway is safe and whether any of the wall is dead; the questions later are strictures and, decades on, cancer.

Must know
  • Alkali = liquefactive necrosis that keeps penetrating; acid = coagulative necrosis that pools in the stomach and poisons the whole body. Concentrated acid destroys the oesophagus too.
  • Do not induce vomiting, neutralise, dilute, give charcoal, or pass a blind nasogastric tube. Stridor, hoarseness or drooling means the larynx is burned — secure the airway under direct vision, early.
  • Contrast CT of the neck, chest and abdomen at 3–6 hours decides surgery (no wall enhancement = transmural necrosis; bronchoscopy before every resection). Endoscopy within 24 hours grades the mucosa (Zargar) for the rest. Never scope a suspected perforation, and never between days 5 and 15.
  • Grade 2b–3: nil by mouth, PPI, enteral nutrition through a tube placed under vision; no routine steroids (laryngeal oedema is the adult indication; a 3-day high-dose course in a child with grade 2b is the exception), no routine antibiotics. Strictures are dilated from 3–6 weeks; squamous cancer surveillance starts 15–20 years on.

AbbreviationsASGE American Society for Gastrointestinal Endoscopy · CT computed tomography · DIC disseminated intravascular coagulation · ECG electrocardiogram · ENT ear, nose and throat · ESGE European Society of Gastrointestinal Endoscopy · ESPGHAN European Society for Paediatric Gastroenterology, Hepatology and Nutrition · ICU intensive care unit · IV intravenous · MRI magnetic resonance imaging · NG nasogastric · PPI proton pump inhibitor · SCC squamous cell carcinoma · WSES World Society of Emergency Surgery

Full detail
Alkali versus acid, and the agents you will meet

Class decides the type of necrosis; strength, volume and form decide how much. The usual thresholds are pH below 2 or above 12 (WSES sets the alkali bar lower, and some agents injure whatever their pH); granules stick in the pharynx, liquids run through to the stomach.

Where it comes fromWhat it does
AlkaliSodium or potassium hydroxide (lye) in drain and oven cleaners; ammonia; dishwasher pods; button batteriesLiquefactive necrosis — saponifies fat, thromboses vessels, keeps penetrating. Tasteless, so larger volumes go down; the oesophagus takes the brunt.
AcidHydrochloric acid in toilet-bowl cleaners; sulfuric acid in drain cleaners and car batteries; hydrofluoric acid in rust removersCoagulative necrosis with an eschar that limits depth. Painful, so less is swallowed; pools in the antrum — gastric necrosis now, outlet obstruction later. Absorbed acid brings acidosis, haemolysis, DIC and renal failure; hydrofluoric acid binds calcium — check calcium and the ECG, give IV calcium gluconate.

Household bleach (3–6% hypochlorite) is usually a mild, self-limited oesophagitis. The phases set the timing of everything else: necrosis in the first days; sloughing and granulation from day 4 to 15, when the wall is thinnest; fibrosis from week 3, when strictures form.

The first hour: airway, resuscitation, what not to do
  • Airway first. Hoarseness, stridor, drooling or respiratory distress means the larynx is burned and swelling: ENT look now, and intubation is early and under direct or fibreoptic vision, never blind. Laryngeal oedema is where WSES accepts steroids.
  • Resuscitate like a burn: IV access, fluid, analgesia, and an antiemetic so vomiting does not drag the agent back up. Send a gas and lactate, chest and abdominal films for free air, and a paracetamol level plus toxicology after intentional ingestion.
  • What not to do: no induced emesis (re-exposes the oesophagus); no neutralising agents (exothermic); no dilution; no charcoal (binds nothing, obscures the view); no blind NG tube or lavage (perforates a necrotic wall). Nil by mouth until graded.
  • Who will be sick: intentional ingestion, a strong agent, a large volume, and any of drooling, stridor, haematemesis, chest or abdominal pain, subcutaneous emphysema, acidosis or a rising lactate — a clean mouth excludes nothing. Peritonitis or instability means a surgeon, not an endoscopy.
CT decides surgery, endoscopy grades the rest

Transmural necrosis needs an operation before it perforates, and endoscopy cannot see depth — contrast-enhanced CT of the neck, chest and abdomen can. In Chirica's 120 patients, CT alone would have spared 19 oesophagectomies and 16 laparotomies, and endoscopy never corrected a wrong CT decision. So WSES 2019 rests the emergency decision on CT at 3–6 hours, operates as soon as possible for transmural necrosis, and reserves emergency endoscopy for when CT is unavailable, contraindicated or equivocal, and for children.

  • Read the CT for wall enhancement. A thickened wall that still enhances is alive; absent post-contrast enhancement is transmural necrosis (CT grade III) and goes to theatre after bronchoscopy — mandatory (WSES) before every emergency resection, whatever the airway looks like — because tracheobronchial necrosis changes the operation to a right thoracotomy with a lung patch.
  • Endoscopy within 24 hours is still how most units grade everyone not going to theatre (the WSES 2015 combined algorithm): it grades the mucosa, says who can eat, and at grade 2b or worse places a nasojejunal feeding tube under direct vision — the only tube that goes in, never blind; WSES advises against nasogastric tubes, which prevent no strictures and add reflux and perforation. Minimal insufflation, no retroflexion in a burned stomach, stop at the first circumferential deep burn. The asymptomatic child who tasted a weak product and swallows normally needs no scope.
  • Do not scope a suspected perforation, an unsecured airway with laryngeal signs, or a CT that already shows transmural necrosis — and not late: after 48 hours the wall is softening, and nobody scopes between day 5 and 15, when the tip goes through granulation. Both windows are conventions from the injury phases, not WSES statements.
Zargar grades and management by grade

Zargar's 81 patients (1991) set the grades: early major complications and deaths were confined to grade 3, grade 0–2a recovered without sequelae, and the outcome counted was oesophageal or gastric scarring needing treatment, not stricture alone.

GradeWhat you seeWhat happensWhat to do
0Normal mucosaNothingFeed, discharge
1Oedema and hyperaemiaHealsFeed, discharge within 24 hours
2aFriability, haemorrhages, erosions, blisters, exudates, superficial ulcersHealsLiquids then diet; home at 24–48 hours
2b2a plus deep discrete or circumferential ulcerationScarring needing treatment in 71%Nil by mouth, PPI, nasojejunal tube at endoscopy; watch for perforation
3aSmall, scattered areas of necrosisScarring in every grade-3 survivor (3a and 3b reported together)As 2b, in a monitored bed
3bExtensive necrosisDeaths and early major complications confined to grade 3ICU; CT decides — resection for transmural necrosis or perforation, otherwise serial CT
  • Corticosteroids are not routine. The classic randomised trial, in children, found no benefit — stricture depended only on the depth of the burn — and steroids mask perforation.TrialAnderson KD, et al. NEJM 1990;323:637–640 — corticosteroids did not prevent strictures A later paediatric trial in grade 2b only (Usta 2014: methylprednisolone 1 g/1.73 m² per day for 3 days) cut strictures from roughly one child in three to one in ten, and the ESPGHAN/ESGE 2017 paediatric guideline adopted it; adults have never been tested, so WSES reserves steroids for laryngeal oedema.
  • Antibiotics are not routine — WSES advises them in grade 3 injury with lung involvement or when steroids are given, otherwise for perforation, aspiration or infection. A PPI is customary from grade 2; the benefit is unproven.
  • Nutrition is enteral, through the tube placed under vision or a jejunostomy. Surgery resects what is dead — oesophagogastrectomy with a cervical oesophagostomy when both organs are necrotic, oesophagectomy alone or total gastrectomy with immediate oesophagojejunostomy when only one is — always with a feeding jejunostomy and never an oesophageal reconstruction, which waits at least 6 months and usually uses colon. Fever, rising lactate or new pain on conservative care means repeat CT the same day.
Strictures, dilation and the late cancer risk
  • Strictures declare from 3 weeks; dysphagia after a grade 2b–3 burn is a contrast study or endoscopy, not a wait-and-see. Acid adds antral scarring and gastric outlet obstruction — why a jejunostomy beats a gastrostomy.
  • Dilation starts at 3–6 weeks, once the injury has healed — a granulating wall perforates. WSES reserves endoscopic dilation for few (fewer than 3), short (under 5 cm) strictures; caustic strictures are long and tortuous, need wire-guided bougies or balloons over many sessions, and perforate more often than peptic ones. Intralesional steroid works less well than in peptic strictures and WSES finds no convincing evidence for stents; self-dilation and a retrograde approach through a gastrostomy are the fall-backs, colon interposition the last resort.
  • Squamous cell carcinoma arises in the scarred segment decades later — a risk put at around 1000-fold, latency 15–40 years. New dysphagia in anyone with a caustic history is a scope, not a dilation; ASGE (2006) suggests surveillance every 1–3 years from 15–20 years after a severe injury.
Button batteries — the two-hour emergency

A lithium coin cell lodged in the oesophagus passes current through the wall and makes hydroxide at its negative pole — an alkali burn that is severe within 2 hours, symptoms or not, and perforates or fistulates over days to weeks. Cells of 20 mm or more (the 3 V coin cell) and children under 6 carry the highest risk.

  • Film, then remove. A double ring on the frontal film and a step-off on the lateral say battery, not coin. In the oesophagus, removal is emergent — within 2 hours, at the latest 6 (ESGE 2016, intubating if the aspiration risk is high), and ESPGHAN says not to wait for fasting. Honey 10 mL every 10 minutes (up to 6 doses) is allowed for a child over 1 year who can swallow, within 12 hours of ingestion and without signs of perforation, and sucralfate 10 mL every 10 minutes (up to 3 doses) in the department — never as a reason to delay.
  • Timing decides the imaging. A cell still in the oesophagus more than 12 hours after ingestion, or any bleeding, gets contrast CT for vascular injury before removal — moving it can open a fistula — with cardiothoracic surgery told first, and never an MRI while the battery is in. After removal, any mucosal injury means admission; significant injury means nil by mouth until a contrast swallow, serial CT, and a watch that lasts weeks: aorto-oesophageal fistula with fatal haemorrhage can present up to 4 weeks later, as can tracheo-oesophageal fistula, vocal cord palsy and spondylodiscitis.
  • Beyond the oesophagus: in adults ESGE wants a gastric battery out within 24 hours; in children ESPGHAN lets an asymptomatic one pass, with a film at 7–14 days, and removes it for symptoms, a co-ingested magnet, or a delayed or unwitnessed ingestion, when the oesophagus it passed through is looked at too.
Intentional ingestion: before they leave

Most adult caustic ingestions are suicide attempts: toxicology on arrival, psychiatry before discharge. Accidental ingestion in a child is a prevention conversation and, where the story does not fit, a safeguarding one. Grade 2b or higher leaves with a 3-week appointment, a warning about dysphagia and a note about cancer surveillance.

Numbers to know
  • CT at 3–6 hours · endoscopy within 24 hours, not after 48 · never between days 5 and 15
  • Zargar 1991: scarring needing treatment in 71% of grade 2b and all grade-3 survivors · Anderson 1990: strictures 10/31 vs 11/29
  • Dilation from 3–6 weeks (WSES: <3 strictures, each <5 cm) · SCC risk about 1000×, latency 15–40 years · surveillance every 1–3 years from 15–20 years
  • Button battery: out of the oesophagus within 2 hours, at the latest 6 · CT first if found after 12 hours · adult stomach within 24 hours · fistula up to 4 weeks after
PitfallThe patient who looks well at two hours is not safe: alkali injury deepens for days, and a soft abdomen on arrival says nothing about the wall on day 5. The reverse trap is treating a Zargar 3b as an automatic oesophagectomy — endoscopy overcalls transmural necrosis; if the wall enhances on CT, most keep their oesophagus.
On rounds, sayShe's 29 and drank about 200 mL of sodium hydroxide drain cleaner two hours ago as a suicide attempt. She's drooling and hoarse but not stridulous, so ENT are looking at her larynx now; she's nil by mouth with no tube, no charcoal and nothing to neutralise it. Her contrast CT shows a thickened oesophagus and stomach, but the wall enhances throughout and there's no free air — no transmural necrosis, so no operation tonight. Once ENT have cleared or secured her airway I'll scope her within 12 hours to grade it; at 2b or 3a she stays nil by mouth on a PPI with a nasojejunal tube placed under vision, no steroids unless the larynx needs them, no antibiotics unless she perforates, and a contrast study at three weeks because most at that grade scar. Psychiatry sees her before she leaves.

H. pylori — the 2024 rewrite that made clarithromycin triple therapy obsolete

ACG Clinical Guideline, Chey et al., Am J Gastroenterol 2024;119:1730–1753

InsideFirst-line optionsThe rules that don't changeWho to test

A gram-negative bacterium that colonises the stomach lining of roughly half the world's population, causing peptic ulcer disease, gastric cancer and MALT lymphoma. Eradicating it is one of the few moments in gastroenterology when a course of tablets actually cures a disease.

Must know
  • Optimized bismuth quadruple therapy for 14 days is first-line for everyone — clarithromycin triple is out unless susceptibility testing proves the strain is susceptible.
  • Test of cure in every treated patient — ≥4 weeks after antibiotics, off PPI for 1–2 weeks. Serology cannot be used.
  • Never repeat clarithromycin or levofloxacin after a failure.

AbbreviationsITP immune thrombocytopenia · MALT mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue · NSAID non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug · PPI proton pump inhibitor

Full detail

This is the highest-yield "did you read anything recent?" topic in general GI, because the answer changed completely and most residents still recite the old triple therapy.

First-line options
RegimenComponents (14 days)Comment
Optimized bismuth quadruplePPI BID + bismuth QID + tetracycline 500 mg QID + metronidazole 500 mg TID–QID (total >1.5 g/day)Preferred first-line for everyone, including penicillin allergy and prior macrolide exposure
Rifabutin tripleOmeprazole 40 mg + amoxicillin 1 g + rifabutin 50 mg, TIDAvailable as a fixed-dose combination; no clarithromycin or metronidazole resistance concern
Vonoprazan dualVonoprazan 20 mg BID + amoxicillin 1 g TIDTrialPHALCON-HP — Chey WD, et al. Gastroenterology 2022;163:608–619Potassium-competitive acid blocker — faster, stronger, more durable acid suppression than PPIs
Vonoprazan tripleVonoprazan 20 mg BID + amoxicillin 1 g BID + clarithromycin 500 mg BIDReasonable where clarithromycin resistance is known to be low
Clarithromycin triplePPI + amoxicillin + clarithromycinRemoved as a first-line option. The guideline states it should not be used unless antibiotic susceptibility testing has demonstrated a clarithromycin-susceptible strain.
The rules that don't change
  • 14 days for essentially all regimens.
  • "Optimized" means specifics. Do not substitute doxycycline for tetracycline, use a metronidazole total dose above 1.5 g/day to overcome in vitro resistance, and prefer a PPI less affected by CYP2C19 polymorphism.
  • Test of cure for every treated patient — urea breath test, fecal antigen, or biopsy-based test. Timing: ≥4 weeks after finishing antibiotics and bismuth, and off PPI for 1–2 weeks. Missing the test of cure is the classic clinic error.
  • Serology is not a test of active infection and has no role in test of cure.
  • Never repeat an antibiotic class that already failed. Clarithromycin and levofloxacin resistance is effectively permanent after exposure. Metronidazole resistance can be overcome with higher dose and bismuth.
  • Penicillin "allergy" should be formally evaluated. Over 90% of labeled patients are not truly allergic, and amoxicillin is central to several good regimens.
Who to test
  • Active or past peptic ulcer disease
  • Gastric MALT lymphoma (eradication alone induces remission in most early, H. pylori-positive cases)
  • Uninvestigated dyspepsia in patients <60 without alarm features — the "test and treat" strategy
  • Gastric intestinal metaplasia, atrophic gastritis, after early gastric cancer resection
  • First-degree relatives of gastric cancer patients; immigrants from high-incidence regions
  • Unexplained iron deficiency anemia; ITP
  • Planned long-term NSAID or aspirin therapy
Numbers to know
  • US clarithromycin resistance cited by the guideline: 22.2–31.5%; levofloxacin 37.6% — this is why both fell out of empiric use
  • Target eradication rate for an acceptable regimen: ≥90%
  • Optimized bismuth quadruple eradication: ~90%
  • Lifetime gastric cancer risk in infected patients: ~1–3%
On rounds, sayGiven US clarithromycin resistance, I'd go straight to optimized bismuth quadruple for 14 days rather than triple therapy, and I've already scheduled the urea breath test for four weeks after he finishes — with instructions to hold the PPI for the two weeks before it.

Dyspepsia — test and treat, or scope?

ACG/CAG Clinical Guideline, Moayyedi et al., Am J Gastroenterol 2017;112:988–1013

InsideAge 60 is the endoscopy thresholdTest and treat under 60When alarm features matterFunctional dyspepsia

Discomfort centred on the upper abdomen — one of the commonest reasons anyone is referred to gastroenterology. The whole clinical question is which of these patients needs a camera.

Must know
  • Age ≥60 with new dyspepsia → endoscopy.
  • Under 60 → non-invasive test and treat, then an empiric PPI trial.

AbbreviationsPPI proton pump inhibitor

Full detail
  • Age ≥60 with new dyspepsia → EGD, regardless of alarm features.
  • Age <60 → non-invasive H. pylori test and treat. If negative or symptoms persist after eradication → empiric PPI trial.
  • Alarm features in patients <60 do not reliably predict malignancy, but most clinicians still scope for overt bleeding, progressive dysphagia, or significant weight loss. Know that the guideline itself is lukewarm on alarm features under 60.
  • If EGD is negative → functional dyspepsia. Treat with PPI, then a tricyclic antidepressant (amitriptyline low-dose), then prokinetics; psychological therapy has good evidence. Avoid escalating imaging.
  • Do not order routine motility testing or repeated abdominal imaging for functional dyspepsia.
On rounds, sayHe's 44 with no bleeding and no weight loss, so rather than scoping I'd do a stool antigen and treat if positive — the guideline puts the endoscopy threshold at 60 for new-onset dyspepsia.

Peptic ulcer disease & NSAID gastropathy

ACG Upper GI Bleeding Guideline 2021 · ACG H. pylori 2024 · practice synthesis

InsideCauses, in the order you should think of themNSAID ulcer prophylaxis — stratify by both GI and CV risk

A break in the stomach or duodenal lining deep enough to reach the submucosa. Almost always caused by H. pylori or anti-inflammatory drugs; the job is to establish which, and to be certain it is not cancer.

Must know
  • Test every ulcer patient for H. pylori.
  • Biopsy every gastric ulcer. Duodenal ulcers essentially never need it.
  • High GI risk on NSAIDs → COX-2 inhibitor plus PPI, or avoid NSAIDs entirely.

AbbreviationsCMV cytomegalovirus · COX-2 cyclooxygenase-2 · NSAID non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug · PPI proton pump inhibitor

Full detail
Causes, in the order you should think of them
  1. H. pylori — test every ulcer patient
  2. NSAIDs and aspirin, including low-dose
  3. Stress-related mucosal disease in critical illness
  4. Malignancy — biopsy every gastric ulcer, and repeat EGD in 8–12 weeks to confirm healing if malignancy wasn't excluded
  5. Zollinger-Ellison — suspect with multiple ulcers, post-bulbar ulcers, ulcers refractory to PPI, or ulcers with diarrhea. Fasting gastrin off PPI (a PPI raises gastrin and makes the test uninterpretable) plus chromogranin A.
  6. Rare: Crohn's, CMV, ischemia, crack cocaine, radiation
NSAID ulcer prophylaxis — stratify by both GI and CV risk
GI riskDefined byStrategy
LowNo risk factorsNon-selective NSAID alone
Moderate1–2 of: age >65, high-dose NSAID, prior uncomplicated ulcer, concurrent aspirin/anticoagulant/steroidNSAID + PPI, or COX-2 inhibitor alone
HighPrior complicated ulcer, or >2 risk factorsAvoid NSAIDs if possible; if unavoidable, COX-2 inhibitor + PPI

Layer cardiovascular risk on top: if the patient needs cardioprotective aspirin, naproxen is the preferred NSAID and a PPI is added. Avoid COX-2 selective agents in high CV risk.

PitfallA gastric ulcer that wasn't biopsied is an unfinished job. Duodenal ulcers essentially never need biopsy; gastric ulcers essentially always do.

Gastric premalignant conditions — atrophic gastritis and intestinal metaplasia

ACG Clinical Guideline, Morgan et al., Am J Gastroenterol 2025

InsideHigh-quality endoscopySystematic biopsy (updated Sydney protocol)Do not surveil everyoneDysplasiaAutoimmune gastritis

The stepwise progression from chronic inflammation to atrophy, to intestinal metaplasia, to dysplasia, to gastric cancer. Working out where on that ladder a patient sits is what decides whether they need surveillance at all.

Must know
  • Eradicate H. pylori in everyone with intestinal metaplasia, and confirm it.
  • Map with the Sydney protocol in separately labeled jars — that is what lets the pathologist stage extent.
  • Surveillance roughly every 3 years is for higher-risk GIM only, not everyone.

AbbreviationsBLI blue light imaging · GIM gastric intestinal metaplasia · NBI narrow-band imaging

Full detail
  • Eradicate H. pylori in every patient with gastric intestinal metaplasia (GIM) or atrophic gastritis, and confirm eradication.
  • High-quality endoscopy with adequate insufflation, mucosal cleansing, ≥7 minutes of inspection, and virtual chromoendoscopy (NBI/BLI) to find focal lesions.
  • Systematic biopsy (updated Sydney protocol): antrum (greater and lesser curve), incisura, and body (greater and lesser curve) — in separately labeled jars, plus targeted biopsies of any lesion. Separate jars are what allows the pathologist to stage extent.
  • Do not surveil everyone. Surveillance EGD roughly every 3 years is reserved for higher-risk GIM: incomplete-type GIM, extensive/corpus-involving GIM, family history of gastric cancer, first-generation immigrants from high-incidence regions, and autoimmune atrophic gastritis.
  • Dysplasia in the stomach → refer for endoscopic resection at an expert center, not just repeat biopsy.
  • Giant gastric folds have their own differential — Ménétrier disease (hypertrophic protein-losing gastropathy, hypoalbuminaemia, foveolar hyperplasia on deep biopsy), lymphoma, Zollinger-Ellison, and infiltrative carcinoma. Standard mucosal biopsies are often too shallow; take well-type or snare biopsies.
  • Autoimmune gastritis: corpus-predominant atrophy, hypergastrinemia, B12 deficiency, iron deficiency, and a raised risk of both type 1 gastric neuroendocrine tumors and adenocarcinoma.
On rounds, sayHer biopsies show incomplete-type intestinal metaplasia involving the body, so she falls into the higher-risk group — eradicate the H. pylori, confirm it, and put her on roughly three-year surveillance with a proper Sydney-protocol mapping in separate jars.

Gastroparesis

ACG Clinical Guideline, Camilleri et al., Am J Gastroenterol 2022;117:1197–1220

InsideDiagnosis requires all threeGastric emptying scintigraphy over 4 hoursDietProkineticsAntiemetics

Delayed emptying of the stomach without any mechanical blockage. Genuinely disabling when it is real — and substantially over-diagnosed, because several commoner things imitate it.

Must know
  • Four-hour scintigraphy, after holding GLP-1 agonists, opioids, anticholinergics and cannabis 48–72 hours.
  • Delayed = >60% at 2 hours or >10% at 4 hours.
  • Metoclopramide at the lowest effective dose, and not beyond 12 weeks (tardive dyskinesia).

AbbreviationsG-POEM gastric peroral endoscopic myotomy · GLP-1 glucagon-like peptide-1

Full detail
  • Diagnosis requires all three: characteristic symptoms, delayed gastric emptying, and no mechanical obstruction (EGD first).
  • Gastric emptying scintigraphy over 4 hours with a standardized low-fat egg-white meal. Two-hour studies are inadequate. Hold opioids, GLP-1 receptor agonists, anticholinergics, and cannabis for 48–72 hours before the study, and normalize glucose (<275 mg/dL) — otherwise the result is meaningless.
  • Retention >60% at 2 h or >10% at 4 h defines delayed emptying.
  • Diet: small, frequent, low-fat, low-insoluble-fiber meals; blenderized or liquid nutrition when solids fail.
  • Prokinetics: metoclopramide is the only FDA-approved agent — use the lowest effective dose, prefer liquid formulation, and counsel about tardive dyskinesia (avoid beyond 12 weeks). Domperidone via expanded-access; erythromycin works acutely but tachyphylaxis limits chronic use.
  • Antiemetics treat nausea but don't accelerate emptying.
  • Gastric electrical stimulation and G-POEM (gastric peroral endoscopic myotomy) for refractory disease at expert centers.
  • Distinguish from cannabinoid hyperemesis and cyclic vomiting — very commonly mislabeled as gastroparesis, and the treatment is entirely different.
PitfallGLP-1 receptor agonists delay gastric emptying by design. A patient on semaglutide with nausea and early satiety does not automatically have gastroparesis, and their scintigraphy is uninterpretable unless the drug is held.

Nausea and vomiting — a structure for the consult

AGA Technical Review on Nausea and Vomiting, Gastroenterology 2001 · ACG Gastroparesis Guideline 2022 · practice synthesis

InsideTiming tells you the causeWhat to exclude firstCyclic vomitingCannabinoid hyperemesisTreatment

A symptom with an enormous differential spanning the gut, the brain, drugs and metabolic disease. Having a structure beats memorising lists.

Must know
  • Exclude obstruction and raised intracranial pressure before anything else.
  • Timing is the most useful history — vomiting of undigested food hours after eating suggests gastroparesis or obstruction; early-morning vomiting suggests pregnancy, raised intracranial pressure, uraemia or alcohol.
  • Cyclic vomiting and cannabinoid hyperemesis are commonly mislabelled as gastroparesis, and the treatment is entirely different.
  • Always review the medication list — opioids, GLP-1 agonists, chemotherapy, digoxin and dopamine agonists are the usual culprits.
Full detail
Sort by timing and content
PatternSuggests
Undigested food hours after a mealGastroparesis, gastric outlet obstruction
FeculentDistal small bowel obstruction, gastrocolic fistula
Early morning, before eatingPregnancy, raised intracranial pressure, uraemia, alcohol
Immediately after eatingFunctional, or psychogenic
Projectile without nauseaCentral cause — image the head
Stereotyped attacks with well periodsCyclic vomiting syndrome
The three that get confused
  • Gastroparesis — delayed emptying on a 4-hour study with no mechanical obstruction, with drugs held.
  • Cyclic vomiting syndrome — discrete, stereotyped episodes with symptom-free intervals; migraine association; responds to tricyclics as prophylaxis and triptans acutely.
  • Cannabinoid hyperemesis — chronic heavy cannabis use, relief with hot showers or bathing, resolution with cessation. Antiemetics work poorly; topical capsaicin helps acutely. Cessation is the treatment, and the diagnosis is missed constantly because patients under-report use.
Rumination syndrome
  • Effortless regurgitation of recently swallowed food within minutes of eating, without retching, often re-chewed and re-swallowed.
  • Diagnosed clinically; high-resolution manometry with impedance confirms it if needed.
  • Treated with diaphragmatic breathing retraining, which is highly effective and completely unlike anything used for gastroparesis.
Symptomatic treatment
  • Match the drug to the mechanism: ondansetron (5-HT3) for chemotherapy and gastroenteritis; metoclopramide or prochlorperazine (dopamine) for gastroparesis and drug-induced; antihistamines and anticholinergics for vestibular causes; aprepitant (NK1) for refractory or chemotherapy-related.
  • Correct hypokalaemia, metabolic alkalosis and volume depletion; give thiamine before glucose in prolonged vomiting.

Subepithelial lesions — what that bump actually is

ACG Clinical Guideline, Jacobson et al., Am J Gastroenterol 2023;118:46–58

InsideEUS defines the layer of originLipomaLeiomyomaGranular cell tumorDuplication cystGISTGastric neuroendocrine tumors

A bump in the gut wall covered by normal-looking mucosa, almost always found by accident. Most are harmless; the point of the workup is to identify the minority that are not.

Must know
  • EUS layer of origin is the whole diagnosis.
  • Layer 4 hypoechoic gastric lesion = GIST until proven otherwise.
  • Resect GIST if ≥2 cm, symptomatic, or with high-risk features.

AbbreviationsEUS endoscopic ultrasound · GIST gastrointestinal stromal tumour · MEN1 multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 · ZES Zollinger-Ellison syndrome

Full detail
  • EUS defines the layer of origin, which is the whole game. Layer 4 (muscularis propria) hypoechoic lesion in the stomach = GIST until proven otherwise.
  • Lipoma (layer 3, hyperechoic, "pillow sign") and pancreatic rest need no follow-up.
  • Leiomyoma — layer 2 or 4, more common in the esophagus; GIST is more common in the stomach.
  • Granular cell tumor — layer 2/3, distal esophagus, usually benign.
  • Duplication cyst — anechoic, layer 3; don't puncture it.
  • Tissue via EUS-guided fine needle biopsy; standard forceps biopsies of a subepithelial lesion usually return normal mucosa.
  • GIST: resect if ≥2 cm, symptomatic, or with high-risk EUS features (irregular border, cystic spaces, echogenic foci, ulceration, growth). CD117/KIT and DOG1 positive; imatinib for advanced disease.
  • Gastric neuroendocrine tumors: Type 1 (atrophic gastritis, hypergastrinemia, multiple, indolent — endoscopic resection/surveillance), Type 2 (ZES/MEN1), Type 3 (sporadic, normal gastrin, solitary, aggressive — surgical resection).

03GI Bleeding

Upper · lower · small bowel · anticoagulation on board

4 topics in this chapter
  1. 01Upper GI bleeding — the resuscitation and timing decisions you'll actually make
  2. 02Lower GI bleeding — CTA before colonoscopy in the unstable patient
  3. 03Small bowel (obscure) bleeding
  4. 04Anticoagulants and antiplatelets around a GI bleed

Upper GI bleeding — the resuscitation and timing decisions you'll actually make

ACG Clinical Guideline, Laine et al., Am J Gastroenterol 2021;116:899–917

InsideRisk stratification before anything elseTransfusionPre-endoscopic drugsTimingForrest classification and what it obligates you to doEndoscopic techniqueAfter hemostasis

Bleeding from anywhere above the ligament of Treitz. One of the commonest emergency consults you will take, and most of the decisions that change outcome are made before the endoscope is picked up.

Must know
  • Transfuse at hemoglobin <7, target 7–9.
  • Endoscopy within 24 hours — not within 12. Resuscitate first.
  • Epinephrine injection alone is never adequate — always add a second modality.
  • Restart cardioprotective aspirin early.

AbbreviationsINR international normalised ratio · PPI proton pump inhibitor · UGIB upper gastrointestinal bleeding

Full detail

The presentation is haematemesis — vomiting fresh blood or coffee-ground material — or melena, or, when bleeding is brisk enough, haematochezia from an upper source.

Risk stratification before anything else
  • Glasgow-Blatchford score ≤1 identifies very low-risk patients who can be discharged with outpatient endoscopy. This is the score to quote — it uses only clinical and lab variables, no endoscopy.
  • Rockall and AIMS65 exist; Blatchford is the one the guideline endorses for the discharge decision.
Transfusion
  • Restrictive strategy: transfuse at hemoglobin <7 g/dL, target 7–9 g/dL.TrialVillanueva C, et al. NEJM 2013;368:11–21 — restrictive transfusion improved 6-week survival in acute upper GI bleeding Liberal transfusion increases mortality in variceal bleeding by raising portal pressure. Exceptions where a higher threshold is reasonable: ongoing massive bleeding, acute coronary syndrome.
  • Platelets and plasma are given for specific defects, not reflexively by INR. A mildly elevated INR in cirrhosis does not mean the patient is auto-anticoagulated and does not need correction before endoscopy.
Pre-endoscopic drugs
  • IV PPI before endoscopy — suggested; it downstages lesions but doesn't change mortality or rebleeding. Don't delay endoscopy for it.
  • Erythromycin 250 mg IV, 30–120 minutes before EGD — a prokinetic dose that clears the stomach and meaningfully improves visualization and reduces repeat endoscopy. Underused; mentioning it makes you sound experienced.
  • If cirrhosis is suspected: add octreotide and IV ceftriaxone 1 g daily for up to 7 days immediately — antibiotic prophylaxis in variceal bleeding reduces mortality, not just infection.
Timing

Endoscopy within 24 hours of presentation for patients admitted with UGIB. The guideline specifically does not recommend endoscopy within 12 hoursTrialLau JYW, et al. NEJM 2020;382:1299–1308 — urgent (<6 h) endoscopy did not reduce 30-day mortality versus early (<24 h) — the randomized data showed no benefit and a signal toward harm in high-risk patients who weren't adequately resuscitated first. Resuscitate, then scope.

Forrest classification and what it obligates you to do
ClassAppearanceRebleed risk untreatedEndoscopic therapy?
IaSpurting arterial bleeding~90%Yes
IbOozing~50%Yes
IIaNon-bleeding visible vessel~40–50%Yes
IIbAdherent clot~20–30%Consider removal and treat underlying stigma
IIcFlat pigmented spot~10%No
IIIClean ulcer base~3–5%No — can feed and discharge early
Endoscopic technique
  • Epinephrine injection alone is never adequate. It must be combined with a second modality — thermal contact (bipolar/heater probe), clips, or sclerosant.
  • Over-the-scope clips and hemostatic spray/powder are the salvage tools for refractory or recurrent bleeding.
  • Variceal bleeding: band ligation for esophageal varices; cyanoacrylate injection for gastric varices.
After hemostasis
  • High-dose PPI for 3 days after successful therapy of a high-risk stigma — continuous infusion (80 mg bolus then 8 mg/h) or intermittent high-dose IV/oral. Then twice-daily oral PPI for 2 weeks, then daily.
  • Recurrent bleeding → repeat endoscopy first. If that fails, transcatheter arterial embolization is preferred over surgery.
  • Test for H. pylori, and if negative during acute bleeding, retest later — false negatives are common in the acute setting.
  • Restart cardioprotective aspirin early (within 1–7 days, ideally as soon as hemostasis is secure). Withholding it kills more patients from cardiovascular events than it saves from rebleeding.
On rounds, sayBlatchford is 12 so he stays; I'd hold transfusion until hemoglobin is under 7 unless he's actively bleeding, give erythromycin 250 IV about 45 minutes before the scope for visualization, and target endoscopy within 24 hours rather than rushing it before he's resuscitated.

Lower GI bleeding — CTA before colonoscopy in the unstable patient

ACG Clinical Guideline, Sengupta et al., Am J Gastroenterol 2023;118:208–231

InsideOakland score ≤8Restrictive transfusion at Hb &lt;7Diverticular bleedingAngioectasiaPost-polypectomy bleeding

Bleeding from below the ligament of Treitz, usually appearing as fresh blood per rectum in an older patient. Most stops by itself — the skill is identifying who cannot wait.

Must know
  • Unstable or brisk bleeding → CT angiography, then embolization.
  • Stable → prepped, non-urgent colonoscopy. Urgent colonoscopy has no proven benefit.
  • Brisk hematochezia with instability can still be an upper source.

AbbreviationsCTA CT angiography · LGIB lower gastrointestinal bleeding · NG nasogastric

Full detail
  • Hemodynamically unstable or ongoing brisk bleeding → CT angiography first, then transcatheter embolization. Do not drag an unstable patient to an unprepped colonoscopy.
  • Hemodynamically stable → colonoscopy after adequate preparation, on a non-emergent basis. Multiple trials show no benefit to urgent (<24 h) colonoscopy over elective inpatient colonoscopy for outcomes that matter.
  • Bowel preparation: 4–6 L of PEG-based solution over 3–4 hours, via NG tube if needed. An unprepped colon in LGIB is a wasted procedure.
  • Brisk hematochezia with hemodynamic instability may be an upper source (roughly 10–15%) — a negative NG lavage doesn't exclude it, so have a low threshold for EGD first.
  • Oakland score ≤8 identifies patients safe for outpatient management.
  • Restrictive transfusion at Hb <7 (higher threshold with cardiovascular disease).
  • Diverticular bleeding: through-the-scope clips are first line. Most stop spontaneously (~75%), but rebleeding is common.
  • Angioectasia: argon plasma coagulation. Consider associated aortic stenosis (Heyde syndrome) and von Willebrand factor destruction.
  • Post-polypectomy bleeding: clips. Occurs up to 2 weeks out.
PitfallDon't order a tagged RBC scan reflexively. It's sensitive to slow bleeding (0.1 mL/min) but poorly localizing; CTA (needs ~0.3–0.5 mL/min) localizes well and leads directly to intervention. If the plan is embolization, go to CTA.

Small bowel (obscure) bleeding

ACG Clinical Guideline, Gerson et al., Am J Gastroenterol 2015;110:1265–1287 · ESGE Technical Review 2018

InsideOccult bleeding and iron-deficiency anaemia

Bleeding from the stretch of small intestine between the ampulla and the ileocaecal valve, which a standard gastroscope and colonoscope cannot reach.

Must know
  • Repeat the upper and lower exams first — many missed lesions are within reach.
  • Capsule endoscopy is the first small bowel test, highest yield close to the bleed.
  • Contraindicated if a stricture is suspected — image or use a patency capsule first.

AbbreviationsCKD chronic kidney disease · GIST gastrointestinal stromal tumour · LVAD left ventricular assist device · NET neuroendocrine tumour · NSAID non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug

Full detail
  • Terminology: "small bowel bleeding" replaced "obscure GI bleeding." Reserve obscure for bleeding that remains unexplained after full evaluation including small bowel imaging.
  • Repeat the upper and lower exams first. A meaningful fraction of missed lesions are within reach of a standard scope — Cameron lesions in a large hiatal hernia, Dieulafoy, angioectasia, a right-sided colonic lesion behind a fold.
  • Video capsule endoscopy is the first small bowel test. Highest yield when performed close to the bleeding episode. Contraindicated with suspected stricture or obstruction — use a patency capsule or CT/MR enterography first if Crohn's or NSAID stricture is possible.
  • Device-assisted (deep) enteroscopy — double-balloon, single-balloon, spiral — for therapy after capsule localizes the lesion. Route (antegrade vs retrograde) is chosen by capsule transit timing.
  • CT enterography is better than capsule for mass lesions; capsule is better for flat mucosal lesions.
  • Meckel's scan (99mTc-pertechnetate) in young patients with unexplained bleeding.
  • Intraoperative enteroscopy is the last resort.
    • Occult bleeding and iron-deficiency anaemia
    • Occult means no visible blood — a positive faecal immunochemical test, or iron-deficiency anaemia with no other explanation. Obscure means bleeding that stays unexplained after a full evaluation. The two are not interchangeable.
    • Iron-deficiency anaemia in a man of any age, or a postmenopausal woman, is a GI lesion until proven otherwise and earns bidirectional endoscopy — upper and lower at the same sitting.
    • Take duodenal biopsies at the same time and send coeliac serology; coeliac disease is a recurring cause of unexplained iron deficiency.
    • If both exams are negative, proceed to capsule endoscopy. Consider H. pylori, which itself causes iron deficiency, and autoimmune atrophic gastritis.
    • A positive stool test is never explained by haemorrhoids. It earns a colonoscopy.
  • Most common causes: angioectasia (older adults, particularly with CKD, aortic stenosis, LVAD), NSAID ulcers, small bowel tumors (GIST, NET, adenocarcinoma, lymphoma — the leading cause in patients under 50), Crohn's, Dieulafoy.

Anticoagulants and antiplatelets around a GI bleed

ACG–CAG Clinical Practice Guideline, Abraham et al., Am J Gastroenterol 2022;117:542–558

InsideDo not delay endoscopy to normalize the INRResume anticoagulationContinue cardioprotective aspirinDo not interrupt aspirinDOACsWarfarin

The recurring bedside conflict between stopping the bleeding in front of you and preventing the stroke or clot you cannot see.

Must know
  • No routine FFP, vitamin K, or reversal agents. Hold the drug and support.
  • Do not delay endoscopy to normalize the INR in a stable patient.
  • Resume anticoagulation — and never interrupt aspirin for polypectomy.

AbbreviationsINR international normalised ratio · PCC prothrombin complex concentrate · VTE venous thromboembolism

Full detail
  • Do not routinely give fresh frozen plasma or vitamin K to reverse warfarin in GI bleeding. For life-threatening bleeding, 4-factor PCC plus vitamin K.
  • Do not routinely use andexanet alfa or idarucizumab — reserve for life-threatening bleeding on the relevant agent. Most DOAC-associated GI bleeding is managed with drug cessation and supportive care because of the short half-lives.
  • Do not delay endoscopy to normalize the INR in a patient who is otherwise stable; endoscopic hemostasis is safe at INR up to about 2.5.
  • Resume anticoagulation. The mortality and thromboembolic penalty for not resuming exceeds the rebleeding risk. Typical resumption is within days of hemostasis, individualized.
  • Continue cardioprotective aspirin (secondary prevention) through a GI bleed; if held, restart within a few days.
  • Dual antiplatelet therapy after recent stenting: involve cardiology; do not stop the P2Y12 inhibitor unilaterally.
Periprocedural management for elective endoscopy
  • Do not interrupt aspirin for routine endoscopy including polypectomy.
  • DOACs: hold 1–2 days before a high-risk procedure (longer for dabigatran with reduced creatinine clearance). No bridging needed — the whole point of DOACs is the rapid on/off.
  • Warfarin: low thromboembolic risk → hold 5 days, no bridge. High risk (mechanical mitral valve, recent VTE, AF with prior stroke) → consider bridging, though bridging itself increases bleeding.
  • Diagnostic endoscopy with or without biopsy is low risk — anticoagulation generally continues.
On rounds, sayHe's on apixaban, so I'd hold the drug and support him rather than reaching for andexanet — the half-life does most of the work — and I want a plan on the chart today for when we restart, because the thromboembolic risk of not resuming outweighs the rebleeding risk.
