Chronic diarrhea — a framework you can say out loud

Practice synthesis

InsideWatery — secretoryWatery — osmoticFattyInflammatoryThe baseline panel

Loose or frequent stools for more than four weeks. The differential looks unmanageable until you classify it, at which point it collapses to a short list.

Must know
  • Classify first: watery (secretory vs osmotic), fatty, or inflammatory.
  • Fecal calprotectin is what separates IBS from IBD before you scope everyone.
  • Random biopsies of normal-appearing mucosa is how microscopic colitis is found.

AbbreviationsCRP C-reactive protein · IBD inflammatory bowel disease · IBS irritable bowel syndrome · PEG polyethylene glycol · SIBO small intestinal bacterial overgrowth · TSH thyroid stimulating hormone

Full detail

Classify before testing. Attendings care much more that you have a structure than that you list every etiology.

TypeCluesThink
Watery — secretoryPersists with fasting, large volume, nocturnalMicroscopic colitis, bile acid diarrhea, neuroendocrine tumor/VIPoma, carcinoid, laxative abuse
Watery — osmoticImproves with fasting, elevated stool osmotic gapLactose/fructose intolerance, sugar alcohols, magnesium, PEG
FattySteatorrhea, weight loss, fat-soluble vitamin deficiencyCeliac, exocrine pancreatic insufficiency, SIBO, giardia, short bowel
InflammatoryBlood, mucus, fever, elevated calprotectin/lactoferrinIBD, invasive infection, ischemia, radiation, neoplasia
  • Baseline labs: CBC, CMP, CRP, TSH, celiac serology, fecal calprotectin, stool studies including C. difficile and Giardia antigen.
  • Fecal calprotectin is the workhorse for separating IBS from IBD before you scope everyone.
  • Colonoscopy with random biopsies of normal-appearing mucosa if chronic watery diarrhea — that's how you find microscopic colitis.

Celiac disease

ACG Clinical Guideline, Rubio-Tapia et al., Am J Gastroenterol 2023;118:59–76

InsideTest on a gluten-containing dietConfirm with duodenal biopsy in adultsHLA-DQ2/DQ8Screen at diagnosisNon-responsive celiac disease

An immune reaction to gluten that flattens the small bowel villi and causes malabsorption. It affects about 1% of people and remains substantially underdiagnosed.

Must know
  • Test on a gluten-containing diet — this is the most common error.
  • tTG-IgA plus a total IgA; IgA deficiency produces false negatives.
  • Confirm with ≥4 distal duodenal biopsies plus 1–2 from the bulb.
  • Non-responsive disease is usually ongoing gluten exposure.

AbbreviationsDEXA dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry · EMA endomysial antibody · IBS irritable bowel syndrome · SIBO small intestinal bacterial overgrowth · tTG-IgA tissue transglutaminase IgA antibody

Full detail
  • Test on a gluten-containing diet. This is the single most common error. If already gluten-free, either do a gluten challenge (3 g/day for 2 weeks minimum, ideally 6–8 weeks) or use HLA-DQ2/DQ8 testing to exclude the diagnosis.
  • First test: tissue transglutaminase IgA (tTG-IgA) plus a total IgA level. Selective IgA deficiency is over-represented in celiac and produces false negatives — then use IgG-based testing (DGP-IgG or tTG-IgG).
  • Confirm with duodenal biopsy in adults: ≥4 biopsies from the distal duodenum plus 1–2 from the bulb. Marsh classification.
  • A "non-biopsy" pathway (tTG-IgA >10× upper limit of normal with confirmatory EMA) is accepted in children and is an option in selected adults, but adult practice in the US still favors biopsy.
  • HLA-DQ2/DQ8: useful only for its high negative predictive value — a negative essentially rules out celiac. About 30–40% of the general population carries it, so a positive means little.
  • Screen at diagnosis: CBC, iron studies, B12, folate, vitamin D, calcium, LFTs; DEXA for bone density.
  • Non-responsive celiac disease: most common cause is continued gluten exposure. Then consider lactose intolerance, SIBO, microscopic colitis, pancreatic insufficiency, IBS — and only then refractory celiac disease (types I and II; type II carries risk of enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma).
  • Associated conditions: dermatitis herpetiformis (pathognomonic — treat with gluten-free diet ± dapsone), type 1 diabetes, autoimmune thyroid disease, Down and Turner syndromes, unexplained transaminitis, IgA nephropathy.
On rounds, sayBefore I interpret that negative tTG I want to know two things — whether she was eating gluten when it was drawn, and whether we have a total IgA, because selective IgA deficiency is common enough in this population to explain a false negative.

Irritable bowel syndrome

ACG Clinical Guideline, Lacy et al., Am J Gastroenterol 2021;116:17–44

InsideMake a positive diagnosisLimited testingLow-FODMAP dietSoluble fiber (psyllium)

A disorder of gut-brain interaction producing abdominal pain with altered bowel habit, without structural disease. Extremely common, and diagnosed positively rather than by exhausting every test.

Must know
  • Make a positive Rome IV diagnosis, not a diagnosis of exclusion.
  • Soluble fiber only — insoluble fiber worsens symptoms.
  • Gut-directed psychotherapy and hypnotherapy are guideline-recommended.
  • FMT is recommended against.

AbbreviationsFMT faecal microbiota transplantation · IBD inflammatory bowel disease · IBS irritable bowel syndrome · PEG polyethylene glycol

Full detail
  • Make a positive diagnosis using Rome IV criteria — recurrent abdominal pain ≥1 day/week for 3 months, related to defecation and/or a change in stool frequency or form. Do not diagnose by exclusion after an exhaustive negative workup.
  • Limited testing: celiac serology in IBS-D, fecal calprotectin to exclude IBD, CBC. Do not routinely order colonoscopy in patients under 45 without alarm features, food allergy testing, or stool ova and parasites.
  • Low-FODMAP diet — limited-duration elimination followed by structured reintroduction, ideally with a dietitian. It is not a permanent diet.
  • Soluble fiber (psyllium) helps; insoluble fiber (bran) does not and often worsens symptoms.
SubtypeOptions
IBS-DRifaximin (repeatable), eluxadoline, alosetron (women, severe, restricted), loperamide (symptom control only), TCAsTrialTARGET 1 and 2 — Pimentel M, et al. NEJM 2011;364:22–32 — rifaximin in non-constipated IBS
IBS-CLinaclotide, plecanatide, lubiprostone, tegaserod (women <65 without cardiovascular risk — withdrawn from the US market again in 2022, so effectively unavailable), PEG (helps stool form, not pain)TrialLembo AJ, et al. NEJM 2011;365:527–536 — linaclotide in IBS with constipation
Pain-predominant, any subtypeTricyclic antidepressants, antispasmodics/peppermint oil, gut-directed psychotherapy and hypnotherapy
  • The guideline explicitly recommends gut-directed psychotherapy — cognitive behavioral therapy and gut-directed hypnotherapy have effect sizes comparable to drugs. Say this rather than implying the symptoms are "in their head."
  • Do not use fecal microbiota transplantation for IBS. Explicitly recommended against.

Chronic abdominal pain — when the pain has become the disease

Rome IV · ACG and AGA guidance on centrally mediated abdominal pain · practice synthesis

InsideCentrally mediated abdominal pain syndromeNarcotic bowel syndromeHow to talk about itNeuromodulatorsWhat not to repeat

Pain that has outlived whatever started it and become a disorder of central pain processing in its own right. The commonest error is to keep investigating.

Must know
  • Centrally mediated abdominal pain syndrome is near-constant pain, poorly localised, with little relation to eating or defecation — a positive diagnosis, not a leftover.
  • Escalating opioids with worsening pain is narcotic bowel syndrome — the opioid is causing it. The treatment is a planned taper, not a higher dose.
  • Repeat imaging and repeat endoscopy cause harm once the workup is complete — cumulative radiation, incidentalomas, and reinforcement of the search for a structural cause.
  • Tricyclic antidepressants and SNRIs are the evidence-based treatment, given as neuromodulators at gut-directed doses, alongside psychological therapy.
Full detail
Recognising it
  • Pain present most days for at least 6 months, poorly localised, with minimal relationship to meals or bowel movements — this is what separates it from IBS and functional dyspepsia.
  • Frequently accompanied by depression, anxiety, sleep disturbance, and a long history of negative investigations.
  • A history of escalating opioid use with worsening rather than improving pain is the signature of narcotic bowel syndrome and opioid-induced hyperalgesia.
  • Look for the treatable mimics before settling: chronic mesenteric ischaemia, median arcuate ligament syndrome, abdominal wall pain (a positive Carnett sign — tenderness that worsens on tensing the abdominal wall — points to the wall, not the viscera), porphyria, adhesive disease, and chronic pancreatitis.
How you talk about it matters
  • Name it as a real, physiological diagnosis of altered central pain processing. Patients who feel disbelieved keep seeking tests.
  • Set the goal explicitly as improved function rather than abolition of pain.
  • Agree a stopping point for investigation, and say plainly that further imaging is more likely to harm than help.
Treatment
  • Tricyclic antidepressants (amitriptyline, nortriptyline, desipramine) at low, gut-directed doses — the best evidence base.
  • SNRIs (duloxetine, venlafaxine) where there is comorbid depression or neuropathic quality.
  • Gut-directed cognitive behavioural therapy and hypnotherapy — effect sizes comparable with drug therapy.
  • Consider gabapentinoids and mirtazapine as adjuncts, particularly with nausea or weight loss.
  • Taper opioids with a written schedule and support; expect a transient worsening before improvement.
  • Avoid benzodiazepines entirely.
PitfallThe reflex on a busy service is to order one more scan because the patient is distressed. Every additional negative test reinforces the belief that something structural has been missed, and makes the eventual conversation harder.
On rounds, sayHer workup is complete and negative, and the pain is constant and poorly localised rather than related to meals — I'd call this centrally mediated abdominal pain, start a low-dose tricyclic as a neuromodulator, refer for gut-directed therapy, and I'd stop imaging rather than repeat the CT.

SIBO

ACG Clinical Guideline, Pimentel et al., Am J Gastroenterol 2020;115:165–178

InsideDiagnosisTest the people with a reason to have itTreatment: rifaximinFix the substrate

Too many bacteria in the small intestine, producing bloating, diarrhoea and malabsorption. Real, but over-diagnosed unless there is a structural or motility reason for it to happen.

Must know
  • Test the people with a structural or motility reason to have it.
  • Rifaximin is the best-studied treatment.
  • Relapse is the rule unless you address the underlying cause.

AbbreviationsCFU colony-forming units · PPI proton pump inhibitor · SIBO small intestinal bacterial overgrowth

Full detail
  • Diagnosis: glucose or lactulose breath testing (rise in hydrogen ≥20 ppm above baseline within 90 minutes) or small bowel aspirate culture ≥10³ CFU/mL. Breath testing is imperfect — a fast oro-cecal transit produces false positives.
  • Test the people with a reason to have it: prior GI surgery (Roux-en-Y, blind loop, ileocecal valve resection), motility disorders (scleroderma, diabetic autonomic neuropathy, chronic intestinal pseudo-obstruction), structural disease (strictures, diverticulosis of small bowel, fistula), and cirrhosis.
  • Treatment: rifaximin is the best-studied. Alternatives include amoxicillin-clavulanate, ciprofloxacin, metronidazole, and TMP-SMX.
  • Fix the substrate — long-term PPI, narcotics, and unaddressed strictures cause relapse. Recurrent courses are common.

Clostridioides difficile infection

ACG Clinical Guideline, Kelly et al., Am J Gastroenterol 2021;116:1124–1147 · IDSA/SHEA focused update

InsideWho to test — and not testing for cureFirst episodeFulminant diseaseRecurrenceWhy IV metronidazole only in fulminant

A toxin-producing bacterium that overgrows once antibiotics have cleared the competition, causing colitis that ranges from mild diarrhoea to toxic megacolon. Recurrence is the defining problem.

Must know
  • Only test clinically significant diarrhea, and never test for cure.
  • First episode: oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin. Metronidazole only if neither is available.
  • IV metronidazole belongs only in fulminant disease — IV vancomycin never works.

AbbreviationsGDH glutamate dehydrogenase · NAAT nucleic acid amplification test · NG nasogastric

Full detail
  • Only test patients with clinically significant diarrhea — ≥3 unformed stools in 24 hours — and do not test for cure. Toxin/PCR positivity persists for weeks in colonized patients.
  • Two-step testing (GDH + toxin EIA, with NAAT to arbitrate) reduces overtreatment of colonization.
  • Stop the inciting antibiotic where possible. Highest-risk agents: clindamycin, fluoroquinolones, cephalosporins, carbapenems.
ScenarioTreatment
Initial, non-severe or severeTrialLouie TJ, et al. NEJM 2011;364:422–431 — fidaxomicin was non-inferior to vancomycin with fewer recurrencesOral vancomycin 125 mg QID × 10 days or fidaxomicin 200 mg BID × 10 days. Metronidazole only if neither is available.
Fulminant (hypotension, shock, ileus, megacolon)Oral/NG vancomycin 500 mg QID + IV metronidazole 500 mg q8h; add vancomycin retention enema if ileus. Early surgical consultation.
First recurrenceFidaxomicin, or a tapered-pulsed vancomycin regimen
Second or later recurrenceFecal microbiota transplantation (or an FDA-approved live biotherapeutic), after an antibiotic courseTrialvan Nood E, et al. NEJM 2013;368:407–415 — trial stopped early for efficacy
High recurrence riskConsider adjunctive bezlotoxumab (anti-toxin B monoclonal) — caution in heart failureTrialMODIFY I and II — Wilcox MH, et al. NEJM 2017;376:305–317
PitfallFulminant disease is the one place IV metronidazole belongs, because it reaches the colon through the inflamed mucosa. IV vancomycin does nothing for C. difficile — it never reaches the lumen. Stating this correctly is a small thing that lands well.

Acute infectious diarrhea

ACG Clinical Guideline, Riddle et al., Am J Gastroenterol 2016;111:602–622

InsideTestLoperamidePost-infectious IBS

Diarrhoea lasting less than two weeks, usually viral and self-limiting. The clinical skill here is restraint — knowing who to test and who to leave alone.

Must know
  • Rehydration is the treatment for most acute diarrhea.
  • No empiric antibiotics for bloody diarrhea until Shiga toxin–producing E. coli is excluded — they precipitate HUS.

AbbreviationsHUS haemolytic uraemic syndrome · IBS irritable bowel syndrome

Full detail
  • Most acute diarrhea is viral and self-limited. Rehydration is the treatment.
  • Test when there is dysentery (bloody stool), fever, severe illness, immunocompromise, recent hospitalization or antibiotics, or symptoms >7 days. Multiplex PCR panels find organisms you may not need to treat — interpret in clinical context.
  • Do not give empiric antibiotics for bloody diarrhea in a well-appearing patient until Shiga toxin–producing E. coli is excluded — antibiotics increase the risk of hemolytic uremic syndrome.
  • Loperamide is fine for watery traveler's diarrhea alongside an antibiotic, but avoid in dysentery or suspected C. difficile.
  • Traveler's diarrhea: azithromycin is preferred in Southeast Asia (fluoroquinolone resistance in Campylobacter); fluoroquinolone or rifaximin elsewhere.
  • Post-infectious IBS follows ~10% of bacterial gastroenteritis — worth naming when a patient's symptoms persist after a documented infection.

Microscopic colitis

Practice synthesis · AGA guideline

InsideStop the culprit drugBudesonide 9 mg daily

Chronic watery diarrhoea in a patient whose colonoscopy looks completely normal. The disease exists only under the microscope, which is why it is missed unless you biopsy.

Must know
  • Chronic watery diarrhea with a normal-looking colonoscopy.
  • Diagnosis is made only on random biopsies from right and left colon.
  • Stop the culprit drug (PPI, NSAID, SSRI), then budesonide 9 mg.

AbbreviationsNSAID non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug · PPI proton pump inhibitor · SSRI selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor

Full detail
  • Chronic watery, non-bloody diarrhea in an older adult — often a woman — with a normal-appearing colonoscopy. Diagnosis is made only by random biopsies from both right and left colon.
  • Two subtypes: collagenous (thickened subepithelial collagen band >10 μm) and lymphocytic (>20 intraepithelial lymphocytes per 100 epithelial cells). Management is identical.
  • Stop the culprit drug: PPIs, NSAIDs, SSRIs, ranitidine, acarbose, ticlopidine.
  • Budesonide 9 mg daily is first-line inductionTrialMiehlke S, et al. Gastroenterology 2014;146:1222–1230; relapse after stopping is common and low-dose maintenance is often needed.
  • Strong association with celiac disease — check serology.

Colonic ischemia and acute mesenteric ischemia

ACG Clinical Guideline, Brandt et al., Am J Gastroenterol 2015;110:18–44

InsideColonic ischemiaCT with IV contrastAcute mesenteric ischemiaIsolated right-sided colonic ischemia

Two different diseases that share a name. Colonic ischaemia is common and usually settles on its own; acute mesenteric ischaemia kills within hours. Telling them apart is the entire topic.

Must know
  • Colonic ischemia: mild pain relative to findings, bloody diarrhea, watershed distribution, rectal sparing.
  • Acute mesenteric ischemia: pain out of proportion to exam → CT angiography now. Normal lactate does not exclude it.
  • Isolated right-sided colonic ischemia is SMA territory — treat it as a red flag.

AbbreviationsSMA superior mesenteric artery

Full detail
  • Colonic ischemia is the common one: sudden crampy left-sided abdominal pain followed within 24 hours by bloody diarrhea, in an older patient. Pain is mild relative to findings.
  • Watershed areas — splenic flexure (Griffiths point) and rectosigmoid junction (Sudeck point). Rectal sparing is typical because of dual blood supply.
  • CT with IV contrast shows segmental wall thickening; colonoscopy within 48 hours confirms. Avoid over-insufflation.
  • Most cases are non-gangrenous and resolve with supportive care, bowel rest, and IV fluids. Antibiotics for moderate–severe disease.
  • Acute mesenteric ischemia is a different, lethal entity: pain out of proportion to exam, in a patient with atrial fibrillation (embolic), atherosclerosis (thrombotic), or shock/pressors (non-occlusive). CT angiography immediately, surgery on board. Lactate rises late and a normal lactate does not exclude it.
  • Isolated right-sided colonic ischemia shares the SMA supply with the small bowel — treat it as a marker of possible acute mesenteric ischemia and image the vessels.
On rounds, sayThe distribution matters here — isolated right-sided colonic ischemia is SMA territory, so I wouldn't manage this as ordinary colonic ischemia; I'd get CT angiography and involve surgery.

Acute colonic pseudo-obstruction and colonic volvulus — the 12 cm cecum, the neostigmine dose, and the volvulus you must not scope

AJR Am J Roentgenol 1985;145:1211–1217 · Sgouros SN, et al. Gut 2006;55:638–642

InsideWho gets pseudo-obstruction and whyProving it is not mechanicalThe perforation thresholdsThe escalation ladderNeostigmine — how to give itColonoscopic decompression, cecostomy and surgerySigmoid versus cecal volvulusSigns that mean surgery now

Two ways a colon becomes massively dilated without a tumour in the way: pseudo-obstruction, where nothing is blocking it and the bowel has simply stopped moving (Ogilvie syndrome), and volvulus, where a loop has twisted on its own mesentery. Both usually turn up as a distended abdomen in an older, sicker patient — cecal volvulus, typically in a younger woman, is the exception — and both perforate if left alone. The endoscopist is the first call for one form of each, and must know which one to decline.

Must know
  • Pseudo-obstruction is a diagnosis of exclusion: CT to rule out a mechanical block or a twist, then 48–72 hours of conservative measures — nil by mouth, nasogastric and rectal tubes, replace potassium and magnesium, stop opioids and anticholinergics, no oral laxatives, mobilize, treat the illness that caused it. Most resolve here.
  • Cecal diameter of 12 cm or more, or distension beyond about 6 days, is where perforation risk climbs. Do not wait out the 72 hours once you are there — and involve the surgeons at 12 cm even while you treat.
  • Neostigmine 2 mg IV over 3–5 minutes on a cardiac monitor with atropine at the bedside; about nine in ten decompress within minutes. Colonoscopic decompression with a tube when it fails or is contraindicated.
  • Sigmoid volvulus: endoscopic detorsion first, then sigmoid colectomy in the same admission. Cecal volvulus: surgery, not a scope. Peritonitis or ischemia in either means surgery without an attempt at detorsion.

AbbreviationsACPO acute colonic pseudo-obstruction · ASCRS American Society of Colon and Rectal Surgeons · ASGE American Society for Gastrointestinal Endoscopy · CT computed tomography · ECG electrocardiogram · IV intravenous · NG nasogastric · PEG polyethylene glycol

Full detail
Who gets pseudo-obstruction and why

The working model is autonomic imbalance: sacral parasympathetic supply to the distal colon fails, that segment goes atonic, and everything proximal dilates — so the apparent "transition" on imaging often sits near the splenic flexure and can fool you into calling it mechanical.

  • Almost every patient has a reason: recent surgery (hip, spine, cardiac, cesarean); critical illness (sepsis, pneumonia, myocardial infarction, trauma); neurological disease (Parkinson's, spinal cord injury, dementia, stroke); low potassium, magnesium or calcium; and drugs — opioids, anticholinergics, calcium-channel blockers, clonidine, antipsychotics. Most patients are elderly with several of these.
  • Presentation: distension building over days, a tympanic abdomen with only mild discomfort, bowel sounds present, nausea and vomiting in about half. Diarrhea and passing flatus do not exclude it. Fever, marked tenderness, a rising white count or peritonitis suggest ischemia and mean an urgent surgical review.
Proving it is not mechanical
  • A plain film shows a diffusely dilated colon with haustra preserved and gas reaching the rectum, but it cannot reliably separate this from a distal mechanical obstruction — and neostigmine given to a colon blocked by a cancer or a twist is the error the work-up exists to prevent. CT, with IV contrast when the kidneys allow, settles it; both guidelines note it has replaced the water-soluble contrast enema, which remains the fallback. You want dilatation with no obstructing lesion at the apparent transition, no mass, no whirl, and no free air or pneumatosis.
  • Rule out the look-alikes: toxic megacolon (colitis plus systemic toxicity — never neostigmine), volvulus, fecal impaction, a stricture or cancer, and chronic intestinal pseudo-obstruction, a motility disorder with a history.
  • Measure the cecal diameter and write it in the note: the cecum has the widest radius and highest wall tension, so it perforates first, and you will track it on a daily film. ASCRS adds that how fast it is changing matters as much as the number.
The perforation thresholds

In Vanek and Al-Salti's 400-case review, ischemia or perforation rose with cecal diameter — none below 12 cm, 7% at 12–14 cm, 23% above 14 cm — and they called for decompression once the cecum reached 12 cm. Duration matters at least as much: in Johnson and Rice's radiological series, perforation tracked how long the cecum had been distended, beyond about 6 days, more than its size. ASGE quotes both thresholds. Mortality is about 15% when the syndrome is recognized and managed early and 36–44% once the bowel is ischemic or perforated (Vanek); ASGE quotes up to 50% after a perforation. That gap is the whole argument for a stepwise plan with a clock on it.

The 12 cm figure is a ceiling, not a target. ASGE strongly recommends conservative management for uncomplicated ACPO — no ischemia, perforation or peritonitis, no significant abdominal pain, cecum under 12 cm — and escalation when that fails at 48–72 hours or the cecum reaches 12 cm sooner; Ponec's trial enrolled at 10 cm after 24 hours. A cecum past 12 cm is also, in the ASGE text, a reason on its own to involve the surgeons — a consult, not yet an operation.

The escalation ladder
StepWhatWhenNotes
0CT, with IV contrast if the kidneys allowEvery patient, before anything aimed at motilityExcludes mechanical obstruction and volvulus; shows ischemia and free air. Water-soluble contrast enema if CT is unavailable
1Conservative measures for 48–72 hoursUncomplicated ACPO: cecum under 12 cm, no ischemia, peritonitis or significant painNil by mouth; NG and rectal tubes; IV fluids; replace potassium, magnesium and calcium; stop opioids, anticholinergics and calcium-channel blockers; no oral laxatives, osmotic or stimulant; mobilize, or alternate knee-chest and prone positioning; treat the cause. Daily film and examination. Resolves roughly 70–95%
2Neostigmine 2 mg IV over 3–5 minutesFailure at 48–72 hours, or cecum at or above 12 cm, no contraindicationCardiac monitor, atropine at the bedside; repeat once. ASCRS puts the scope after neostigmine fails or is contraindicated; ASGE allows colonoscopic decompression as an alternative here and notes retrospective series favouring it — but neostigmine needs no endoscopist
2bNeostigmine by another routeNo response to bolus dosingASGE suggests (weak) subcutaneous dosing or a continuous infusion of 0.4–0.8 mg/h before the scope; more bradycardia with the infusion
3Colonoscopic decompression with a decompression tubeNeostigmine fails, recurs after a second dose, or is contraindicatedNo prep, non-opioid sedation, water not gas, tube left in the right colon; stop if the mucosa is ischemic. Can be repeated
4Percutaneous endoscopic or radiological cecostomyKeeps re-dilating after endoscopic decompression; poor operative candidate; viable bowelA vent, not a cure, with its own complication rate
5SurgeryIschemia, perforation, peritonitis, or failure of everything aboveTube cecostomy if the bowel is viable; resection, usually with a stoma, if not. Mortality is the highest of any step
AfterDaily PEG for a weekOnce decompressed by any routeCut recurrence from 5 of 15 to 0 of 15 in a small randomized trial (Sgouros, Gut 2006); the ASGE algorithm ends with it
Neostigmine — how to give it

A reversible acetylcholinesterase inhibitor that restores parasympathetic drive to the colon. It is off-label here — its approval is for reversing neuromuscular blockade, as ASCRS notes — but the evidence is a 21-patient placebo-controlled trial with one of the cleanest results in the specialty: 10 of 11 patients given 2 mg of neostigmine decompressed promptly, versus none of 10 on placebo, with a median time to response of 4 minutes.TrialPonec RJ, et al. N Engl J Med 1999;341:137–141 — neostigmine vs placebo for acute colonic pseudo-obstruction The three placebo-controlled trials put the response at 85–94%; a 2014 meta-analysis pooled it at 89% versus 15% for placebo.

  • Dose: 2 mg IV over 3–5 minutes, the patient supine on continuous ECG and blood pressure monitoring during and after the dose until the heart rate and the response have settled — ASGE sets no fixed window. Bedpan ready: the response is often an immediate, large bowel movement. Replace the potassium and magnesium first — electrolyte imbalance, the post-operative state and a recently restarted opioid or anticholinergic all predict failure.
  • Atropine 0.5–1 mg drawn up at the bedside for symptomatic bradycardia; two patients in the trial needed it (19 doses were given once open-label rescue is counted). Glycopyrrolate given alongside is an alternative that blunts salivation and bronchospasm. Cramps, salivation and vomiting are expected and short-lived.
  • Contraindications: absolute — mechanical bowel or urinary obstruction, ischemia, perforation or peritonitis, hypersensitivity. Relative (ASGE) — bradycardia, recent myocardial infarction, asthma or active bronchospasm, renal insufficiency, peptic ulcer disease, acidosis. The trial also excluded a heart rate under 60, a systolic pressure under 90 mmHg, pregnancy and a creatinine above 3 mg/dL. Beta-blockers are a reason for caution, not a bar.
  • No response: a second dose after about 3 hours, which works in 40–100% across series; if that fails, ASGE suggests subcutaneous or continuous-infusion neostigmine before the scope. Recurrence after a response happens in a minority — in Ponec's trial two responders re-dilated and needed colonoscopic decompression, one going on to a subtotal colectomy.
Colonoscopic decompression, cecostomy and surgery
  • Colonoscopic decompression is for the patient in whom neostigmine has failed or cannot be given. A plain film within a few hours beforehand to exclude a perforation, especially with fever, a rising white count or worsening pain. No oral prep. Sedate with a benzodiazepine or another non-opioid agent — opioids deepen the atony you are treating. Minimal or no insufflation, carbon dioxide if any, water infusion to see, suction gas as you advance, and reach at least the distal transverse colon. Dusky, ulcerated or bleeding mucosa means ischemia — stop and hand over to surgery. Initial success is roughly 60–95% but recurrence without a tube is around 40%, so leave a decompression tube over a guidewire in the right colon, flushed to keep it patent. The procedure's own perforation rate is about 1–3% with a mortality near 1%, which is why it sits below neostigmine.
  • Cecostomy — percutaneous endoscopic, radiological or surgical — vents the patient who keeps re-dilating and is too sick for a laparotomy, provided the bowel is viable.
  • Surgery is for ischemia, perforation and peritonitis: tube cecostomy when the colon is viable, resection with a stoma when it is not. These patients are frail and septic, and surgical mortality in ACPO is the highest of any step — the reason the earlier rungs are worth doing on time.
Sigmoid versus cecal volvulus
Sigmoid volvulusCecal volvulus
Share of colonic volvulusThe majority — roughly 60–75%Most of the rest; transverse and splenic-flexure volvulus are rare
WhoMen over 70; the debilitated or institutionalized; chronic constipation; neurological or psychiatric disease; diabetes; megacolon (Chagas disease in endemic regions). A long, redundant sigmoid on a narrow mesenteric rootYounger, more often women; a congenitally mobile cecum never fixed to the retroperitoneum; previous surgery; pregnancy
Plain filmMassive loop rising out of the pelvis toward the right upper quadrant — the coffee-bean sign. Diagnostic in only about 60%Dilated cecum displaced to the left upper quadrant or mid abdomen, collapsed distal colon, dilated small bowel. Even less often enough on its own
CTWhirl sign at the mesenteric root, bird-beak transitions; near-100% sensitivity. Look for pneumatosis and free airThe same signs, with the ileocecal valve and terminal ileum in the twist. A cecal bascule — the cecum folded forward without torsion — is a variant
First moveEndoscopic detorsion with a flexible sigmoidoscope and a decompression tube when there is no peritonitis or ischemia — succeeds in 55–95% of seriesSurgery. Endoscopic detorsion worked in only 7 of 51 pooled attempts (14%), risks perforation and delays the operation, and is not recommended by ASGE or ASCRS
Definitive treatmentSigmoid colectomy in the same admission: recurrence after detorsion alone is 43–75%, higher still in some series, and an emergency operation for the recurrence kills far more than an elective resection after the first episode. Percutaneous endoscopic sigmoidopexy or colostomy only when surgery is out of the question — serious complications in around a fifth and mortality of about 5% in the review ASGE citesRight hemicolectomy with a primary ileocolic anastomosis when the patient is stable and the bowel viable; cecopexy alone recurs in roughly one in eight, tube cecostomy has the highest complication rate, resection almost never recurs

Detorsion: no prep, minimal air, advance gently to the twist and through it; the rush of gas and stool tells you it has worked. Inspect the mucosa and leave a tube for 24–72 hours. Then book the surgeon — ASGE recommends surgical consultation during the index admission and ASCRS says these patients should be considered for colectomy in the same admission. The scope turns an emergency operation into an elective one; it does not replace it.

Signs that mean surgery now

Peritonitis, fever, a rising white count or lactate, or hemodynamic instability; free air, pneumatosis, portal venous gas or absent wall enhancement on CT; dusky, black, ulcerated or bleeding mucosa at endoscopy. Stop, do not detorse, do not decompress further — untwisting a gangrenous loop delivers its contents to the circulation.

Numbers to know
  • Perforation thresholds in ACPO: cecal diameter ≥12 cm · duration >6 days · conservative management before escalating 48–72 h
  • Neostigmine: 2 mg IV over 3–5 min · Ponec trial response 10 of 11 vs 0 of 10 placebo · median time to response 4 min · pooled response 89% vs 15%
  • Mortality: about 15% with early appropriate management · 36–44% with ischemia or perforation
  • Sigmoid volvulus: 60–75% of colonic volvulus · recurrence after detorsion alone 43–75% · endoscopic detorsion of cecal volvulus succeeds in 14%
PitfallThree ways to hurt these patients: an oral laxative or a prep into a colon that is not moving; neostigmine before CT has excluded a mechanical block; a scope pushed through a sigmoid volvulus whose mucosa was already black. And one way to lose them slowly — "still passing flatus" is not a reason to let day 7 arrive with a 13 cm cecum.
On rounds, sayShe's day 5 after a hip replacement, on hydromorphone, potassium 3.0, cecum 10 cm on CT with no obstructing lesion, no whirl and no free air — that's Ogilvie's. I'd stop the opioid and the oxybutynin, replace potassium and magnesium, put in a rectal tube, get her out of bed, and repeat the film tomorrow. If she's still 10 cm at 48 to 72 hours, or hits 12 cm sooner, she gets 2 mg of neostigmine over 3 to 5 minutes on a monitor with atropine drawn up — nine in ten respond within minutes — and at 12 cm I'd let surgery know the same day. If two doses fail, we scope her with water and minimal gas under non-opioid sedation, leave a tube in the right colon, then a week of daily PEG. If she turns peritonitic at any point, she goes to the operating room, not endoscopy.

The advanced therapy landscape — know the mechanisms, not just the names

ACG Clinical Guideline: Ulcerative Colitis, Rubin et al., 2025 · ACG Clinical Guideline: Crohn's Disease, Lichtenstein et al., 2025 · AGA living guidelines

InsidePositioning principles the guidelines actually stateTreat to target — STRIDE-II

The drug landscape in inflammatory bowel disease. Six mechanisms are now in routine use, and understanding what each one blocks is far more useful than memorising brand names.

Must know
  • Early advanced therapy beats step-up in moderate-to-severe disease.
  • No 5-ASA in Crohn's disease. Steroids are never maintenance.
  • Anti-TNF is the class with perianal fistula data and the class for acute severe UC rescue.
  • Treat to target: symptoms → CRP/calprotectin → endoscopic healing.

AbbreviationsCRP C-reactive protein · JAK Janus kinase · MACE major adverse cardiovascular events · NUDT15 nudix hydrolase 15 · S1P sphingosine-1-phosphate · TPMT thiopurine methyltransferase · UC ulcerative colitis · VTE venous thromboembolism · VZV varicella zoster virus

Full detail
ClassAgentsWhere they sit
Anti-TNFInfliximab, adalimumab, golimumab (UC), certolizumab (CD)Highest-efficacy tier; the only class with good data in perianal fistulizing Crohn's and in acute severe UC rescue. Combining with a thiopurine reduces immunogenicity (SONIC).TrialSONIC — Colombel JF, et al. NEJM 2010;362:1383–1395
Anti-integrinVedolizumab (α4β7)Gut-selective — the safest option in older patientsTrialGEMINI 1 and 2 — Feagan BG, NEJM 2013;369:699–710; Sandborn WJ, NEJM 2013;369:711–721, malignancy history, or infection risk. Slower onset; better as maintenance than for a sick inpatient.
IL-12/23UstekinumabExcellent safety; useful in both CD and UC, and in patients with psoriasis.TrialUNITI — Feagan BG, et al. NEJM 2016;375:1946–1960
Selective IL-23Risankizumab, mirikizumab, guselkumabThe newest class and increasingly high on the list — strong efficacy signals against ustekinumab and adalimumab in head-to-head work.TrialSEQUENCE — Peyrin-Biroulet L, et al. NEJM 2024;391:213–223 — risankizumab versus ustekinumab in Crohn's
JAK inhibitorsTofacitinib (UC), upadacitinib (UC and CD)Oral, very fast onset — valuable when you need a response in days. Carry boxed warnings (MACE, VTE, malignancy, mortality) derived from the rheumatoid arthritis population; generally positioned after anti-TNF failure.TrialOCTAVE — Sandborn WJ, et al. NEJM 2017;376:1723–1736 (tofacitinib); U-ACHIEVE / U-ACCOMPLISH — Danese S, et al. Lancet 2022;399:2113–2128 (upadacitinib)
S1P modulatorsOzanimod, etrasimod (UC)Oral. Requires baseline ECG, ophthalmologic assessment in at-risk patients, and VZV serology/vaccination. Watch bradycardia at initiation and macular edema.
Positioning principles the guidelines actually state
  • Early advanced therapy beats step-up in moderate-to-severe disease. The old "climb the pyramid" approach is out; delaying effective therapy accrues irreversible bowel damage.
  • Do not use 5-ASA in Crohn's disease. It has no meaningful efficacy for induction or maintenance. Continuing mesalamine in a Crohn's patient is a very visible tell.
  • Corticosteroids are never maintenance therapy. If a patient can't come off steroids, that is by definition a failure requiring escalation, not a dose to be continued.
  • Thiopurine monotherapy is not recommended for induction; it has a role in maintenance and in combination with anti-TNF. Check TPMT and NUDT15 before starting — NUDT15 matters especially in patients of East Asian and Hispanic ancestry.
  • Therapeutic drug monitoring for loss of response: low drug level + no antibodies → dose escalate; low drug + high antibodies → switch within or out of class; adequate drug + active inflammation → change mechanism.
Treat to target — STRIDE-II
  • Short term: clinical response, then symptomatic remission
  • Intermediate: normalization of CRP and fecal calprotectin
  • Long term: endoscopic healing, normalized quality of life, absence of disability. Transmural healing in Crohn's is an emerging target.
  • Symptoms alone are a poor proxy — objective reassessment (calprotectin, endoscopy, or cross-sectional imaging) is expected at defined intervals.
On rounds, sayHe's steroid-dependent, which by definition means the current regimen has failed, so rather than another taper I'd move to an advanced therapy now — and given his fistulizing disease I'd favor an anti-TNF, since that's the class with the fistula data.

Acute severe ulcerative colitis — the inpatient algorithm

ACG UC Guideline 2025 · Truelove & Witts criteria · Oxford (Travis) index

InsideDefining it: Truelove and WittsDay 1Day 3 — the decision point

A medical emergency — severe colitis with systemic toxicity, carrying genuine mortality and a high chance of losing the colon. It runs on a strict clock, and the day-3 decision is the one that matters.

Must know
  • Truelove & Witts defines it: ≥6 bloody stools/day plus a marker of systemic toxicity.
  • Day 3 Oxford index — >8 stools, or 3–8 stools with CRP >45 — predicts ~85% colectomy. Start rescue therapy that day.
  • Give VTE prophylaxis. Bloody stool is not a contraindication.
  • Surgery consulted on day 1, unprepped flexible sigmoidoscopy with CMV biopsies, no opioids or antidiarrheals.

AbbreviationsCMV cytomegalovirus · CRP C-reactive protein · ESR erythrocyte sedimentation rate · TPN total parenteral nutrition · UC ulcerative colitis · VTE venous thromboembolism

Full detail
Defining it: Truelove and Witts

≥6 bloody stools per day plus at least one marker of systemic toxicity: temperature >37.8 °C, heart rate >90, hemoglobin <10.5 g/dL, or ESR >30 mm/h.

Day 1
  • IV methylprednisolone 60 mg/day (or hydrocortisone 100 mg q6–8h). Higher doses add nothing.
  • Flexible sigmoidoscopy without prep, limited insufflation, to confirm severity and biopsy for CMV. Do not do a full colonoscopy — perforation risk.
  • Stool studies including C. difficile — superinfection is common and changes management.
  • Prophylactic-dose heparin. Active UC is a strongly prothrombotic state; the bloody stool is not a contraindication. This is the item most often missed by residents and most often noticed by attendings.
  • Stop antidiarrheals, anticholinergics, opioids, and NSAIDs — all precipitate toxic megacolon.
  • Surgery consulted on day 1, not on day 5. Early colorectal surgery involvement improves outcomes and is a marker of a well-run service.
  • Nutrition assessment; no need for bowel rest or TPN unless obstructed.
Day 3 — the decision point

Oxford criteria: on day 3 of IV steroids, >8 stools per day, or 3–8 stools per day with CRP >45 mg/L, predicts roughly 85% likelihood of colectomy during that admissionTrialTravis SPL, et al. Gut 1996;38:905–910 — the original Oxford day-3 index. That patient needs rescue therapy now.

  • Infliximab — often accelerated/intensified dosing given the fecal drug losses of severe colitisTrialJärnerot G, et al. Gastroenterology 2005;128:1805–1811 — infliximab rescue reduced colectomy in steroid-refractory severe UC
  • Cyclosporine — equally effective; requires level monitoringTrialCYSIF — Laharie D, et al. Lancet 2012;380:1909–1915 — ciclosporin and infliximab were equivalent as rescue therapy, and a plan for what maintains remission afterward
  • Tofacitinib or upadacitinib — increasingly used for their speed of onset
  • If rescue fails within another 5–7 days → colectomy. A delayed colectomy in a deteriorating patient is far more dangerous than a timely one.
PitfallToxic megacolon = transverse colon diameter >6 cm on plain film plus systemic toxicity. Serial abdominal films, serial exams, and no anticholinergics. If it's not improving in 24–72 hours, that's a surgical colon.
On rounds, sayShe's on day 3 of IV methylprednisolone with nine stools and a CRP of 60 — that's Oxford criteria, roughly an 85% colectomy risk this admission, so I'd start rescue infliximab today and I've already asked colorectal surgery to see her.

Crohn's disease — phenotype drives everything

ACG Clinical Guideline, Lichtenstein et al., Am J Gastroenterol 2025

InsideMontreal classificationInflammatory vs fibrotic stricturePerianal fistulizing diseaseSmoking cessationPost-operative recurrenceIleal Crohn's after resectionBudesonide

Transmural, patchy inflammation that can occur anywhere from mouth to anus. Where it is and how it behaves — inflammatory, stricturing or penetrating — drives every management decision.

Must know
  • State the Montreal phenotype — location and behaviour — when you present.
  • Inflammatory vs fibrotic stricture is the decisive question; imaging answers it.
  • Drain the perianal abscess and map with MRI before you immunosuppress.
  • Smoking cessation is disease-modifying. Scope at 6–12 months post-resection (Rutgeerts).

AbbreviationsUC ulcerative colitis

Full detail
  • Montreal classification: age at diagnosis (A), location (L1 ileal, L2 colonic, L3 ileocolonic, L4 upper GI), behavior (B1 inflammatory, B2 stricturing, B3 penetrating, +p perianal). Say the phenotype out loud when presenting — it's how GI physicians think.
  • Inflammatory vs fibrotic stricture is the key management question. MR enterography or CT enterography distinguishes them; inflammation responds to drugs, fibrosis needs dilation or resection.
  • Perianal fistulizing disease: MRI pelvis + examination under anesthesia to map the tracts and drain abscess with setons before immunosuppressing. Then anti-TNF (infliximab has the strongest data), often with an antibiotic (ciprofloxacin/metronidazole). Drugs on top of an undrained abscess is a real and avoidable harm.
  • Smoking cessation is disease-modifying in Crohn's — arguably the highest-yield intervention available and free. (Note the paradox: smoking is protective in UC.)
  • Post-operative recurrence: colonoscopy at 6–12 months after ileocolonic resection, graded by the Rutgeerts scoreTrialRutgeerts P, et al. Gastroenterology 1990;99:956–963. i2b or higher predicts clinical recurrence and prompts escalation. High-risk patients (smokers, penetrating disease, prior resection, young age at surgery) get prophylactic therapy started within weeks of surgery.
  • Ileal Crohn's after resection → bile acid diarrhea (treat with a bile acid sequestrant) and B12 malabsorption.
  • Budesonide (ileal-release) for mild-to-moderate ileal/right colonic disease — high first-pass metabolism, fewer systemic effects, but still not a maintenance drug.

Preventive care in IBD — the checklist that makes you look like a fellow

ACG Clinical Guideline Update, Farraye et al., Am J Gastroenterol 2025

InsideColorectal cancer surveillance in IBDPregnancy

The routine maintenance that quietly gets forgotten while everyone concentrates on the biologic: vaccines, cancer screening, bone density and mental health.

Must know
  • Recombinant zoster vaccine at age ≥18 on immunosuppression — not the old age-50 rule.
  • No live vaccines on biologics. Screen TB and hepatitis B before anti-TNF.
  • CRC surveillance 8 years after diagnosis — but immediately and annually with PSC.
  • Annual dermatology and cervical screening; continue biologics through pregnancy.

AbbreviationsCRC colorectal cancer · HPV human papillomavirus · IBD inflammatory bowel disease · JAK Janus kinase · PSC primary sclerosing cholangitis · TB tuberculosis

Full detail
  • Vaccinate before immunosuppression where possible. Inactivated vaccines are safe on therapy. Live vaccines are contraindicated while on biologics or significant immunosuppression.
  • Recombinant zoster vaccine (Shingrix) for all IBD patients ≥18 on immunosuppression — not the old age-50 threshold. Especially important before a JAK inhibitor.
  • Also: annual influenza, pneumococcal, hepatitis B (check titers — response is blunted on immunosuppression), HPV, COVID-19.
  • Screen for latent TB and hepatitis B before anti-TNF.
  • Skin cancer: annual dermatologic exam. Thiopurines → non-melanoma skin cancer; anti-TNF → melanoma. Counsel on sun protection.
  • Cervical cancer: annual screening for women on immunosuppression.
  • Bone density for those with steroid exposure, and vitamin D/calcium repletion.
  • Depression and anxiety screening — prevalence is high and it drives symptom burden independent of inflammation.
  • Smoking cessation counselling documented at every visit for Crohn's.
Colorectal cancer surveillance in IBD
  • Begin surveillance 8 years after diagnosis of colitis (extent beyond the rectum), then every 1–3 years depending on risk.
  • With PSC: start immediately at IBD diagnosis, then annually. PSC-IBD is the highest-risk group.
  • Use high-definition white light with targeted biopsies, or dye-spray chromoendoscopy. Perform when in remission — inflammation obscures dysplasia.
  • Visible dysplastic lesions that are endoscopically resectable can be removed and surveilled; invisible or unresectable high-grade dysplasia → colectomy discussion.
Pregnancy
  • Continue biologics through pregnancy. Active disease is far more dangerous to the pregnancy than the drug. (ACG Global Consensus on Pregnancy in IBD, 2025.)
  • Methotrexate is absolutely contraindicated — stop ≥3 months before conception in both partners.
  • Anti-TNF crosses the placenta in the third trimester; the infant should avoid live vaccines (rotavirus, BCG) in the first 6 months. Inactivated vaccines proceed normally.

Pouchitis

Practice synthesis · AGA guideline on pouchitis

InsideConfirm endoscopically with biopsiesAcuteChronic antibiotic-dependentChronic antibiotic-refractory

Inflammation of the ileal reservoir built after the colon is removed for ulcerative colitis. It is the commonest late complication of that operation.

Must know
  • Confirm endoscopically with biopsies before treating repeatedly.
  • Acute: ciprofloxacin or metronidazole for 2 weeks.
  • Consider cuffitis, Crohn's of the pouch, and mechanical problems in the differential.

AbbreviationsUC ulcerative colitis

Full detail
  • The most common late complication after ileal pouch–anal anastomosis for UC — roughly half of patients within 5 years.
  • Increased stool frequency, urgency, abdominal cramping, bleeding, incontinence, fever.
  • Confirm endoscopically with biopsies before treating repeatedly — the differential includes cuffitis (retained rectal cuff — treat with topical mesalamine or steroid), irritable pouch syndrome, Crohn's of the pouch, and mechanical problems (stricture, afferent limb syndrome).
  • Acute: ciprofloxacin or metronidazole, 2 weeks. Ciprofloxacin is better tolerated.
  • Chronic antibiotic-dependent: maintenance or rotating antibiotics; probiotics (VSL#3-type formulations) for prevention.
  • Chronic antibiotic-refractory: vedolizumab has randomized data; also anti-TNF and ustekinumab.
