Screening — start at 45

ACG Clinical Guideline, Shaukat et al., Am J Gastroenterol 2021;116:458–479 · USMSTF focused update 2022

InsideAverage-risk screening begins at age 45Stop at 75Family historyAspirin

Colorectal cancer is one of the few cancers you can genuinely prevent rather than merely detect early, because you can remove the precursor lesion.

Must know
  • Average-risk screening starts at 45.
  • Colonoscopy every 10 years or annual FIT are the preferred modalities.
  • Any positive stool test needs a prompt colonoscopy. Stop screening at 75.

AbbreviationsCRC colorectal cancer · FIT faecal immunochemical test · USMSTF US Multi-Society Task Force on Colorectal Cancer

Full detail
  • Average-risk screening begins at age 45 (strong recommendation for 50–75; conditional for 45–49).
  • Preferred modalities: colonoscopy every 10 years, or annual FIT. Everything else is an alternative when the patient declines these.
  • Alternatives: multitarget stool DNA every 3 years, CT colonography every 5 years, flexible sigmoidoscopy every 5–10 years, colon capsule, blood-based cell-free DNA tests.
  • Any positive non-colonoscopy test requires a diagnostic colonoscopy — and it should happen promptly; delay past a year measurably increases cancer risk.
  • Stop at 75; individualize from 76–85 based on comorbidity, life expectancy (>10 years), and prior screening history; do not screen beyond 85.
  • Family history: one first-degree relative with CRC or advanced adenoma diagnosed <60, or two first-degree relatives at any age → start at age 40 or 10 years before the youngest diagnosis, whichever is earlier, and repeat every 5 years.
  • Aspirin is not recommended purely as a CRC-prevention strategy in this guideline.

Post-polypectomy surveillance — the table you will be quizzed on

USMSTF Consensus Update, Gupta et al., Am J Gastroenterol 2020;115:415–434 · Gastroenterology 2020

InsideThe full interval tablePiecemeal resection of large lesionsInadequate preparationSerrated polyposis syndrome

How soon the patient comes back after polyps are removed. You will use this table in clinic more often than almost anything else in this module.

Must know
  • 1–2 small tubular adenomas → 7–10 y; 3–4 → 3–5 y; 5–10 → 3 y.
  • ≥10 mm, villous, or high-grade dysplasia → 3 years.
  • Piecemeal resection of a lesion ≥20 mm → 6 months.
  • Inadequate prep means repeat the exam — do not apply the interval table.

AbbreviationsSSL sessile serrated lesion · USMSTF US Multi-Society Task Force on Colorectal Cancer

Full detail
Index colonoscopy findingNext colonoscopy
Normal exam10 years
1–2 tubular adenomas <10 mm7–10 years
3–4 tubular adenomas <10 mm3–5 years
5–10 adenomas3 years
Adenoma ≥10 mm3 years
Adenoma with villous/tubulovillous histology3 years
Adenoma with high-grade dysplasia3 years
>10 adenomas1 year (and consider genetic evaluation)
Piecemeal resection of an adenoma ≥20 mm6 months — to inspect and treat the scar
Sessile serrated lesion <10 mm, no dysplasia5–10 years
SSL ≥10 mm, SSL with dysplasia, or traditional serrated adenoma3 years
Hyperplastic polyp(s) <10 mm, rectosigmoid10 years
Hyperplastic polyp ≥10 mm3–5 years
PitfallSurveillance intervals assume the index exam was complete to the cecum with adequate preparation. If the prep was inadequate, the correct answer is to repeat the exam — typically within a year, and sooner if the prep was poor — not to apply the interval table.

Serrated polyposis syndrome (WHO 2019): ≥5 serrated lesions proximal to the rectum, all ≥5 mm with ≥2 being ≥10 mm; or >20 serrated lesions of any size distributed throughout the colon with ≥5 proximal to the rectum. Surveillance every 1–3 years, and screen first-degree relatives.

Colonoscopy quality indicators — 2024 changed all the numbers

ASGE–ACG Task Force, Rex et al., Am J Gastroenterol 2024;119:1754–1780 / Gastrointest Endosc 2024;100:352–381

InsidePriority indicatorsADR exclusions

A colonoscopy only prevents cancer if it is done well. These are the measurable numbers that separate an examination that protects a patient from one that reassures them falsely.

Must know
  • ADR ≥35% (men 40, women 30), across all outpatient colonoscopies aged ≥45.
  • Sessile serrated lesion detection rate ≥6% — new in 2024.
  • Cecal intubation ≥95% · bowel prep adequacy ≥90% · withdrawal time ≥8 minutes.
  • Every one of these numbers changed in 2024.

AbbreviationsADR adenoma detection rate · ASGE American Society for Gastrointestinal Endoscopy · CRC colorectal cancer · IBD inflammatory bowel disease · SSLDR sessile serrated lesion detection rate

Full detail

If you have any interest in endoscopy quality, these are the figures to have cold — nearly every one moved from the 2015 version.

Indicator2015 target2024 target
Adenoma detection rate≥25% (M ≥30 / F ≥20), screening exams only≥35% (M ≥40 / F ≥30), all outpatient colonoscopies in age ≥45
Sessile serrated lesion detection rate—≥6% — brand new outcome indicator
ADR after a positive stool test—≥50%
Cecal intubation rate≥90% all / ≥95% screening≥95% for all colonoscopies, with photodocumentation of landmarks
Bowel preparation adequacy≥85%≥90%, preferably scored by Boston Bowel Preparation Scale (≥2 in each of 3 segments)
Withdrawal time≥6 minutes≥8 minutes in normal exams, applied to all endoscopists regardless of ADR
  • Priority indicators — the five everyone should measure: ADR, SSLDR, bowel preparation adequacy rate, adherence to recommended screening/surveillance intervals, and cecal intubation rate.
  • ADR exclusions: positive non-colonoscopy screening tests, IBD, hereditary polyposis syndromes, and exams done to treat known neoplasia.
  • A case counts toward ADR only if a conventional adenoma is confirmed by pathology — a sessile serrated lesion alone doesn't count toward ADR (it counts toward SSLDR).
Numbers to know
  • Corley (NEJM 2014): each 1% rise in ADR → 3% lower interval cancer risk and 5% lower fatal interval cancer riskTrialCorley DA, et al. NEJM 2014;370:1298–1306
  • Post-colonoscopy CRC accounts for roughly 6–9% of colorectal cancers
  • Adenoma miss rates: ~26% for 1–5 mm, ~13% for 5–10 mm, ~2% for ≥10 mm
On rounds, sayWorth noting the 2024 task force moved the ADR floor from 25 to 35 percent and expanded the denominator to all outpatient colonoscopies, added sessile serrated lesion detection rate at 6 percent, and raised minimum withdrawal time from 6 to 8 minutes.

Hereditary colorectal cancer syndromes

ACG Clinical Guideline, Syngal et al., 2015 · USMSTF Lynch Syndrome 2014 · Am J Gastroenterol 2017 primer

InsideUniversal tumor testingLoss of MLH1 on IHCAspirin

The roughly 5% of colorectal cancer driven by an inherited mutation, where diagnosing one patient protects an entire family.

Must know
  • Universal MMR immunohistochemistry or MSI testing on every colorectal and endometrial cancer.
  • MLH1 loss → check BRAF V600E and promoter methylation first — if present it's sporadic.
  • Lynch surveillance: colonoscopy every 1–2 years from age 20–25.

AbbreviationsAPC argon plasma coagulation · CHRPE congenital hypertrophy of the retinal pigment epithelium · CRC colorectal cancer · FAP familial adenomatous polyposis · IHC immunohistochemistry · MMR mismatch repair · MSI microsatellite instability · USMSTF US Multi-Society Task Force on Colorectal Cancer

Full detail
SyndromeGeneticsHallmarksSurveillance
Lynch (HNPCC)MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2, EPCAM — autosomal dominantRight-sided CRC, young onset, endometrial cancer, MSI-high/dMMR. Also ovarian, gastric, urothelial, small bowel, pancreas, sebaceous neoplasms.Colonoscopy every 1–2 years starting age 20–25 (or 2–5 years before the earliest family diagnosis). Gene-specific: MSH6/PMS2 start later.
FAPAPCHundreds to thousands of adenomas; near-100% CRC risk untreated. Duodenal/ampullary adenomas, desmoids, CHRPE, osteomas, thyroid cancer.Annual sigmoidoscopy/colonoscopy from age 10–12; colectomy when polyp burden becomes unmanageable. Upper endoscopy with side-viewing scope, staged by Spigelman.
Attenuated FAPAPC (5'/3' ends)10–100 adenomas, right-sided, later onsetColonoscopy every 1–2 years from age 18–20
MUTYH-associatedMUTYH — autosomal recessiveAttenuated-FAP-like phenotype with no vertical family historyColonoscopy every 1–2 years from age 25–30
Peutz-JeghersSTK11Hamartomatous polyps, mucocutaneous pigmentation, intussusception; broad cancer risk (breast, pancreas, gynecologic)Small bowel imaging/capsule and colonoscopy from the teens
Juvenile polyposisSMAD4, BMPR1AJuvenile hamartomas; SMAD4 overlaps with hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasiaColonoscopy and EGD from age 12–15
  • Universal tumor testing — IHC for mismatch repair proteins or MSI testing on every colorectal and endometrial cancer — is the standard entry point to Lynch diagnosis. Amsterdam II and Bethesda criteria are historical.
  • Loss of MLH1 on IHC → check BRAF V600E and MLH1 promoter hypermethylation first; if present, it's sporadic, not Lynch.
  • Aspirin reduces CRC incidence in Lynch syndrome (CAPP2) — worth discussing.TrialCAPP2 — Burn J, et al. Lancet 2011;378:2081–2087
  • Refer to genetic counseling before testing, not after.

Malignant polyps and endoscopic resection

USMSTF, Shaukat et al., 2020 · USMSTF Endoscopic Removal of Colorectal Lesions, Kaltenbach et al., 2020

InsideDo not use hot forcepsLesions ≥20 mmAdverse features on a malignant polypParis classification

How lesions are actually taken out, and the features that mean endoscopic removal was not enough.

Must know
  • Cold snare for lesions <10 mm. Never hot forceps.
  • Adverse features on a malignant polyp — poor differentiation, lymphovascular invasion, budding, margin <1 mm, depth >1000 µm — argue for surgery.
  • Tattoo distal to the lesion, never on it.

AbbreviationsEMR endoscopic mucosal resection · USMSTF US Multi-Society Task Force on Colorectal Cancer

Full detail
  • Cold snare polypectomy is preferred for lesions <10 mm. Cold forceps only for lesions ≤2 mm — anything larger is incompletely removed by forceps.
  • Do not use hot forceps. High complication rate, poor histology, incomplete removal.
  • Lesions ≥20 mm: EMR at a center with expertise; avoid piecemeal removal where en bloc is achievable; tattoo the site (3 cm distal, in three quadrants, and never on the lesion).
  • Adverse features on a malignant polyp that argue for surgical resection: poorly differentiated histology, lymphovascular invasion, tumor budding, positive or <1 mm deep margin, and submucosal invasion depth >1000 μm (or Haggitt level 4 for pedunculated lesions).
  • Paris classification (0-Ip pedunculated, 0-Is sessile, 0-IIa slightly elevated, 0-IIb flat, 0-IIc depressed) — depressed lesions carry disproportionate submucosal invasion risk.
  • Post-CRC-resection surveillance: colonoscopy at 1 year after resection (or after the clearing exam if obstructed at diagnosis), then 3 years, then 5 years.

07Constipation & Anorectal Disorders

Where most consults are actually about pelvic floor function

2 topics in this chapter
  1. 01Chronic idiopathic constipation
  2. 02Benign anorectal disorders

Chronic idiopathic constipation

ACG–AGA Clinical Practice Guideline, Chey et al., Am J Gastroenterol 2023;118:936–954

InsideTreatment ladderWhen to testOpioid-induced constipation

Infrequent or difficult defecation without a structural cause. Very common — and a large minority is a pelvic floor problem wearing the costume of slow transit.

Must know
  • PEG 3350 is first-line; stimulant laxatives are safe and guideline-supported.
  • Refractory constipation → anorectal manometry with balloon expulsion. Up to half have a defecatory disorder.
  • Dyssynergia is treated with biofeedback, not more laxative.

AbbreviationsCIC chronic idiopathic constipation · PEG polyethylene glycol

Full detail
  • Rome IV: hard/lumpy stools, straining, incomplete evacuation, sensation of blockage, manual maneuvers, or <3 spontaneous bowel movements per week — for at least 3 months.
  • Exclude secondary causes: medications (opioids, anticholinergics, calcium channel blockers, iron, ondansetron), hypothyroidism, hypercalcemia, diabetes, Parkinson's, and mechanical obstruction. Alarm features (bleeding, weight loss, anemia, new onset over 45) → colonoscopy.
Treatment ladder
  1. Fiber — soluble (psyllium). Insoluble fiber tends to worsen bloating.
  2. PEG 3350 — first-line osmotic laxative with the best evidence base.
  3. Stimulants — bisacodyl, senna. The guideline supports these; the old fear of "cathartic colon" and dependence is not evidence-based.
  4. Secretagogues — linaclotide, plecanatide (guanylate cyclase-C agonists), lubiprostone (chloride channel activator). Recommended.
  5. Prucalopride — 5-HT4 agonist; recommended, and cardiovascularly safe unlike its predecessors.
  6. Tenapanor — NHE3 inhibitor, for IBS-C.
  7. The guideline recommends against routine probiotics for CIC.
When to test
  • Anorectal manometry with balloon expulsion testing for anyone failing initial therapy — defecatory disorders (dyssynergia) are present in up to half of refractory constipation and do not respond to laxatives.
  • Treatment for dyssynergia is anorectal biofeedback, which outperforms laxatives in randomized trials.
  • Colonic transit study only after outlet obstruction has been excluded — otherwise a slow transit result is misleading.
Opioid-induced constipation
  • Distinct entity. Peripherally acting mu-opioid receptor antagonists: naloxegol, naldemedine, methylnaltrexone. These don't reverse analgesia because they don't cross the blood-brain barrier.
On rounds, sayShe's failed fiber, PEG, and a secretagogue, so before adding a fourth drug I'd get anorectal manometry with a balloon expulsion test — if this is dyssynergic defecation, the answer is biofeedback, not more laxative.

Benign anorectal disorders

ACG Clinical Guideline, Wald et al., Am J Gastroenterol 2021;116:1987–2008

InsideHemorrhoidsAnal fissureFecal incontinenceLevator ani syndrome and proctalgia fugax

Haemorrhoids, fissures and incontinence. Common, under-reported by patients out of embarrassment, and frequently mismanaged because someone assumed rather than looked.

Must know
  • Never attribute rectal bleeding to hemorrhoids without examining and, where warranted, scoping.
  • Fissure: topical nifedipine or diltiazem first-line.
  • Off-midline or irregular fissure → think Crohn's, HIV, TB, syphilis, malignancy.

AbbreviationsTB tuberculosis

Full detail
Hemorrhoids
  • Internal (above dentate line, painless bleeding, visceral innervation) vs external (below dentate line, painful, somatic innervation).
  • Grade I–II → fiber, water, sitz baths, avoid straining and prolonged toilet sitting. Grade II–III → rubber band ligation, the most effective office procedure. Grade IV or failed ligation → surgery.
  • Thrombosed external hemorrhoid: excision (not simple incision) gives the best outcome if within 72 hours; after that, conservative care.
  • Never attribute rectal bleeding to hemorrhoids without examining and, when age or features warrant, scoping. This is the single most consequential anorectal error.
Anal fissure
  • Posterior midline in ~90%. Severe tearing pain with defecation plus bright blood.
  • First-line: sitz baths, fiber, topical nifedipine or diltiazem (fewer headaches than nitroglycerin).
  • Refractory: botulinum toxin injection; then lateral internal sphincterotomy — highly effective but carries an incontinence risk.
  • Off-midline, multiple, or irregular fissures → think Crohn's disease, HIV, tuberculosis, syphilis, or malignancy.
Fecal incontinence
  • Ask directly — patients almost never volunteer it. Distinguish urge from passive incontinence.
  • Optimize stool consistency first (fiber to bulk, loperamide titrated), then pelvic floor biofeedback.
  • Anorectal manometry and endoanal ultrasound to define sphincter defects; sacral nerve stimulation for refractory cases.
  • Always exclude overflow from fecal impaction — the treatment is disimpaction, not antidiarrheals.
Levator ani syndrome and proctalgia fugax
  • Levator ani: chronic dull rectal ache >30 min, tenderness on posterior traction of the puborectalis. Treat with biofeedback, digital massage, and muscle relaxation.
  • Proctalgia fugax: brief, severe, self-limited episodes. Reassurance is the mainstay.

08Diverticulitis

Rewritten by ACG in July 2026 — the newest guideline in this module

Colonic diverticulitis

ACG Clinical Guideline, Peery et al., Am J Gastroenterol, July 2026 (DOI 10.14309/ajg.0000000000004047)

InsidePhenotypesDiagnosisAntibiotics — the recommendation people get wrongIf you do treat — 4 to 7 daysColonoscopy afterwardNatural history and surgeryPrevention

Inflammation of the small outpouchings that form in the colon wall with age. Common, and the management changed substantially with the 2026 guideline.

Must know
  • CT at the first presentation — clinical diagnosis alone is unreliable.
  • Selected uncomplicated patients can be managed without antibiotics: immunocompetent, stable, tolerating oral intake, not frail, no SIRS, reliable follow-up.
  • Colonoscopy afterward only for complicated disease, alarm symptoms, or overdue screening.
  • Complication risk is highest at the first episode and falls with recurrences — episode count does not drive surgery.

AbbreviationsCRC colorectal cancer · NSAID non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug · SIRS systemic inflammatory response syndrome

Full detail
Phenotypes
PhenotypeDefinition
UncomplicatedLocalized inflammation of colonic diverticula without abscess, perforation, stricture, or fistula
Chronic / smolderingInflammation persisting for weeks to months; often improves on antibiotics and relapses when they stop
ComplicatedPhlegmon, abscess, or perforation; strictures and fistulas may emerge as delayed complications
Diagnosis
  • Clinical diagnosis alone is unreliable. Obtain CT at the first presentation to confirm the diagnosis, exclude alternatives, assess severity, and localize disease.
Antibiotics — the recommendation people get wrong

Acute uncomplicated diverticulitis can be managed without antibiotics in patients who are all of: immunocompetent, hemodynamically stable, being managed as an outpatient, able to tolerate oral intake, without SIRS or complicated disease, not medically frail, and able to follow up reliably.TrialAVOD — Chabok A, et al. Br J Surg 2012;99:532–539; DIABOLO — Daniels L, et al. Br J Surg 2017;104:52–61

Give antibiotics when the patient is immunocompromised, frail, medically complex, unable to tolerate oral intake, clinically worsening, has markedly elevated inflammatory markers or higher-risk imaging findings, or lacks reliable follow-up and support.

If you do treat — 4 to 7 days
  • Monotherapy: amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg PO q12h, or moxifloxacin 400 mg PO daily
  • Combination: metronidazole 500 mg PO q8h plus either TMP-SMX 1 DS tablet q12h, ciprofloxacin 500 mg PO q12h, or levofloxacin 500 mg daily
Colonoscopy afterward
  • After complicated diverticulitis → colonoscopy to exclude a missed cancer or premalignant lesion.
  • After uncomplicated diverticulitis → colonoscopy only if alarm symptoms are present or the patient is not up to date on CRC screening. Alarm symptoms: unintentional weight loss, change in bowel habits, iron-deficiency anemia, bloody stools, persistent abdominal pain.
  • Wait roughly 6–8 weeks after the acute episode resolves.
Natural history and surgery
Numbers to know
  • Risk of complicated disease is highest with the first episode and falls with subsequent recurrences — the opposite of the old teaching that drove prophylactic resection
  • Recurrence after a first episode: ~22%
  • Recurrence after a second episode: ~55%
  • After three or more episodes: recurrence risk is high
  • Elective resection is a quality-of-life decision, not a number-of-episodes decision. Refer for surgical discussion when recurrent uncomplicated diverticulitis meaningfully impairs quality of life. Resection lowers but does not eliminate recurrence.
Prevention
  • High-fiber, plant-forward diet
  • Do not routinely avoid nuts, seeds, corn, or popcorn — this myth persists in patient handouts and is explicitly rejected
  • Avoid regular NSAID use where possible
  • Moderate alcohol; lose weight if overweight or obese; regular physical activity; smoking cessation
On rounds, sayShe's immunocompetent, afebrile, tolerating oral intake, and has good follow-up — under the 2026 ACG guideline that's a patient we can manage without antibiotics. And since this is uncomplicated and she's current on screening, she doesn't need a follow-up colonoscopy either.

09Pancreas & Biliary

Acute pancreatitis · exocrine insufficiency · cysts · stones · strictures

5 topics in this chapter
  1. 01Acute pancreatitis — the fluid recommendation reversed in 2024
  2. 02Chronic pancreatitis
  3. 03Pancreatic cystic lesions
  4. 04Autoimmune pancreatitis
  5. 05Choledocholithiasis, cholangitis, and biliary strictures

Acute pancreatitis — the fluid recommendation reversed in 2024

ACG Clinical Guideline, Tenner et al., Am J Gastroenterol 2024;119:419–437 · WATERFALL trial, NEJM 2022

InsideDiagnosis — two of threeEtiology — work it up in this orderFluids — the changeFeedingAntibioticsERCP and cholecystectomyPost-ERCP pancreatitis prophylaxis

Sudden inflammation of the pancreas, usually from gallstones or alcohol. Most cases are mild and settle — but the first 48 hours determine which ones will not.

Must know
  • Diagnosis needs 2 of 3: pain, lipase >3× ULN, imaging. Do not trend the lipase.
  • Moderate goal-directed lactated Ringer's, not aggressive fluids (WATERFALL).
  • Feed within 24 hours with a low-fat solid diet. No prophylactic antibiotics.
  • Cholecystectomy during the index admission for mild biliary pancreatitis.

AbbreviationsBISAP Bedside Index of Severity in Acute Pancreatitis · ERCP endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography · EUS endoscopic ultrasound · IgG4 immunoglobulin G subclass 4 · MRCP magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography · ULN upper limit of normal

Full detail
Diagnosis — two of three
  1. Characteristic epigastric pain radiating to the back
  2. Lipase or amylase >3× the upper limit of normal
  3. Characteristic findings on imaging

Lipase level does not correlate with severity — do not trend it, and do not repeat it daily.

Etiology — work it up in this order
  • Right upper quadrant ultrasound in every patient — gallstones are the most common cause and the one with a specific intervention.
  • Alcohol; triglycerides >1000 mg/dL; hypercalcemia; drugs; post-ERCP; autoimmune (IgG4); genetic (PRSS1, SPINK1, CFTR); tumor/obstruction.
  • Idiopathic pancreatitis in a patient over 40 warrants imaging to exclude malignancy — CT or MRCP, and often EUS.
Fluids — the change

Moderate, goal-directed resuscitation with lactated Ringer's, not aggressive fluids. The WATERFALL trial found aggressive resuscitation caused fluid overload without improving outcomes.TrialWATERFALL — de-Madaria E, et al. NEJM 2022;387:989–1000 Typical approach: a 10 mL/kg bolus only if hypovolemic, then roughly 1.5 mL/kg/hour, reassessed at 6–12 hours by hemodynamics, urine output, BUN, and hematocrit. Lactated Ringer's is preferred over normal saline.

Feeding
  • Start oral feeding within 24 hours as tolerated. "Nil per os until the lipase normalizes" is obsolete and harmful.
  • A low-fat solid diet is as safe as clear liquids and shortens length of stay.TrialPYTHON — Bakker OJ, et al. NEJM 2014;371:1983–1993 — early nasoenteric feeding was not superior to an oral diet at 72 h
  • If oral intake fails, use enteral (nasogastric is as good as nasojejunal) rather than parenteral nutrition.
Antibiotics
  • No prophylactic antibiotics, even in severe necrotizing pancreatitis.
  • Treat only for infected necrosis (gas in the collection, or clinical deterioration after the first week) or an extrapancreatic infection.
  • Infected necrosis: antibiotics first, then a step-up approach — percutaneous or endoscopic drainage before necrosectomy, and delay intervention ≥4 weeks to allow the collection to wall offTrialPANTER — van Santvoort HC, et al. NEJM 2010;362:1491–1502 — step-up approach reduced major complications versus open necrosectomy.
ERCP and cholecystectomy
  • Urgent ERCP only for concurrent cholangitis or persistent biliary obstruction. Gallstone pancreatitis by itself is not an ERCP indication — most stones pass.
  • Cholecystectomy during the index admission for mild biliary pancreatitis. Discharging without it produces a high readmission rateTrialPONCHO — da Costa DW, et al. Lancet 2015;386:1261–1268 for recurrent pancreatitis and cholangitis.
  • In necrotizing biliary pancreatitis, delay cholecystectomy until inflammation settles.
Post-ERCP pancreatitis prophylaxis
  • Rectal indomethacin or diclofenac 100 mg immediately before or after ERCP in high-risk patientsTrialElmunzer BJ, et al. NEJM 2012;366:1414–1422
  • Aggressive periprocedural lactated Ringer's
  • Prophylactic pancreatic duct stent in high-risk cases (young women, sphincter of Oddi dysfunction, difficult cannulation, pancreatic duct injection)
Numbers to know
  • Revised Atlanta: mild (no organ failure/complications), moderately severe (transient organ failure <48 h or local complications), severe (persistent organ failure >48 h)
  • Overall mortality ~2–5%; severe/necrotizing with infection up to 20–30%
  • BISAP ≥3 predicts severe disease; BUN rise at 24 h is the single best lab predictor of mortality
  • Triglyceride threshold to implicate as the cause: >1000 mg/dL
On rounds, sayI'd give lactated Ringer's at a moderate goal-directed rate rather than the old aggressive protocol — WATERFALL showed that just produces fluid overload — start him on a low-fat solid diet today rather than keeping him NPO, and book cholecystectomy this admission.

Chronic pancreatitis

ACG Clinical Guideline, Gardner et al., Am J Gastroenterol 2020;115:322–339

InsideDiagnosisExocrine pancreatic insufficiencyPancreatic enzyme replacement therapyType 3c diabetesComplete alcohol and tobacco cessationPainScreen for pancreatic cancer

Irreversible scarring of the pancreas producing chronic pain, failure to digest food, and diabetes.

Must know
  • Fecal elastase <100 µg/g diagnoses exocrine insufficiency.
  • 40,000–50,000 lipase units with each meal, taken during the meal.
  • Complete alcohol and tobacco cessation is the highest-value intervention.

AbbreviationsDEXA dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry · EUS endoscopic ultrasound · MRCP magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography

Full detail
  • Diagnosis: CT or MRI/MRCP first; EUS (Rosemont criteria) when cross-sectional imaging is non-diagnostic but suspicion remains. Do not diagnose chronic pancreatitis on symptoms alone. Secretin-enhanced MRCP for early disease.
  • Exocrine pancreatic insufficiency: screen with fecal elastase-1 (<100 μg/g is diagnostic; 100–200 is indeterminate — sample must be formed stool, and the test is falsely low in watery diarrhea).
  • Pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy: roughly 40,000–50,000 lipase units with each main meal, half that with snacks, taken during the meal, not before or after. Add acid suppression if the response is inadequate — enteric coating needs adequate duodenal pH.
  • Fat-soluble vitamin (A, D, E, K) monitoring and DEXA — osteoporosis is markedly under-recognized in these patients.
  • Type 3c diabetes — from loss of both insulin and glucagon, so hypoglycemia risk is high and management differs from type 2.
  • Complete alcohol and tobacco cessation — smoking is an independent driver of progression and of pancreatic cancer risk, and cessation is the highest-value intervention available.
  • Pain: a multimodal, non-opioid-first approach. Adjuvants (pregabalin, TCAs), then celiac plexus block (EUS-guided), endoscopic therapy for an obstructed dilated duct, and surgery (Frey or Puestow) for large-duct disease — surgery outperforms endotherapy for durable pain relief in dilated-duct disease.
  • Screen for pancreatic cancer in hereditary pancreatitis; chronic pancreatitis raises risk substantially.

Pancreatic cystic lesions

ACG Clinical Guideline, Elta et al., 2018 (update in progress) · Fukuoka/International consensus · Nat Rev Gastro Hep 2019

InsideHigh-risk stigmata (resect)Worrisome features (EUS ± FNA)Cyst fluid

Fluid-filled pancreatic lesions, found increasingly often on scans done for something else. The question is always the same: which of these can turn into cancer?

Must know
  • Main-duct IPMN and mucinous cystic neoplasm get resected. Serous cystadenoma needs nothing.
  • Know high-risk stigmata (jaundice, mural nodule ≥5 mm, main duct ≥10 mm) vs worrisome features.
  • Low cyst-fluid glucose is a cheap, accurate marker of a mucinous cyst.

AbbreviationsCEA carcinoembryonic antigen · EUS endoscopic ultrasound · FNA fine needle aspiration · IPMN intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasm

Full detail
LesionKey featuresMalignant potential
Serous cystadenomaMicrocystic/honeycomb, central scar; older womenEssentially none
Mucinous cystic neoplasmBody/tail, unilocular, ovarian-type stroma, women 40–50, no duct communicationYes — resect
Branch-duct IPMNCommunicates with the pancreatic duct, often multifocalModerate — surveillance
Main-duct IPMNDiffuse duct dilation, "fish-mouth" ampullaHigh — resect
PseudocystHistory of pancreatitis, no epithelial lining, high amylaseNone
  • High-risk stigmata (resect): obstructive jaundice with a head cyst, enhancing mural nodule ≥5 mm, main pancreatic duct ≥10 mm, or cytology positive for high-grade dysplasia/malignancy.
  • Worrisome features (EUS ± FNA): cyst ≥3 cm, thickened enhancing walls, main duct 5–9 mm, non-enhancing mural nodule, abrupt duct caliber change with distal atrophy, lymphadenopathy, elevated CA 19-9, rapid growth (>5 mm in 2 years), new-onset diabetes, pancreatitis.
  • Cyst fluid: CEA distinguishes mucinous from non-mucinous (elevated = mucinous) but does not predict malignancy; amylase is high in pseudocysts and duct-communicating lesions; glucose <50 mg/dL is a newer, cheap, accurate marker of a mucinous cyst; molecular testing (KRAS, GNAS) supports IPMN.

Autoimmune pancreatitis

Practice synthesis

InsideType 1Type 2Dramatic response to corticosteroids

A steroid-responsive inflammatory pancreatitis that imitates pancreatic cancer closely. The one diagnosis you must not get wrong in either direction.

Must know
  • Type 1 is IgG4-related: sausage-shaped pancreas, rim, other organ involvement, relapses.
  • The differential is pancreatic adenocarcinoma — get tissue when there is any doubt.
  • Dramatic corticosteroid response is characteristic and diagnostic.

AbbreviationsIBD inflammatory bowel disease · IgG4 immunoglobulin G subclass 4

Full detail
  • Type 1 — the pancreatic manifestation of IgG4-related disease. Older men, painless obstructive jaundice, "sausage-shaped" pancreas with a peripheral rim on CT, elevated serum IgG4, and other organ involvement (sclerosing cholangitis, retroperitoneal fibrosis, salivary gland enlargement, tubulointerstitial nephritis). Relapses frequently.
  • Type 2 — idiopathic duct-centric pancreatitis, granulocytic epithelial lesions, normal IgG4, younger patients, strongly associated with IBD, rarely relapses.
  • The critical differential is pancreatic adenocarcinoma. Both cause a mass and painless jaundice. Obtain tissue when there is any doubt — treating cancer with steroids is a catastrophic error.
  • Dramatic response to corticosteroids (prednisone 40 mg daily, tapered over weeks) is characteristic and is part of the diagnostic criteria. Rituximab for relapsing type 1.

Choledocholithiasis, cholangitis, and biliary strictures

ASGE risk stratification (updated 2019) · Tokyo Guidelines 2018 · ACG Biliary Strictures Guideline, Elmunzer et al., 2023

InsideStratify before you order ERCPAcute cholangitisBiliary strictures

Stones, infection and narrowing in the bile ducts — and the discipline of not using ERCP as a diagnostic test when a scan would answer the question.

Must know
  • High probability → ERCP: stone seen on imaging, cholangitis, or bilirubin >4 with a dilated duct.
  • Intermediate probability → EUS or MRCP first. ERCP is therapeutic, not a diagnostic test.
  • Cholangitis needs drainage, within 24 hours — antibiotics alone will not clear an obstructed system.
  • Assume a biliary stricture is malignant until proven otherwise.

AbbreviationsASGE American Society for Gastrointestinal Endoscopy · CBD common bile duct · ERCP endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography · EUS endoscopic ultrasound · IOC intraoperative cholangiography · MRCP magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography · PSC primary sclerosing cholangitis

Full detail
Stratify before you order ERCP
  • High probability (→ ERCP): a visualized common bile duct stone on imaging, clinical ascending cholangitis, or total bilirubin >4 mg/dL with a dilated CBD.
  • Intermediate probability (→ EUS or MRCP first, then ERCP if positive): abnormal liver tests, age >55, or a dilated CBD on ultrasound. Gallstone pancreatitis on its own was dropped from the 2019 criteria — pancreatitis with normal liver tests and a normal-calibre duct is low probability.
  • Low probability: proceed to cholecystectomy with intraoperative cholangiography if indicated.
  • ERCP is a therapeutic procedure with real risk — it should not be used as a diagnostic test when MRCP or EUS will answer the question.
Acute cholangitis
  • Charcot's triad — fever, jaundice, right upper quadrant pain. Reynolds' pentad adds hypotension and altered mental status (suppurative cholangitis).
  • Tokyo Guidelines grade severity: Grade III (organ dysfunction) demands urgent biliary drainage within 24 hours, and sooner if in shock.
  • Antibiotics plus drainage — antibiotics alone in an obstructed system will not clear the infection.
Biliary strictures
  • Assume malignancy until proven otherwise. ERCP brushings have poor sensitivity (~40–50%); add FISH and consider cholangioscopy with directed biopsy, or EUS-FNA of an associated mass.
  • Do not stent a potentially resectable hilar cholangiocarcinoma before surgical evaluation — get the multidisciplinary discussion first.
  • Benign causes: post-cholecystectomy injury, post-transplant anastomotic stricture, chronic pancreatitis, IgG4-related sclerosing cholangitis, PSC.
  • Benign strictures are treated with multiple side-by-side plastic stents or a fully covered metal stent, exchanged over roughly a year.
On rounds, sayHis bilirubin is 2.8 with a dilated duct but no stone seen and no cholangitis — that's intermediate risk, so I'd get an MRCP or EUS rather than sending him straight to ERCP and accepting a post-ERCP pancreatitis risk for a diagnostic question.

Abnormal liver chemistries — read the pattern first

ACG Clinical Guideline, Kwo et al., Am J Gastroenterol 2017;112:18–35

InsideHepatocellular patternCholestatic patternAST:ALT ratio &gt;2:1 with AST &lt;400ALT/AST &gt;1000Isolated hyperbilirubinemia

The commonest reason a patient is referred to hepatology. Recognising the pattern of the abnormality narrows the differential far faster than ordering every test at once.

Must know
  • True normal ALT is 29–33 U/L in men and 19–25 U/L in women — far below most lab ranges.
  • Read the pattern first: hepatocellular vs cholestatic vs isolated bilirubin.
  • AST:ALT >2 with AST <400 is alcohol. ALT >1000 has a short list — ischemia, acetaminophen, acute viral, autoimmune, Budd-Chiari, passing stone.

AbbreviationsALP alkaline phosphatase · ALT alanine aminotransferase · AMA anti-mitochondrial antibody · ANA antinuclear antibody · AST aspartate aminotransferase · CK creatine kinase · GGT gamma-glutamyl transferase · MASLD metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease · MRCP magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography · PBC primary biliary cholangitis · PSC primary sclerosing cholangitis · TSH thyroid stimulating hormone

Full detail
  • True upper limit of normal ALT is 29–33 U/L in men and 19–25 U/L in women — far lower than most lab reference ranges, which were derived from populations that included undiagnosed fatty liver. Quote this and you'll immediately sound like you read the guideline.
  • Hepatocellular pattern (ALT/AST predominant): viral hepatitis, MASLD, alcohol, drugs, autoimmune, Wilson, hemochromatosis, α1-antitrypsin, celiac, thyroid disease, muscle injury (check CK).
  • Cholestatic pattern (ALP predominant): confirm hepatic origin with GGT or fractionated ALP, then image the biliary tree. Consider PBC (AMA), PSC (MRCP), drugs, infiltrative disease.
  • AST:ALT ratio >2:1 with AST <400 is the classic alcohol signature.
  • ALT/AST >1000: a short list — ischemic hepatitis ("shock liver"), acetaminophen, acute viral hepatitis, autoimmune hepatitis, acute Budd-Chiari, and acute biliary obstruction from a passing stone.
  • Isolated hyperbilirubinemia: fractionate. Unconjugated → Gilbert (fasting, illness, stress), hemolysis. Conjugated → Dubin-Johnson, Rotor, or hepatobiliary disease.
A first-pass panel for unexplained elevation

Hepatitis B and C serologies, hepatitis A IgM if acute; iron studies with transferrin saturation and ferritin; ANA, anti-smooth muscle antibody, quantitative IgG; ceruloplasmin if under 40; α1-antitrypsin phenotype; celiac serology; TSH; a full medication and supplement history; and right upper quadrant ultrasound.

Hepatitis B and C — who to screen, who to treat, and the reactivation question

AASLD Hepatitis B Guidance, Terrault et al., Hepatology 2018 · AASLD–IDSA HCV Guidance (hcvguidelines.org, living document) · CDC universal screening: HCV 2020, HBV 2023 · ACIP universal adult hepatitis B vaccination 2022

InsideScreen every adult onceHepatitis C — treat everyoneHepatitis B — reading the serologyHepatitis B — who to treatReactivation — the consult that must not be missedPregnancy, vaccination, HDV, A and E

Two chronic viral infections of the liver that between them account for most cirrhosis and liver cancer worldwide. One is now curable with tablets; the other is controllable but never truly cleared, which is why it comes back when the immune system is switched off.

Must know
  • Screen every adult once: HCV antibody with reflex RNA, and the hepatitis B triple panel — HBsAg, anti-HBs, total anti-HBc.
  • HCV: treat everyone with viraemia. Glecaprevir/pibrentasvir for 8 weeks or sofosbuvir/velpatasvir for 12; SVR12 is cure; F3–F4 keep HCC surveillance for life.
  • HBV: the treatment decision is ALT + HBV DNA + fibrosis, treated with entecavir or tenofovir. Cirrhosis with detectable DNA is treated regardless of ALT.
  • Before rituximab, chemotherapy, anti-TNF or high-dose steroids, check HBsAg and anti-HBc. HBsAg-positive patients, and anti-HBc-positive patients on B-cell depletion, get prophylaxis — not monitoring.

AbbreviationsALT alanine aminotransferase · DAA direct-acting antiviral · HBIG hepatitis B immune globulin · HCC hepatocellular carcinoma · HDV hepatitis D virus · SVR12 sustained virological response 12 weeks after treatment · TAF tenofovir alafenamide · TDF tenofovir disoproxil fumarate · ULN upper limit of normal

Full detail
Screen every adult once
  • HCV: all adults at least once, every pregnancy, and periodically with ongoing risk (CDC 2020). Order the antibody with reflex RNA — antibody-positive, RNA-negative means resolved or cured infection (or a false positive), not active disease.
  • HBV: all adults at least once with the triple panel (HBsAg, anti-HBs, total anti-HBc), every pregnancy, and before any immunosuppressive therapy (CDC 2023).
  • Also test anyone with abnormal liver tests, HIV, injection drug use, dialysis, birth in a region of intermediate or high endemicity, or a household or sexual contact with hepatitis B.
Hepatitis C — treat everyone
  • Roughly three-quarters of exposures become chronic. Every patient with detectable RNA is treated, including active drug use and acute infection — waiting for spontaneous clearance is no longer recommended.
  • Before treatment: HCV RNA, HBsAg and anti-HBc (HBV reactivation during DAA therapy carries a boxed warning — treat HBsAg-positive patients with a nucleoside analogue alongside, monitor those who are anti-HBc-positive only), HIV, CBC, liver panel, eGFR, INR, pregnancy test if ribavirin might be used, and fibrosis staging (FIB-4, then elastography if indeterminate) because cirrhosis changes the regimen and the follow-up. Genotype is not needed for the simplified pangenotypic pathway.
  • Simplified treatment (treatment-naive, no prior transplant or HCC, no decompensation, not pregnant): glecaprevir/pibrentasvir for 8 weeks in all genotypes including compensated cirrhosis, or sofosbuvir/velpatasvir for 12 weeks. Genotype 3 with cirrhosis: check for the NS5A Y93H substitution before sofosbuvir/velpatasvir and add ribavirin or use glecaprevir/pibrentasvir if present.
  • Decompensated cirrhosis (Child-Pugh B or C): sofosbuvir/velpatasvir with ribavirin for 12 weeks (24 weeks without ribavirin if intolerant), in a transplant-capable centre. Protease inhibitors — glecaprevir, voxilaprevir, grazoprevir — are contraindicated in Child-Pugh B and C.
  • Prior DAA failure: sofosbuvir/velpatasvir/voxilaprevir for 12 weeks.
  • Interactions worth knowing: amiodarone with sofosbuvir (symptomatic bradycardia); PPIs reduce velpatasvir absorption (omeprazole no more than 20 mg, taken with the DAA and food); statins, carbamazepine, phenytoin, rifampin and St John's wort; some antiretrovirals. Check every regimen on a drug-interaction checker.
  • SVR12 — undetectable RNA 12 weeks after the end of treatment — is cure, achieved in more than 95%. Nothing further is needed for F0–F2. F3–F4 continue HCC surveillance every 6 months indefinitely and variceal screening per Baveno, because the cancer risk falls but does not disappear. Retest with RNA, not antibody, if there is ongoing risk — the antibody stays positive for life.
  • Extrahepatic disease — cryoglobulinaemic vasculitis, membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis, porphyria cutanea tarda, lichen planus, B-cell lymphoma — is treated by treating the virus.
Hepatitis B — reading the serology
PatternHBsAgAnti-HBsAnti-HBcMeaning
Acute infection+−IgM +HBeAg and DNA high; more than 95% of adults clear it
Chronic infection+ for >6 months−Total +, IgM −Then phase it by HBeAg, DNA and ALT
Resolved infection−++Immune, but cccDNA persists in hepatocytes — can reactivate under immunosuppression
Vaccinated−+−Immune; anti-HBs ≥10 mIU/mL
Isolated anti-HBc−−+Resolved infection with waned anti-HBs, occult infection, or a false positive — check HBV DNA when immunosuppression is planned

HBeAg marks high replication and infectivity; anti-HBe usually marks lower replication, but HBeAg-negative chronic hepatitis (precore or basal core promoter mutants) can be active with a high DNA — which is why DNA, not HBeAg, drives the decision. The ALT upper limit used by AASLD is 35 U/L in men and 25 U/L in women, not the laboratory range.

Hepatitis B — who to treat
PhaseHBeAgHBV DNA (IU/mL)ALTAction
Immune tolerant+>1,000,000NormalMonitor ALT every 6 months; treat if ALT rises, or consider from age 40 with biopsy or elastography evidence of disease
Immune active, HBeAg-positive+>20,000≥2× ULN, or significant fibrosisTreat
Inactive carrier−<2,000NormalMonitor ALT and DNA every 6–12 months; HCC surveillance if it is otherwise indicated
Immune active, HBeAg-negative−>2,000≥2× ULN, or significant fibrosisTreat
Cirrhosiseitherany detectableanyTreat, indefinitely; decompensated disease also goes for transplant evaluation
  • First-line drugs: entecavir, tenofovir alafenamide or tenofovir disoproxil — all high-barrier to resistance. TAF is preferred with reduced eGFR or bone disease; entecavir is avoided after lamivudine exposure because of cross-resistance. Pegylated interferon for 48 weeks is an option in selected non-cirrhotic patients who want finite therapy.
  • Duration: HBeAg-positive patients can stop after HBeAg seroconversion plus at least 12 months of consolidation with undetectable DNA and normal ALT; HBeAg-negative patients are treated indefinitely unless HBsAg is lost; cirrhosis is lifelong. Stopping is followed by flares, so monitor closely.
  • Monitoring on treatment: ALT and HBV DNA every 3–6 months, HBsAg yearly, eGFR and phosphate on tenofovir.
  • HCC surveillance without cirrhosis: Asian men over 40 and Asian women over 50, patients of sub-Saharan African origin (in whom HCC occurs young), anyone with a first-degree relative with HCC, and HDV co-infection — ultrasound with or without AFP every 6 months. Everyone with cirrhosis is surveilled regardless.
  • Acute hepatitis B is supportive care; treat only if it is severe (INR >1.5), protracted beyond four weeks, or evolving into acute liver failure.
Reactivation — the consult that must not be missed

Hepatitis B is never eradicated: covalently closed circular DNA persists in hepatocytes after HBsAg is lost, and anti-HBc-positive patients can reactivate — sometimes fatally — when immunity is removed. Every patient starting immunosuppression or chemotherapy needs HBsAg and anti-HBc first, and the response depends on the risk category (AASLD 2018).

Risk of reactivationWhoWhat to do
High (>10%)HBsAg-positive on B-cell depleting therapy (rituximab, obinutuzumab), anthracyclines, or prednisone ≥20 mg/day for ≥4 weeks; anti-HBc-positive/HBsAg-negative on B-cell depleting therapyProphylaxis — entecavir, TAF or TDF started before the first dose and continued for at least 6 months after immunosuppression ends, at least 12 months after B-cell depleting agents
Moderate (1–10%)HBsAg-positive on anti-TNF, other cytokine or integrin inhibitors, tyrosine kinase inhibitors, or moderate-dose steroids; anti-HBc-positive on anthracyclines or high-dose steroidsProphylaxis for HBsAg-positive patients; prophylaxis or HBV DNA monitoring every 1–3 months for anti-HBc-positive patients
Low (<1%)Azathioprine, 6-mercaptopurine, methotrexate; intra-articular steroids; steroids for a week or lessMonitor ALT and HBV DNA; treat if DNA rises

Direct-acting antivirals for hepatitis C also reactivate hepatitis B (boxed warning). HBsAg-positive patients get a nucleoside analogue for the DAA course; anti-HBc-positive patients are monitored.

Pregnancy, vaccination, HDV, A and E
  • Pregnancy: screen every pregnancy. If HBV DNA is above 200,000 IU/mL, start tenofovir disoproxil at 28–32 weeks to cut vertical transmission; the infant receives HBIG and the first vaccine dose within 12 hours of birth. Breastfeeding is not contraindicated. Hepatitis C is not yet treated during pregnancy outside trials.
  • Vaccination: ACIP (2022) recommends hepatitis B vaccination for all adults aged 19–59, and for those 60 and over with risk factors or on request; everyone with chronic liver disease should be immune to hepatitis A and B. Heplisav-B is a two-dose schedule a month apart. Check anti-HBs one to two months after the series in dialysis, immunocompromised and healthcare workers.
  • Hepatitis D needs HBsAg to replicate and produces the fastest-progressing viral hepatitis. Test anti-HDV in every HBsAg-positive patient at least once (EASL 2023 makes this universal; US practice is moving the same way, with HIV, injection drug use, high ALT with low HBV DNA, and origin in an endemic region the classical triggers), then HDV RNA if positive. Bulevirtide is licensed in Europe but not by the FDA; pegylated interferon is the alternative.
  • Hepatitis A — IgM anti-HAV; self-limited, vaccinate contacts. Hepatitis E — travellers and, in the immunosuppressed and transplant recipients, a cause of chronic hepatitis treated with ribavirin; test for it before calling a hepatitis "drug-induced".
Numbers to know
  • Chronicity after hepatitis C exposure: ~75% · DAA cure: >95%
  • Chronicity after hepatitis B exposure: ~90% perinatal, <5% adult
  • AASLD ALT upper limit: 35 U/L men, 25 U/L women
  • HBV DNA thresholds: 2,000 (HBeAg-negative treatment), 20,000 (HBeAg-positive treatment), 200,000 IU/mL (antiviral in pregnancy)
Pitfall"HBsAg negative, anti-HBc positive" is not the same as "immune". Those patients carry cccDNA and reactivate on rituximab. When oncology or rheumatology asks whether the patient is "cleared to start", the answer is a risk category and a prophylaxis plan, not a reassurance.
On rounds, sayHe's HBsAg-positive with a low DNA and a normal ALT, so on his own he'd just be monitored — but oncology wants to start R-CHOP next week, and rituximab puts him in the highest reactivation category. I'd start entecavir now, before the first cycle, continue it for at least twelve months after the last rituximab dose, and check HBV DNA every three months rather than waiting for the ALT to rise.

MASLD and MASH — new name, and now two approved drugs

AASLD Practice Guidance 2023 + 2024 update · Multi-society nomenclature consensus 2023 · FDA approvals 2024, 2025

InsideNomenclatureRisk stratification — the pathway you should be able to drawTreatment

Fat accumulating in the liver in someone with cardiometabolic risk factors. It is now the commonest liver disease in the world, and most of these patients will die of heart disease rather than their liver.

Must know
  • FIB-4 <1.3 is low risk, >2.67 is high risk — then elastography.
  • ≥10% weight loss is what improves fibrosis.
  • Resmetirom and semaglutide are approved for non-cirrhotic MASH with F2–F3 fibrosis; neither for cirrhosis.
  • Statins are safe and indicated — cardiovascular disease is what kills these patients.

AbbreviationsALT alanine aminotransferase · AST aspartate aminotransferase · BMI body mass index · ELF Enhanced Liver Fibrosis test · FIB-4 Fibrosis-4 index · GLP-1 glucagon-like peptide-1 · HDL high-density lipoprotein · MASH metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis · MASLD metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease · MetALD MASLD with increased alcohol intake · SLD steatotic liver disease

Full detail
Nomenclature
  • MASLD — metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease: hepatic steatosis plus ≥1 cardiometabolic risk factor (elevated BMI or waist circumference, hyperglycemia/diabetes, hypertension, elevated triglycerides, low HDL). Note this is a positive diagnosis, not a diagnosis of exclusion the way NAFLD was.
  • MetALD — MASLD in someone with moderate alcohol intake (roughly 140–350 g/week in women, 210–420 g/week in men).
  • MASH replaces NASH; SLD is the umbrella term.
Risk stratification — the pathway you should be able to draw
  1. FIB-4 in everyone with risk factors. <1.3 → low risk (recheck in 2–3 years). 1.3–2.67 → indeterminate. >2.67 → high risk. FIB-4 loses accuracy over age 65 — use a higher lower-cutoff (~2.0).
  2. Indeterminate or high FIB-4 → vibration-controlled transient elastography (FibroScan) or ELF test.
  3. Persistent uncertainty, or a competing diagnosis → liver biopsy.
Treatment
  • Weight loss remains the foundation: ≥5% improves steatosis, ≥7–10% resolves steatohepatitis, ≥10% improves fibrosis. Mediterranean-style diet, exercise independent of weight loss, avoid fructose-sweetened beverages.
  • Resmetirom (Rezdiffra) — oral thyroid hormone receptor-β agonistTrialMAESTRO-NASH — Harrison SA, et al. NEJM 2024;390:497–509, FDA-approved March 2024 for non-cirrhotic MASH with F2–F3 fibrosis (MAESTRO-NASH).
  • Semaglutide 2.4 mg weekly (Wegovy) — accelerated approval August 2025 for non-cirrhotic MASH with F2–F3 fibrosis, on the ESSENCE trial. At 72 weeks, roughly 63% achieved steatohepatitis resolution without worsening fibrosis versus 34% on placebo. First GLP-1 receptor agonist with this indication.TrialESSENCE — Sanyal AJ, et al. NEJM 2025 — semaglutide 2.4 mg in biopsy-confirmed MASH with F2–F3 fibrosis
  • Neither drug is approved for MASH cirrhosis — that remains an unmet need and a good thing to know when asked.
  • Off-label options with data: vitamin E 800 IU/day in non-diabetic patients with biopsy-proven MASHTrialPIVENS — Sanyal AJ, et al. NEJM 2010;362:1675–1685; pioglitazone, including in those with type 2 diabetes.
  • Statins are safe and indicated in MASLD, including compensated cirrhosis. Cardiovascular disease — not liver disease — is the leading cause of death in this population. Withholding a statin over mild transaminitis is a common, harmful error.
  • Bariatric surgery for eligible patients; consider referral in F2+ with obesity.
On rounds, sayHer FIB-4 is 3.1, so she's high-risk and I'd get elastography rather than repeating labs in a year — and if she turns out to be F2 or F3 without cirrhosis, she's now a candidate for resmetirom or semaglutide, both of which have that specific indication.

Alcohol-associated liver disease and alcohol-associated hepatitis

ACG Clinical Guideline, Shah et al., Am J Gastroenterol 2024;119:30–54

InsideScreen every patient with AUDIT-CAlcohol-associated hepatitisPrednisolone 40 mg daily for 28 daysLille score at day 7N-acetylcysteineEarly liver transplantation

The spectrum from fatty liver through alcohol-associated hepatitis to cirrhosis. It contains one of the few presentations in hepatology with a specific, time-limited drug treatment.

Must know
  • AST:ALT >1.5 with AST <400 and bilirubin >3 within 8 weeks of heavy use.
  • Maddrey DF ≥32 or MELD >20 → prednisolone 40 mg daily for 28 days.
  • Lille score >0.45 at day 7 means non-response — stop the steroid.
  • Alcohol use disorder pharmacotherapy is part of the hepatology plan.

AbbreviationsALT alanine aminotransferase · AST aspartate aminotransferase · AUDIT-C Alcohol Use Disorders Identification Test — Consumption · HRS hepatorenal syndrome · MELD Model for End-Stage Liver Disease · PEth phosphatidylethanol

Full detail
  • Screen every patient with AUDIT-C. Quantify in standard drinks. Phosphatidylethanol (PEth) is an objective biomarker with a 3–4 week window, increasingly used in transplant evaluation.
  • Alcohol-associated hepatitis — clinical diagnosis: onset of jaundice within 8 weeks of heavy use, AST:ALT >1.5 with AST <400 U/L, total bilirubin >3 mg/dL, and exclusion of other causes.
  • Severity: Maddrey discriminant function ≥32, or MELD >20 → severe disease.
  • Prednisolone 40 mg daily for 28 days in severe diseaseTrialSTOPAH — Thursz MR, et al. NEJM 2015;372:1619–1628 — prednisolone improved 28-day but not 90-day or 1-year mortality without contraindications (active infection, GI bleeding, HRS, uncontrolled sepsis). Prednisolone, not prednisone — it doesn't require hepatic conversion.
  • Lille score at day 7TrialLouvet A, et al. Hepatology 2007;45:1348–1354: >0.45 means non-response — stop the steroid. Continuing it only adds infection risk.
  • N-acetylcysteine as an adjunct to steroids has supportive data.
  • Aggressive nutrition — these patients are profoundly malnourished; target 1.2–1.5 g/kg protein and 35 kcal/kg. Thiamine before glucose. Watch for refeeding.
  • Alcohol use disorder pharmacotherapy is part of hepatology care: baclofen has the best safety data in cirrhosis; acamprosate and naltrexone are options (avoid naltrexone in decompensated disease). Pair with behavioral treatment.
  • Early liver transplantation in carefully selected patients with severe alcohol-associated hepatitis is now accepted — the rigid "6 months of sobriety" rule is no longer an absolute requirement.

Portal hypertension and varices — Baveno VII language

Baveno VII Consensus, J Hepatol 2022 · AASLD portal hypertension guidance 2024

InsidecACLDPrimary prophylaxisAcute variceal bleedPre-emptive TIPS within 72 hoursGastric varices

As the liver scars, pressure rises in the portal venous system. That single mechanical fact generates varices, ascites and encephalopathy.

Must know
  • Carvedilol is the preferred non-selective beta-blocker — it prevents decompensation, not just bleeding.
  • LSM ≥25 kPa rules in clinically significant portal hypertension.
  • Baveno VI: LSM <20 kPa and platelets >150,000 lets you skip screening endoscopy.
  • Every variceal bleed gets octreotide and ceftriaxone; consider pre-emptive TIPS within 72 hours in high-risk bleeders.

AbbreviationsAKI acute kidney injury · BRTO balloon-occluded retrograde transvenous obliteration · CSPH clinically significant portal hypertension · EVL endoscopic variceal ligation · HVPG hepatic venous pressure gradient · LSM liver stiffness measurement · NSBB non-selective beta-blocker · TIPS transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt · cACLD compensated advanced chronic liver disease

Full detail
  • cACLD (compensated advanced chronic liver disease) has replaced "compensated cirrhosis" as the working term. Liver stiffness <10 kPa rules it out; 10–15 kPa is suggestive; >15 kPa makes it highly likely.
  • Clinically significant portal hypertension (CSPH) = HVPG ≥10 mmHg. Non-invasively, LSM ≥25 kPa is sufficient to rule CSPH in. ("Rule of 5" — 10, 15, 20, 25 kPa.)
  • Baveno VI criteria to skip screening endoscopy: LSM <20 kPa and platelets >150,000. Those patients have a very low probability of high-risk varices.
  • Carvedilol is the preferred non-selective beta-blocker in CSPH — it has additional α1-blockade and, per PREDESCI, prevents decompensation, not just variceal bleedingTrialPREDESCI — Villanueva C, et al. Lancet 2019;393:1597–1608. Typical dose 6.25–12.5 mg daily.
  • Primary prophylaxis: NSBB (carvedilol preferred) or endoscopic variceal ligation for medium/large varices. NSBB is preferred where tolerated because of the broader benefit.
  • Secondary prophylaxis (after a bleed): NSBB plus serial EVL — combination therapy, not either alone.
  • Acute variceal bleed: restrictive transfusion to Hb 7, octreotide, ceftriaxone 1 g daily up to 7 days, endoscopy within 12 hours, band ligation.
  • Pre-emptive TIPS within 72 hours (ideally 24) in high-risk bleedersTrialGarcía-Pagán JC, et al. NEJM 2010;362:2370–2379 — early TIPS reduced treatment failure and mortality in Child B with active bleeding or Child C — Child-Pugh C 10–13, or Child B with active bleeding at endoscopy.
  • Gastric varices: cyanoacrylate injection or BRTO; isolated gastric varices should prompt evaluation for splenic vein thrombosis (left-sided portal hypertension — cured by splenectomy).
PitfallThe old "stop beta-blockers in refractory ascites" teaching is now nuanced: continue carvedilol/NSBB unless the patient has hypotension (systolic <90), hyponatremia, or AKI. Reduce or hold in that setting, then rechallenge.

Vascular liver disease — Budd-Chiari and portal vein thrombosis: anticoagulate, find the cause, and know when the clot is a tumour

ACG Clinical Guideline, Simonetto et al., Am J Gastroenterol 2020;115:18–40 · AASLD Vascular Liver Disorders and PVT Guidance, Northup et al., Hepatology 2021;73:366–413 · EASL Vascular Diseases of the Liver CPG, Rautou et al., J Hepatol 2026;84:399–456 · AGA Clinical Practice Update on PVT in Cirrhosis, Davis et al., Gastroenterology 2025;168:396–404 · Baveno VII, J Hepatol 2022 · Baveno VIII, J Hepatol 2026 · Smalberg et al., Blood 2012 · EBMT SOS criteria, Mohty et al., Bone Marrow Transplant 2016 and 2023

InsideBudd-Chiari — recognising outflow obstructionBudd-Chiari — the cause hunt and the thrombophilia work-upBudd-Chiari — the stepwise treatmentCirrhotic PVT — bland or tumour, and how to describe itCirrhotic PVT — who to anticoagulate, with what, for how longNon-cirrhotic portal vein thrombosis — acute and chronicSinusoidal obstruction, ischaemic hepatitis and congestive hepatopathy

Three ways the blood supply of the liver fails: the hepatic veins block (Budd-Chiari), the portal vein clots (portal vein thrombosis, with or without cirrhosis), or the sinusoids themselves are injured or congested. They are uncommon, they turn up as unexplained ascites, a tender big liver or an incidental finding on a surveillance scan, and two of them — Budd-Chiari and non-cirrhotic portal vein thrombosis — share a rule: anticoagulate, then find the clotting tendency that caused it. In cirrhosis the clot is usually the liver's own doing and the decision is selective.

Must know
  • Budd-Chiari is hepatic venous outflow obstruction. Doppler ultrasound first, then CT or MR venography. Everyone is anticoagulated for life, and everyone is tested for JAK2 V617F — a myeloproliferative neoplasm underlies about 40%, and hypersplenism hides it behind normal blood counts.
  • Budd-Chiari treatment is stepwise: anticoagulation and treatment of the cause → angioplasty or stent for a short-segment stenosis → TIPS for non-responders → transplant. Followed in order, it keeps roughly three-quarters of patients alive at 5 years.
  • Portal vein thrombosis in cirrhosis: first decide bland or tumour. Enhancement, an expanded vein, arterial flow inside the thrombus and a raised AFP mean HCC invading the vein — not a clot to anticoagulate.
  • Anticoagulate bland cirrhotic PVT when it is recent (within 6 months) and blocks more than half the main trunk, or is symptomatic, progressing, into the SMV, or in a transplant candidate — with the varices covered first; it is safe once they are. Non-cirrhotic acute PVT: anticoagulate everyone for at least 6 months.

AbbreviationsAFP alpha-fetoprotein · ALT alanine aminotransferase · BCLC Barcelona Clinic Liver Cancer staging · CALR calreticulin · DOAC direct oral anticoagulant · EBMT European Society for Blood and Marrow Transplantation · HCC hepatocellular carcinoma · HSCT haematopoietic stem cell transplantation · INR international normalised ratio · IVC inferior vena cava · JAK2 Janus kinase 2 · LDH lactate dehydrogenase · LI-RADS Liver Imaging Reporting and Data System · LMWH low-molecular-weight heparin · MPN myeloproliferative neoplasm · PNH paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria · PVT portal vein thrombosis · SAAG serum-ascites albumin gradient · SMV superior mesenteric vein · SOS sinusoidal obstruction syndrome · TIPS transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt

Full detail
Budd-Chiari — recognising outflow obstruction

Hepatic venous outflow obstruction from the small hepatic veins to the IVC–right atrial junction, by thrombosis (primary) or by tumour or abscess compressing or invading the veins (secondary); sinusoidal obstruction and cardiac congestion are a different block. Fulminant disease (acute liver failure within days) is rare — emergency TIPS if feasible, transplant centre on day one; acute disease is days to weeks of right upper quadrant pain, tender hepatomegaly, fast ascites and transaminases in the thousands; subacute and chronic disease, the commonest, is months of ascites, splenomegaly and varices mimicking cirrhosis until someone images the hepatic veins.

  • High-SAAG, high-protein ascites (above 2.5 g/dL), like cardiac ascites; cirrhotic ascites is low-protein, so a high protein in a "cirrhotic" means image the hepatic veins and the heart.
  • Caudate hypertrophy is the signature — it drains straight into the IVC. Chronic disease grows large benign regenerative nodules that enhance without washout, so LI-RADS does not apply; HCC occurs even without cirrhosis, so all chronic Budd-Chiari gets six-monthly surveillance and a growing or atypical nodule is biopsied.
  • Doppler ultrasound first — absent or reversed hepatic vein flow, spider-web collaterals, an IVC web — then CT or MR venography to map the extent and find a stenosis short enough to open, and an echocardiogram, because right heart failure and constrictive pericarditis give the same picture.
Budd-Chiari — the cause hunt and the thrombophilia work-up

Most patients have a prothrombotic factor and at least a quarter have more than one — oral contraceptives and pregnancy are usually the second hit — so finding one does not end the search.

  • Myeloproliferative neoplasms are the big one: about 40% of Budd-Chiari and a third of non-cirrhotic PVT (Smalberg meta-analysis), JAK2 V617F-positive in most. Haemodilution and hypersplenism keep the blood count normal, so test JAK2 V617F in everyone; if negative and suspicion remains, add CALR (with haematology, JAK2 exon 12 or a myeloid sequencing panel) and discuss a marrow whatever the counts.
  • PNH — high-sensitivity flow cytometry in everyone; it changes treatment (eculizumab or ravulizumab). Antiphospholipid syndrome — lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin, anti-β2-glycoprotein I, confirmed 12 weeks apart; confirmed means a vitamin K antagonist, not a DOAC.
  • Inherited — factor V Leiden, prothrombin G20210A, protein C, S and antithrombin; the last three fall with liver dysfunction and on warfarin or heparin, so a low level in a sick liver proves nothing.

Draw protein C, S, antithrombin and the lupus anticoagulant before anticoagulation where you can — heparin, warfarin and above all DOACs interfere; the solid-phase antibodies can go off at once. The AASLD is more selective: the inherited panel rarely changes management, and none of the panel is needed when a fresh operation, trauma or inflammation explains the clot. In cirrhotic PVT no panel is routine (AGA 2025) unless the counts are unexpectedly normal for the portal hypertension — then JAK2.

Budd-Chiari — the stepwise treatment

ACG, AASLD and EASL endorse the same escalation, moving up only when the step below has failed — ascites, bilirubin, creatinine and INR not settling over the first weeks.

  • Step 1, everyone: lifelong anticoagulation — LMWH, then a vitamin K antagonist to an INR of 2–3; DOAC data are growing — and treat the cause: cytoreduction and aspirin for an MPN, complement inhibition for PNH, stop the oestrogen.
  • Step 2: angioplasty, usually with a stent, for a short-segment stenosis or web — the rule in membranous obstruction of the IVC (common in parts of Asia), a minority otherwise.
  • Step 3: TIPS for non-responders who cannot be recanalised; with obliterated hepatic veins the radiologist punctures straight from the IVC into the portal vein.
  • Step 4: transplantation for fulminant disease, failed TIPS or decompensated cirrhosis. An MPN is not a contraindication, and anticoagulation continues afterwards — the clotting tendency travels with the patient, not the liver.

Followed in order, this kept 77% of 157 patients alive at a median of 50 months in the multicentre European EN-Vie cohort (Seijo 2013); the single-centre series that pioneered it reported close to 90% at 5 years. Pregnancy is possible once stable — LMWH from before conception, because warfarin is teratogenic in the first trimester — and oestrogen-containing contraception is off for good.

Cirrhotic PVT — bland or tumour, and how to describe it

Roughly 5% of compensated cirrhotics by one year and 10% by five, mostly found on the surveillance scan: slow portal flow (a Doppler velocity below 15 cm/s predicts it) on haemostasis that is rebalanced, not anticoagulated — the raised INR is not protection (the cirrhosis topic).

FeatureBland thrombusTumour thrombus (HCC with macrovascular invasion)
EnhancementNone, on every phaseArterial enhancement and washout, like the parent tumour
Vein calibreNormal or contractedExpanded by tumour growing along it
DopplerNo flow in the clotPulsatile arterial signal inside it; AFP often raised
ConsequenceAn anticoagulation decisionBCLC C — systemic therapy, no listing, no anticoagulation

Contrast CT or MRI confirms it, and once bland you describe it as the AASLD asks: timing — recent (found within 6 months, or absent on a scan in the last 6 months) versus chronic (older, or a cavernoma replacing the vein); site — trunk, intrahepatic branches, splenic vein, SMV; degree — minimal (under 50% of the lumen), partial (more than 50%) or occlusive; and symptoms. Each changes management, and an occluded SMV can make a standard portal anastomosis impossible.

Cirrhotic PVT — who to anticoagulate, with what, for how long
SituationWhat to do
Recent, completely or >50% occluding the main trunkAnticoagulate
Into the SMV, or symptomaticAnticoagulate — bowel and future anastomosis at stake
Transplant candidate, any recent thrombusAnticoagulate until transplant
Minimal (under 50%), asymptomatic, not a candidateObserve; reimage at 3 months, treat if it progresses — many regress
Chronic, with cavernomaAnticoagulation will not reopen it; give it for a prothrombotic disorder, progression or past mesenteric ischaemia, and consider it — or TIPS recanalisation — in a transplant candidate
Tumour thrombusTreat the HCC
  • Cover the varices, then start — quickly. Carvedilol by preference — the ACG puts the beta-blocker first when anticoagulation is coming, because banding may force a pause in it — and band ligation if beta-blockade is contraindicated or not tolerated. Book the scope within days and start LMWH straight after; the AGA says "avoid delays". The AASLD's read: portal-hypertensive bleeding is unchanged by anticoagulation and other bleeding matches the general population; pooled data show recanalisation in 71% treated against 42% untreated with no excess bleedingTrialLoffredo L, et al. Gastroenterology 2017;153:480–487 — meta-analysis of anticoagulation versus none in cirrhotic PVT. Platelets under 50,000 weigh against it.
  • Which drug. LMWH, weight-based, is the usual starter — once daily when creatinine clearance is under 30; anti-Xa levels read low in cirrhosis because the assay needs antithrombin, so do not chase them. Vitamin K antagonists work, but the INR is a poor guide from a baseline of 1.5. DOACs: AASLD 2021 and AGA 2025 accept them in Child-Pugh A and selected B, never in C (Baveno VII adds caution below a creatinine clearance of 30); ACG 2020 avoids them in B too, as do rivaroxaban's and apixaban's own labels.
  • How long. At least 6 months, reimaging every 3 months (AGA); until transplant in candidates; indefinite after SMV involvement or a prothrombotic disorder. In the others, continuing after recanalisation is a case-by-case weighing of recurrence — common after stopping — against bleeding; a thrombus unmoved after 6 months is a reason to stop.
  • TIPS when anticoagulation fails or is contraindicated, and first choice with a second indication — refractory ascites or recurrent variceal bleeding; recanalisation through the TIPS can restore transplant candidacy.
  • Prevention is not practice. Prophylactic enoxaparin in one small open-label trial prevented PVT and, unexpectedly, decompensationTrialVilla E, et al. Gastroenterology 2012;143:1253–1260 — enoxaparin 4000 IU daily prevented PVT and decompensation; the placebo-controlled sequel, rivaroxaban 10 mg in Child-Pugh 7–10, missed its primary endpoint with more than double the non-portal-hypertensive bleedingTrialCIRROXABAN — Puente Á, et al. J Hepatol 2025;83:1069–1076 — rivaroxaban versus placebo to prevent portal hypertensive complications. No guideline recommends it outside a trial.
Non-cirrhotic portal vein thrombosis — acute and chronic
  • Acute: days of abdominal pain, fever and ileus with near-normal liver tests because the liver is healthy; contrast CT makes the diagnosis and maps the extent. Look for a local cause — pancreatitis, intra-abdominal infection, abdominal surgery (splenectomy above all), trauma, an occult HCC — and a systemic one: the Budd-Chiari list, MPN and JAK2 V617F again at the top. Bacteraemia from an abdominal source makes it septic pylephlebitis: weeks of antibiotics, drain any abscess. Splenic vein thrombosis alone, after pancreatitis, gives isolated gastric varices — left-sided portal hypertension, cured by splenectomy (the portal hypertension topic).
  • Anticoagulate at once, for at least 6 months (LMWH, then a vitamin K antagonist or, increasingly, a DOAC — not in antiphospholipid syndrome): started early, roughly 40% of portal trunks reopen and the splenic and mesenteric veins do better. Go indefinite with a permanent prothrombotic condition, past intestinal ischaemia or recurrent thrombosis; many centres also continue when the SMV was involved. Reimage with contrast CT at about 6 months — a vein still closed by then will not reopen.
  • Intestinal ischaemia is the emergency. With the SMV involved, worsening pain, rectal bleeding, rising lactate, or bowel wall thickening and pneumatosis on CT mean venous infarction — surgical review now. Catheter-directed thrombolysis is for the patient deteriorating on anticoagulation without established infarction, in a centre that does it, because its bleeding complications are frequent; the mesenteric ischaemia topic covers the arterial side.
  • Chronic means a cavernoma of periportal collaterals has replaced the vein, which takes only weeks: portal hypertension with a normal liver — varices and splenomegaly, preserved synthetic function, little ascites. Screen for and treat varices as in cirrhosis; bleeds are tolerated better because the liver works. Anticoagulate long-term only for a permanent prothrombotic state (above all an MPN) or past intestinal ischaemia. Portal biliopathy — bile ducts compressed by the cavernoma, symptomatic in a minority — is treated endoscopically, with portal decompression if it keeps recurring; never let a surgeon explore the duct through a cavernoma. The mimic is porto-sinusoidal vascular disorder — portal hypertension with a patent portal vein and a non-cirrhotic biopsy — which itself predisposes to PVT.
Sinusoidal obstruction, ischaemic hepatitis and congestive hepatopathy
  • Sinusoidal obstruction syndrome (veno-occlusive disease): toxic injury to the sinusoidal endothelium after myeloablative conditioning for HSCT, oxaliplatin, inotuzumab ozogamicin or pyrrolizidine alkaloids. Usually within three weeks of transplant — the Baltimore criteria are bilirubin ≥2 mg/dL by day 21 plus two of painful hepatomegaly, weight gain over 5% and ascites — but the EBMT criteria (2016, refined 2023) recognise late-onset disease after day 21 and grade severity by the speed of the bilirubin rise, transaminases, weight gain and kidney function. Doppler shows patent hepatic veins and, when severe, reversed portal flow. With multi-organ failure most die; defibrotide 6.25 mg/kg IV every 6 hours for at least 21 days is the only approved treatmentTrialRichardson PG, et al. Blood 2016;127:1656–1665 — defibrotide in severe SOS with multi-organ failure.
  • Ischaemic hepatitis ("shock liver"): transaminases in the thousands with a high LDH a day or two after shock, sepsis, respiratory failure or an arrhythmia, usually in an already congested liver. ALT:LDH below 1.5 favours ischaemia over viral hepatitis; the enzymes normalise within a week or two. Restore perfusion and oxygen, check a paracetamol level; the mortality belongs to the cause.
  • Congestive hepatopathy — right heart failure, tricuspid regurgitation, constrictive pericarditis or a Fontan circulation: mild cholestasis, high-SAAG high-protein ascites like Budd-Chiari, dilated hepatic veins and IVC with "nutmeg" enhancement. Years of it produce cardiac cirrhosis, and Fontan-associated liver disease earns HCC surveillance. Treat the heart.
Numbers to know
  • MPN in about 40% of Budd-Chiari and a third of non-cirrhotic PVT · stepwise treatment: 77% of 157 alive at a median of 50 months (EN-Vie)
  • Recent PVT = within 6 months · treat a recent trunk thrombus at >50% of the lumen · anticoagulate for at least 6 months · reimage every 3 months · recanalisation 71% vs 42% with bleeding 11% in both groups
  • Ascitic protein in Budd-Chiari and cardiac ascites >2.5 g/dL with SAAG ≥1.1 · defibrotide 6.25 mg/kg every 6 h for ≥21 days · ischaemic hepatitis ALT:LDH <1.5
PitfallTwo mistakes in opposite directions. Anticoagulating a tumour thrombus — the "clot" that enhances, expands the vein and comes with an AFP in the hundreds is HCC, and heparin only makes it bleed. And withholding anticoagulation because the INR is 1.8 and the platelets are 90 — that patient is not auto-anticoagulated, and a recent occlusive thrombus in a transplant candidate is exactly who the guidance says to treat once the varices are covered.
On rounds, sayShe's 58 with Child-Pugh B8 alcohol-related cirrhosis, listed for transplant, and the surveillance MRI shows a thrombus filling most of the main portal vein and reaching the SMV confluence. It doesn't enhance, the vein isn't expanded and her AFP is 3, so it's bland clot, and it wasn't on the scan six months ago, so it's recent. Recent, more than 50% of the trunk, heading into the SMV, in a transplant candidate — four separate reasons to anticoagulate. Her last scope showed small varices, so I'd start carvedilol today, get her scoped this week to be sure nothing needs banding, and begin weight-based enoxaparin straight after — she's Child B, so I'm not reaching for rivaroxaban. Then reimage at three months and keep her anticoagulated until she's transplanted.

Ascites and spontaneous bacterial peritonitis

AASLD guidance on ascites and SBP · practice synthesis

InsideSAAG = serum albumin − ascitic albuminManagementAvoid NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, and ARBsRefractory ascitesDiagnosis: ascitic PMN count ≥250/mm³Treat empirically with IV cefotaximeAlbumin 1.5 g/kg on day 1 and 1 g/kg on day 3

Fluid accumulating in the abdominal cavity, and the infection that develops within it. Both mark a decisive step down in prognosis and should prompt thoughts of transplantation.

Must know
  • Diagnostic paracentesis on every cirrhotic admitted with ascites. Coagulopathy is not a contraindication.
  • SAAG ≥1.1 = portal hypertension. Spironolactone:furosemide 100:40.
  • Ascitic PMN ≥250 = SBP. Treat empirically; albumin 1.5 g/kg day 1 and 1 g/kg day 3.
  • LVP >5 L → 6–8 g albumin per litre removed. Secondary SBP prophylaxis is lifelong.

AbbreviationsAKI acute kidney injury · HRS hepatorenal syndrome · LVP large-volume paracentesis · PMN polymorphonuclear neutrophil · SAAG serum-ascites albumin gradient · SBP spontaneous bacterial peritonitis · TIPS transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt

Full detail
  • Diagnostic paracentesis on every cirrhotic admitted with ascites, regardless of the reason for admission. Coagulopathy is not a contraindication and routine plasma/platelet transfusion before paracentesis is not indicated.
  • SAAG = serum albumin − ascitic albumin. ≥1.1 g/dL = portal hypertension (cirrhosis, heart failure, Budd-Chiari, portal vein thrombosis). <1.1 = non-portal (peritoneal carcinomatosis, tuberculosis, pancreatic, nephrotic). Add ascitic total protein: >2.5 g/dL with a high SAAG points to cardiac ascites.
  • Management: sodium restriction to 2 g/day, and spironolactone:furosemide in a 100:40 ratio titrated together to preserve potassium balance. Fluid restriction only for sodium <125.
  • Large-volume paracentesis >5 L → albumin 6–8 g per liter removed to prevent post-paracentesis circulatory dysfunction.
  • Avoid NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, and ARBs in patients with ascites — they precipitate AKI.
  • Refractory ascites: serial LVP or TIPS. Consider transplant evaluation — refractory ascites carries roughly 50% one-year mortality.
SBP
  • Diagnosis: ascitic PMN count ≥250/mm³. Inoculate culture bottles at the bedside to improve yield.
  • Treat empirically with IV cefotaxime (or ceftriaxone) — do not wait for cultures.
  • Albumin 1.5 g/kg on day 1 and 1 g/kg on day 3 reduces HRS and mortalityTrialSort P, et al. NEJM 1999;341:403–409 — the albumin-in-SBP paper flagged in your syllabus. Indicated when creatinine >1 mg/dL, BUN >30 mg/dL, or total bilirubin >4 mg/dL — many services simply give it to everyone with SBP.
  • Secondary prophylaxis after an episode of SBP is lifelong — daily norfloxacin, ciprofloxacin, or TMP-SMX, until transplant.
  • Primary prophylaxis for ascitic fluid protein <1.5 g/dL with advanced liver or renal dysfunction, and for 7 days after any GI bleed (ceftriaxone).
