  • Secondary bacterial peritonitis — suspect with polymicrobial culture, PMN in the thousands, and ascitic protein >1 g/dL with glucose <50 and LDH above serum. That patient needs imaging and surgery, not just antibiotics.
On rounds, sayPMN count is 380, so this is SBP — I'd start ceftriaxone now rather than waiting on culture, give albumin at 1.5 grams per kilo today and 1 gram per kilo on day 3, and once he's through this he needs lifelong secondary prophylaxis.

Hepatorenal syndrome — AKI

AASLD guidance · ICA criteria · FDA approval of terlipressin 2022

InsideHRS-AKIAlways look for a precipitant firstTerlipressin plus albuminNorepinephrine plus albuminMidodrine + octreotide + albuminRefer for liver transplantation

Kidney failure caused by the circulatory collapse of advanced liver disease, in kidneys that are structurally entirely normal. It is a diagnosis of exclusion with a specific treatment.

Must know
  • Requires no improvement after 2 days of albumin 1 g/kg with diuretics withdrawn, no shock, no structural kidney disease.
  • Always hunt the precipitant — SBP, bleeding, over-diuresis, NSAIDs.
  • Terlipressin plus albumin is first-line (watch respiratory failure); norepinephrine is the ICU alternative.

AbbreviationsACLF acute-on-chronic liver failure · AKI acute kidney injury · HRS hepatorenal syndrome · ICA International Club of Ascites · SBP spontaneous bacterial peritonitis

Full detail
  • HRS-AKI replaced "type 1 HRS." Diagnosis requires: cirrhosis with ascites, AKI by ICA criteria, no improvement after 2 days of diuretic withdrawal plus albumin 1 g/kg/day, absence of shock, no recent nephrotoxins, and no structural kidney injury (no significant proteinuria, hematuria, or abnormal renal ultrasound).
  • Always look for a precipitant first — SBP, GI bleeding, over-diuresis, large-volume paracentesis without albumin, NSAIDs, contrast, sepsis.
  • Terlipressin plus albumin is now FDA-approved and is first-line in the US.TrialCONFIRM — Wong F, et al. NEJM 2021;384:818–828 Watch for respiratory failure — the boxed warning — and avoid in patients with hypoxia or ACLF grade 3.
  • Norepinephrine plus albumin in an ICU setting is an effective alternative.
  • Midodrine + octreotide + albumin is the least effective of the three; use it only when the others aren't available.
  • Refer for liver transplantation — that is the definitive therapy. Dialysis is a bridge.

Hepatic encephalopathy — the newest ACG guideline

ACG Clinical Guideline, Bajaj et al., Am J Gastroenterol 2026;121:588–618 (March 2026) — 24 recommendations

InsideAmmoniaCovert and minimal HEInpatient management of overt HEPreventing recurrenceNutrition and sarcopeniaTIPS and transplant

Reversible brain dysfunction caused by liver failure and by blood bypassing the liver. Ranges from subtle inattention to coma.

Must know
  • Do not trend serum ammonia — the 2026 guideline suggests against using it to guide treatment.
  • Do not restrict protein. Target 1.2–1.5 g/kg/day, plus a late-night snack.
  • Lactulose titrated to 2–3 soft stools daily; add rifaximin for acute overt HE and for recurrence.
  • Rifaximin 14 days before elective TIPS, continued ≥6 months.

AbbreviationsHE hepatic encephalopathy · MELD Model for End-Stage Liver Disease · TIPS transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt

Full detail

This guideline landed in March 2026 and contains several statements that contradict common ward practice. Knowing them is the fastest way to demonstrate you're reading current literature.

Ammonia
  • Do not use serum ammonia alone to diagnose minimal or covert HE.
  • Do not routinely check ammonia to guide treatment decisions in patients with HE. Trending ammonia daily is a habit the guideline explicitly discourages.
Covert and minimal HE
  • A single-test strategy is suggested over a two-test combination for diagnosis.
  • Lactulose is suggested over no treatment for minimal/covert HE, though evidence is insufficient to recommend routine treatment specifically to prevent overt HE.
Inpatient management of overt HE
  • Lactulose is recommended to improve outcomes and prevent recurrence.
  • High-volume polyethylene glycol is suggested as an alternative to lactulose — a useful option that many residents don't know is guideline-supported.
  • Add rifaximin to lactulose in acute overt HE, rather than lactulose alone.
  • Do not routinely obtain brain imaging in a cirrhotic patient with confusion and no new focal neurologic deficit.
Preventing recurrence
  • After a first episode of overt HE: lactulose titrated to 2–3 soft bowel movements per day as outpatient first-line.TrialSharma BC, et al. Gastroenterology 2009;137:885–891 — lactulose for secondary prophylaxis
  • Use the Bristol Stool Scale together with stool frequency to titrate lactulose — this reduces readmissions.
  • Rifaximin in the outpatient setting to prevent recurrenceTrialBass NM, et al. NEJM 2010;362:1071–1081 — rifaximin maintained remission and reduced HE-related hospitalisation; add rifaximin for anyone recurring on lactulose maintenance.
  • Zinc supplementation in patients with persistent symptoms despite lactulose and rifaximin who have low blood zinc.
  • Shunt embolization for refractory HE on optimized therapy with adequate hepatic function.
Nutrition and sarcopenia
  • Protein target 1.2–1.5 g/kg/day. Do not restrict protein — it increases muscle breakdown and does not shorten HE.
  • Branched-chain amino acid supplementation when protein needs can't be met with food.
  • Late-night snack to reduce frailty and HE.
  • Exercise — reduces falls, lowers portal pressure, and increases skeletal muscle capacity for ammonia metabolism.
TIPS and transplant
  • Start rifaximin 14 days before elective TIPS and continue at least 6 months in decompensated cirrhosis, with or without prior overt HE.
  • Embolize extrahepatic collaterals at the time of TIPS to reduce post-TIPS HE.
  • Multiple HE episodes with MELD <15 → evaluate for living donor liver transplantation, since MELD alone under-prioritizes these patients.
On rounds, sayI wouldn't trend the ammonia — the 2026 ACG guideline suggests against using it to guide treatment. He's on lactulose titrated to two or three soft stools a day, I'd add rifaximin now given this is a recurrence, and we should stop restricting his protein and target 1.2 to 1.5 grams per kilogram instead.

Cirrhosis: scoring, surveillance, and the things that get missed

MELD 3.0 (2023) · AASLD HCC guidance · ACG Perioperative Risk in Cirrhosis, Mahmud et al., 2025

InsideChild-PughMELD 3.0VaccinateScreen for varicesAvoidPerioperative risk (ACG 2025)

End-stage scarring of the liver. This topic covers how it is scored, what surveillance it earns, and the things that routinely get missed.

Must know
  • HCC surveillance: ultrasound ± AFP every 6 months.
  • Acetaminophen up to 2 g/day is preferred over NSAIDs — most people get this backwards.
  • INR does not predict bleeding in cirrhosis. Don't correct it reflexively; do give VTE prophylaxis.

AbbreviationsAFP alpha-fetoprotein · CSPH clinically significant portal hypertension · HCC hepatocellular carcinoma · INR international normalised ratio · MELD Model for End-Stage Liver Disease · VTE venous thromboembolism

Full detail
  • Child-Pugh — bilirubin, albumin, INR, ascites, encephalopathy. Class A 5–6, B 7–9, C 10–15.
  • MELD 3.0 is the current allocation score: creatinine, bilirubin, INR, sodium, albumin, and female sex — the last two added to correct a documented disadvantage for women on the waitlist.
  • HCC surveillance: abdominal ultrasound ± AFP every 6 months in all patients with cirrhosis, and in selected non-cirrhotic hepatitis B carriers. Use CT or MRI if ultrasound is inadequate (obesity, nodular liver).
  • Vaccinate: hepatitis A and B, pneumococcal, annual influenza, COVID-19.
  • Screen for varices per Baveno VII; screen for osteoporosis; screen for depression.
  • Avoid: NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, and unnecessary sedatives. Acetaminophen up to 2 g/day is safe in cirrhosis and is preferred over NSAIDs — patients and clinicians both get this backwards.
  • Perioperative risk (ACG 2025): use the VOCAL-Penn score rather than Child-Pugh or MELD alone for surgical risk prediction; it outperforms the older tools. Assess for CSPH before elective abdominal surgery.
  • The INR in cirrhosis does not predict bleeding. These patients have rebalanced hemostasis with reduced pro- and anticoagulant factors and are at real risk of thrombosis — including portal vein thrombosis. Do not correct INR before procedures reflexively, and do give VTE prophylaxis when indicated.

Hepatocellular carcinoma — stage the tumour, the liver and the patient, then match the treatment

AASLD Practice Guidance on Prevention, Diagnosis, and Treatment of Hepatocellular Carcinoma, Singal AG et al., Hepatology 2023;78:1922–1965 · AASLD Critical Update to the HCC guidance, Hepatology 2025 · BCLC strategy for prognosis prediction and treatment recommendation: the 2022 update, Reig M et al., J Hepatol 2022;76:681–693, and the 2026 update, Reig M et al., J Hepatol 2026 · EASL Clinical Practice Guidelines on the management of hepatocellular carcinoma, J Hepatol 2025 · ACR LI-RADS CT/MRI v2018 · Mazzaferro V, et al. NEJM 1996;334:693–699 · IMbrave150, Finn RS et al., NEJM 2020 · HIMALAYA, Abou-Alfa GK et al., NEJM Evid 2022 · CheckMate 9DW, Yau T et al., Lancet 2025

InsideDiagnosis: LI-RADS and when to biopsyStaging: BCLC and stage migrationCurative options: ablation, resection, transplantLocoregional therapy: TACE, Y-90, SBRTSystemic therapy: first and second lineNon-cirrhotic HCC and fibrolamellar carcinoma

The commonest primary liver cancer, and one that grows almost always out of cirrhosis or chronic hepatitis B. It is unusual among cancers in that the liver disease underneath decides the treatment as much as the tumour does: a patient can die of the cirrhosis before the cancer matters, and a curative operation can tip a borderline liver into failure. Staging therefore weighs three things at once — tumour burden, liver function and how well the patient is — and every stage maps to a treatment.

Must know
  • LR-5 on multiphase CT or MRI is HCC without a biopsy. LR-M, LR-TIV, an LR-4 whose result would change management, and a mass in a non-cirrhotic liver that imaging cannot call benign (haemangioma and focal nodular hyperplasia are imaging diagnoses) need tissue.
  • BCLC stages 0–D combine tumour burden, liver function and performance status, and each maps to a treatment: ablation or resection for 0/A, transplant within Milan, TACE for B, systemic therapy for C, supportive care for D.
  • Milan criteria: one tumour ≤5 cm, or up to three each ≤3 cm, no vascular invasion, no spread. Transplant within Milan gives 5-year survival of roughly 70% and treats the cirrhosis as well.
  • First-line systemic therapy is an immunotherapy doublet: atezolizumab–bevacizumab (median survival 19.2 vs 13.4 months with sorafenib) after an endoscopy with varices treated; durvalumab–tremelimumab or nivolumab–ipilimumab when the bleeding risk is high; sorafenib or lenvatinib when immunotherapy is contraindicated.

AbbreviationsAFP alpha-fetoprotein · ALBI albumin–bilirubin grade · anti-HBc hepatitis B core antibody · BCLC Barcelona Clinic Liver Cancer · CSPH clinically significant portal hypertension · CT computed tomography · CTLA-4 cytotoxic T-lymphocyte-associated antigen 4 · ECOG Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status · EGD oesophagogastroduodenoscopy · HBsAg hepatitis B surface antigen · HCC hepatocellular carcinoma · HVPG hepatic venous pressure gradient · LI-RADS Liver Imaging Reporting and Data System · LR-TR LI-RADS treatment response · MASLD metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease · MELD Model for End-Stage Liver Disease · MMaT median MELD at transplant · mRECIST modified Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors · MRI magnetic resonance imaging · MWA microwave ablation · OPTN Organ Procurement and Transplantation Network · PD-1/PD-L1 programmed death-1 / programmed death-ligand 1 · RFA radiofrequency ablation · SBRT stereotactic body radiotherapy · TACE transarterial chemoembolisation · TARE transarterial radioembolisation · TKI tyrosine kinase inhibitor · VEGF vascular endothelial growth factor · Y-90 yttrium-90

Full detail
Diagnosis: LI-RADS and when to biopsy

Surveillance is in the cirrhosis topic and the no-biopsy rule in the focal liver lesion topic; LI-RADS puts numbers on that rule. It applies only to cirrhosis, chronic hepatitis B and a prior HCC — not to cirrhosis from Budd-Chiari or cardiac congestion, where benign hypervascular nodules mimic cancer.

  • LR-5 (definitely HCC): ≥20 mm with non-rim arterial hyperenhancement plus washout, an enhancing capsule or threshold growth (≥50% in 6 months); or 10–19 mm with hyperenhancement plus washout or threshold growth — a capsule alone at that size is only LR-4. Positive predictive value around 94%: treat, list, never biopsy.
  • LR-4 (about three-quarters HCC): repeat imaging within 3 months, biopsy, or treat after tumour-board review — biopsy when the answer changes the plan, because LR-4 earns no transplant exception points. LR-3 (about a third HCC): repeat in 3–6 months.
  • LR-M (rim enhancement, peripheral washout, a targetoid look): mostly cholangiocarcinoma or metastasis. Biopsy, because cholangiocarcinoma removes transplant candidacy.
  • LR-TIV (tumour in vein): an enhancing, expanding thrombus contiguous with a tumour is macrovascular invasion, BCLC C — but cholangiocarcinoma invades veins too, so AASLD advises a biopsy before committing to systemic therapy. Bland thrombus neither enhances nor precludes transplant.

AFP is not a diagnostic test: it supports the diagnosis above 400 ng/mL, selects for ramucirumab, and above 1000 ng/mL blocks MELD exception unless treatment brings it under 500. Staging adds a chest CT, Child-Pugh and MELD, ECOG status, an EGD if resection or bevacizumab is on the table, and HBsAg with anti-HBc — doxorubicin, TKIs and checkpoint blockade all reactivate hepatitis B, so an HBsAg-positive patient starts entecavir or tenofovir before the first treatment, not after.

Staging: BCLC and stage migration

BCLC stages by three axes at once and attaches a treatment to each stage. It dropped "Child-Pugh A" for "preserved liver function" in 2018; the 2022 update spells out how to judge it (Child-Pugh, MELD, ALBI grade, bilirubin), and any decompensation means function is not preserved whatever the score, because an A7 patient with a low albumin does not tolerate treatment the way an A5 patient does.

StageTumour burdenLiver functionECOGFirst-line treatmentExpected survival
0 — very earlySingle ≤2 cmPreserved0Ablation; resection if ablation is not feasible>5 years
A — earlySingle, any size; or up to three each ≤3 cmPreserved0Single: resection if no CSPH and normal bilirubin, otherwise ablation (≤3 cm) or transplant. Two or three: transplant if a candidate, otherwise ablation>5 years
B — intermediateMultinodular, no vascular invasion or spreadPreserved0Within extended transplant criteria → transplant; well-defined nodules → TACE (or TARE); diffuse or extensive bilobar → systemic therapy>2.5 years
C — advancedPortal vein invasion, extrahepatic spread, or cancer-related symptomsPreserved1–2Atezolizumab–bevacizumab, durvalumab–tremelimumab or nivolumab–ipilimumab; sorafenib or lenvatinib if immunotherapy is contraindicated>2 years
D — terminalAnyEnd-stage, not a transplant candidate3–4Best supportive careMonths, not years

Cancer-related symptoms (ECOG 1–2 from the tumour, not the cirrhosis) make a patient BCLC C whatever the burden. When the treatment for a stage is not feasible — a stage A tumour that cannot be ablated, a stage B patient whose TACE has failed — move to the next stage's treatment (treatment stage migration) rather than force the wrong one. Every new HCC goes to the multidisciplinary tumour board; treat the cause too, because antivirals for hepatitis B reduce recurrence.

Curative options: ablation, resection, transplant
  • Ablation (RFA or MWA) is the treatment for stage 0 and for stage A tumours that cannot be resected. It works best up to 3 cm: below 2 cm complete necrosis is the rule and survival matches resection; above 3 cm local recurrence climbs. Tumours against bowel, the gallbladder or the hilum go to SBRT, radiation segmentectomy or surgery.
  • Resection is for a single tumour with preserved function, no CSPH and a normal bilirubin — CSPH meaning an HVPG ≥10 mmHg, a liver stiffness ≥25 kPa, or in practice platelets under 100 with varices or splenomegaly; operating through portal hypertension buys tumour control at the price of decompensation. Recurrence reaches 50–70% by 5 years, and no adjuvant therapy has a durable benefit — sorafenib failed in STORM, and the early signal with atezolizumab–bevacizumab in IMbrave050 faded with follow-up, so AASLD withdrew it in 2025.
  • Transplantation removes the cancer and the organ that made it. Within the Milan criteria — one tumour ≤5 cm, or up to three each ≤3 cm, no macrovascular invasion, no extrahepatic disease — 5-year survival is around 70% with recurrence under 15%. TrialMazzaferro V, et al. NEJM 1996;334:693–699 — the Milan criteria
  • MELD exception: HCC does not raise the MELD score, so OPTN grants exception points after a 6-month wait — the delay weeds out aggressive biology — set at the median MELD at transplant within 250 nautical miles of the listing hospital, minus 3 (MMaT−3). Only T2 tumours qualify (one lesion 2–5 cm, or two or three each 1–3 cm), so a single tumour under 2 cm is within Milan but earns no points. Downstaging: beyond Milan but within the OPTN limits — one tumour >5 and ≤8 cm; two or three each ≤5 cm; or four or five each ≤3 cm, the multinodular groups with a sum of diameters ≤8 cm — treat with TACE, TARE or ablation and, if the tumour comes inside Milan and stays there, list with exception; roughly two-thirds succeed. Bridge when the expected wait exceeds 6 months.
Locoregional therapy: TACE, Y-90, SBRT
  • TACE injects doxorubicin and embolises the feeding artery as selectively as possible. TrialLlovet JM, et al. Lancet 2002;359:1734–1739 — chemoembolisation improved survival in unresectable HCC Contraindications: decompensated cirrhosis, main portal vein thrombosis (the liver then depends on its artery), extrahepatic disease, biliary obstruction. Repeat on demand, judged by viable enhancing tumour rather than size (mRECIST, or LR-TR on the radiology report), and stop when it is not working: two sessions without response, progression to vascular invasion or spread, or falling liver function is TACE refractoriness, and the answer is systemic therapy, not a third embolisation. Adding systemic therapy to TACE (EMERALD-1, LEAP-012) lengthened progression-free but not yet overall survival, so TACE alone remains the standard for stage B.
  • TARE (Y-90) delivers β-emitting microspheres through the hepatic artery. It is minimally embolic, so it can be given with branch portal vein invasion where TACE cannot, and as radiation segmentectomy it can ablate a solitary tumour a needle cannot reach safely — BCLC allows single tumours up to 8 cm on the LEGACY data. It did not beat sorafenib in advanced disease (SARAH, SIRveNIB), so it is not a substitute for systemic therapy in BCLC C.
  • SBRT gives a few high-dose fractions with local control above 90% in series — for tumours where ablation is anatomically unsafe, as bridging, and for tumour thrombus. The one randomised trial against ablation, in small recurrent HCC, gave better local control but the same survival; there is no phase 3 trial against TACE, and liver function can fall in Child-Pugh B.
Systemic therapy: first and second line

For BCLC C, and for BCLC B that is diffuse or has failed TACE, with preserved liver function and ECOG 0–1 — the drugs do not help a patient who is dying of cirrhosis. Three immunotherapy doublets are approved first line and none has been compared with another; the choice turns on bleeding risk and toxicity.

  • Atezolizumab plus bevacizumab (anti-PD-L1 plus anti-VEGF, every 3 weeks). TrialIMbrave150 — Finn RS, et al. NEJM 2020;382:1894–1905 — atezolizumab–bevacizumab beat sorafenib on survival and progression-free survival Median survival 19.2 vs 13.4 months in the updated analysis, objective response around 30%. Bevacizumab makes varices bleed, so IMbrave150 required an EGD within the preceding 6 months, with varices treated (banded, or a beta-blocker for small ones); AASLD asks for an EGD to find and treat high-risk varices before starting, and most centres keep the trial's window. Bleeding in the last 6 months, uncontrolled hypertension, recent arterial thrombosis or heavy proteinuria also rule bevacizumab out.
  • Durvalumab plus tremelimumab (STRIDE: a single priming dose of anti-CTLA-4 tremelimumab with durvalumab, then durvalumab alone every 4 weeks) is the other preferred option and the one to choose when the bleeding risk is high, since it has no anti-VEGF component. TrialHIMALAYA — Abou-Alfa GK, et al. NEJM Evid 2022;1:EVIDoa2100070 — single-dose tremelimumab plus durvalumab beat sorafenib on survival Median survival 16.4 vs 13.8 months; 3-year survival 30.7% vs 20.2%.
  • Nivolumab plus ipilimumab beat lenvatinib or sorafenib in CheckMate 9DW — median survival 23.7 vs 20.6 months, hazard ratio 0.79, response rate 36% vs 13% — and was FDA-approved first line in 2025. No anti-VEGF, so no endoscopy requirement, but dual checkpoint blockade carries the most immune-related toxicity of the three.
  • When immunotherapy is contraindicated — active autoimmune disease needing systemic treatment, an organ transplant (PD-1/PD-L1 blockade causes graft rejection) — use a TKI. Sorafenib was the first drug to prolong survival in HCC, by under 3 months. TrialSHARP — Llovet JM, et al. NEJM 2008;359:378–390 — the first systemic agent to prolong survival in HCC Lenvatinib (12 mg daily at 60 kg or more, 8 mg below) was non-inferior to sorafenib in REFLECT with more responses and is usually preferred. Selected Child-Pugh B7 patients get a single agent — a TKI, or anti-PD-1/PD-L1 alone (durvalumab by itself was non-inferior to sorafenib in HIMALAYA) — after tumour-board discussion.
  • Second line after sorafenib, each adding one to three months: regorafenib (RESORCE, 10.6 vs 7.8 months; only if sorafenib was tolerated), cabozantinib (CELESTIAL, 10.2 vs 8.0) and ramucirumab (REACH-2, 8.5 vs 7.3; only for AFP ≥400 ng/mL); pembrolizumab and nivolumab–ipilimumab also hold approvals here. After atezolizumab–bevacizumab the one phase 3 trial, IMbrave251, found that continuing atezolizumab alongside a TKI did not improve survival over the TKI alone, so practice — and the AASLD guidance — is sorafenib or lenvatinib, then one of the above; nivolumab–ipilimumab if a TKI is unsuitable.
Non-cirrhotic HCC and fibrolamellar carcinoma
  • HCC in a non-cirrhotic liver — perhaps one in five HCCs in Western series, more with MASLD — presents late and large because nobody was surveilling. LI-RADS does not apply: haemangioma and focal nodular hyperplasia are imaging diagnoses (focal liver lesion topic); biopsy what imaging cannot call benign. A normal liver tolerates a major hepatectomy, so resection is the mainstay even for big tumours.
  • Fibrolamellar carcinoma: adolescents and young adults, no cirrhosis, a normal AFP, defined by the DNAJB1–PRKACA fusion. A large mass with a central scar can be mistaken for focal nodular hyperplasia; nodal metastases are common. Resection with regional lymphadenectomy, repeated for recurrence; no established systemic regimen.

After any curative or locoregional treatment, re-image with multiphase CT or MRI every 3–6 months for 2 years, when most recurrence happens, then return to 6-monthly surveillance.

Numbers to know
  • Milan: one tumour ≤5 cm or up to three each ≤3 cm · 5-year survival after transplant ~70% · MELD exception after 6 months at MMaT−3, T2 tumours only · AFP >1000 ng/mL blocks it unless it falls below 500
  • Ablation works best up to 3 cm · resection needs no CSPH (HVPG <10 mmHg, liver stiffness <25 kPa) and a normal bilirubin · recurrence after resection 50–70% at 5 years
  • Median survival — IMbrave150 19.2 vs 13.4 months · HIMALAYA 16.4 vs 13.8 · CheckMate 9DW 23.7 vs 20.6 · SHARP 10.7 vs 7.9 · TACE (Llovet 2002) 2-year survival 63% vs 27%
  • Bevacizumab: EGD within 6 months and varices treated first · ramucirumab only if AFP ≥400 ng/mL · lenvatinib 12 mg at ≥60 kg, 8 mg below
PitfallChild-Pugh A on paper is not a liver that will survive treatment: an A7 patient with an albumin of 2.8 g/dL, a bilirubin of 1.9 mg/dL and small varices belongs at the tumour board before any resection or TACE. The mirror-image error is calling a Child-Pugh C patient with a 3 cm HCC "BCLC D, supportive care" — he is inside Milan, the transplant cures both problems, and he needs a referral. And never start bevacizumab without an endoscopy in the last 6 months.
On rounds, sayShe's a 64-year-old with hepatitis C cirrhosis, Child-Pugh A6, ECOG 0, and the MRI shows a single 4 cm LR-5 lesion in segment 6 with no vascular invasion and a clear chest CT, so this is BCLC A. Her platelets are 80 and she has small varices — that's clinically significant portal hypertension, so I wouldn't resect; she'd decompensate. She's within Milan and it's a T2 tumour, so I'd refer her for transplant evaluation today; after 6 months on the list she'll get exception points at the median MELD at transplant within 250 nautical miles of our centre, minus 3. At 4 cm ablation alone is unreliable, so I'd bridge with TACE while she waits and re-image every 3 months. Her AFP is 60, well under the 1000 that would block the exception, her hepatitis B serology is negative, and I'll present her at tumour board on Thursday.

Drug-induced liver injury

ACG Clinical Guideline, Chalasani et al., Am J Gastroenterol 2021;116:878–898

InsideR value = (ALT ÷ ULN) ÷ (ALP ÷ ULN)Hy's LawTake a full supplement historyAcetaminophen

Liver injury caused by a drug, herb or supplement. Always a diagnosis of exclusion, and the supplement history is the part most often skipped.

Must know
  • Calculate the R value: ≥5 hepatocellular, ≤2 cholestatic.
  • Hy's Law — ALT >3× ULN with bilirubin >2× ULN — predicts ~10% mortality.
  • Take a full supplement history. Amoxicillin-clavulanate is the commonest prescription cause.

AbbreviationsALP alkaline phosphatase · ALT alanine aminotransferase · DILI drug-induced liver injury · NAC N-acetylcysteine · RUCAM Roussel Uclaf Causality Assessment Method · ULN upper limit of normal

Full detail
  • R value = (ALT ÷ ULN) ÷ (ALP ÷ ULN). ≥5 hepatocellular, ≤2 cholestatic, 2–5 mixed. Calculate it — it's a one-line way to look organized.
  • Hy's Law: hepatocellular injury with ALT >3× ULN and total bilirubin >2× ULN without significant cholestasis predicts roughly 10% mortality or need for transplant. This is the finding that should raise your alarm level.
  • DILI is a diagnosis of exclusion — rule out viral hepatitis (including hepatitis E), autoimmune hepatitis, biliary obstruction, and ischemia first. RUCAM provides structure.
  • Take a full supplement history. Herbal and dietary supplements now account for a large and growing share of US DILI: green tea extract, garcinia cambogia, ashwagandha, turmeric/curcumin, kava, anabolic androgenic steroids, and multi-ingredient bodybuilding products.
  • Classic culprits: amoxicillin-clavulanate (the most commonly implicated prescription drug in the US), isoniazid, nitrofurantoin, minocycline, azathioprine, methotrexate, allopurinol, and immune checkpoint inhibitors.
  • Acetaminophen: N-acetylcysteine, guided by the Rumack-Matthew nomogram for single acute ingestion. Chronic staggered overdose in a malnourished or alcohol-using patient can be toxic at "therapeutic" doses.
  • NAC is also recommended in non-acetaminophen acute liver failure in adults.TrialLee WM, et al. Gastroenterology 2009;137:856–864 — improved transplant-free survival in early-stage coma
  • Corticosteroids for DILI with autoimmune features or checkpoint-inhibitor hepatitis; otherwise the treatment is withdrawal of the agent and supportive care.

Autoimmune and cholestatic liver disease

ACG PSC Guideline 2015 · AASLD PBC and AIH guidance · FDA approvals 2024

InsideAutoimmune hepatitisPrimary biliary cholangitisPrimary sclerosing cholangitis

Three immune-mediated liver diseases — autoimmune hepatitis attacking hepatocytes, and PBC and PSC attacking bile ducts.

Must know
  • PBC: UDCA 13–15 mg/kg, response assessed at 12 months; elafibranor and seladelpar (2024) are now the second-line drugs — obeticholic acid was withdrawn from the market in 2025.
  • High-dose UDCA is harmful in PSC.
  • PSC needs annual colonoscopy and annual MRI/MRCP with CA 19-9.

AbbreviationsAIH autoimmune hepatitis · ALP alkaline phosphatase · AMA anti-mitochondrial antibody · ANA antinuclear antibody · CRC colorectal cancer · ERCP endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography · IBD inflammatory bowel disease · MRCP magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography · PBC primary biliary cholangitis · PPAR peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor · PSC primary sclerosing cholangitis · TPMT thiopurine methyltransferase · UDCA ursodeoxycholic acid

Full detail
Autoimmune hepatitis
  • Female predominance, elevated IgG, ANA and/or anti-smooth muscle antibody (type 1), anti-LKM-1 (type 2). Interface hepatitis with plasma cells on biopsy.
  • Can present as acute liver failure; a normal ANA doesn't exclude it.
  • Prednisone (or prednisolone) plus azathioprine; budesonide is an alternative in non-cirrhotic patients. Check TPMT before azathioprine. Long taper; relapse on withdrawal is common.
Primary biliary cholangitis
  • Middle-aged women, fatigue and pruritus, cholestatic pattern, anti-mitochondrial antibody in ~95%. Biopsy is not needed if ALP is elevated and AMA is positive.
  • Ursodeoxycholic acid 13–15 mg/kg/day is first-line. Assess biochemical response at 12 months (Paris/POISE criteria — roughly ALP normalization or near-normalization).
  • Second-line, for inadequate UDCA response: the PPAR agonists elafibranor and seladelpar, both given FDA accelerated approval in 2024; bezafibrate is the off-label alternativeTrialPOISE — Nevens F, et al. NEJM 2016;375:631–643 (obeticholic acid); ELATIVE — Kowdley KV, et al. NEJM 2024;390:795–805 (elafibranor); RESPONSE — Hirschfield GM, et al. NEJM 2024;390:783–794 (seladelpar). Obeticholic acid, the original second-line drug from POISE, is no longer available: the EU authorisation was revoked in 2024 and the US accelerated approval was withdrawn in September 2025 after the confirmatory trial failed to confirm clinical benefit — and it was in any case contraindicated in decompensated cirrhosis.
  • Pruritus ladder: cholestyramine (separate from other drugs by 4 hours), then rifampin, then naltrexone, then sertraline; bezafibrate has good data.
  • Monitor for osteoporosis and fat-soluble vitamin deficiency.
Primary sclerosing cholangitis
  • Men, often younger, strongly associated with IBD (usually ulcerative colitis with right-sided predominance and rectal sparing). MRCP shows multifocal strictures and beading.
  • Colonoscopy at PSC diagnosis and annually thereafter — the CRC risk in PSC-IBD is the highest of any IBD group.
  • Cholangiocarcinoma surveillance: annual MRI/MRCP with CA 19-9. Also raised gallbladder cancer risk — a gallbladder polyp in PSC generally means cholecystectomy.
  • Do not use high-dose UDCA (28–30 mg/kg) — it increased mortality and colorectal neoplasia in trialsTrialLindor KD, et al. Hepatology 2009;50:808–814; Eaton JE, et al. Am J Gastroenterol 2011;106:1638–1645. This is a real "know the harm" point.
  • Dominant strictures need ERCP with brushings to exclude malignancy. Liver transplantation is the only therapy that alters natural history.

Genetic and metabolic liver disease

ACG Hereditary Hemochromatosis Guideline, Kowdley et al., 2019 · practice synthesis

InsideHereditary hemochromatosisFerritin is an acute-phase reactantWilson diseaseα1-antitrypsin deficiency

Inherited disorders of iron, copper and protein handling that damage the liver. Individually rare, but worth knowing because several are treatable and one is curable.

Must know
  • Transferrin saturation >45% plus ferritin, then HFE genotyping.
  • Phlebotomy to a ferritin of 50–100.
  • Isolated high ferritin with normal saturation is inflammation, not iron overload. Consider Wilson under 40.

AbbreviationsHCC hepatocellular carcinoma · HFE the homeostatic iron regulator gene · MASLD metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease

Full detail
  • Hereditary hemochromatosis: screen with transferrin saturation >45% and ferritin. Confirm with HFE genotyping — C282Y homozygosity accounts for the majority. Penetrance is incomplete, so genotype alone doesn't equal disease.
  • Treatment is therapeutic phlebotomy to a ferritin target of 50–100 ng/mL, then maintenance. Chelation only if phlebotomy isn't tolerated. Screen first-degree relatives. HCC surveillance if cirrhotic.
  • Ferritin is an acute-phase reactant — an isolated high ferritin with a normal transferrin saturation is usually inflammation, MASLD, or alcohol, not iron overload.
  • Wilson disease: consider in anyone under 40 with unexplained liver disease, especially with neuropsychiatric features or Coombs-negative hemolytic anemia with a low alkaline phosphatase. Low ceruloplasmin, elevated 24-hour urinary copper, Kayser-Fleischer rings on slit lamp. Treat with chelation (penicillamine, trientine) or zinc.
  • α1-antitrypsin deficiency: PiZZ phenotype; liver disease plus early emphysema. Check level and phenotype, not just level (it's an acute-phase reactant).

Acute liver failure and focal liver lesions

ACG Acute Liver Failure Guideline, Shingina et al., 2023 · ACG Focal Liver Lesions Guideline, Frenette et al., 2024

InsideAcute liver failureFocal liver lesions

Two separate problems. Acute liver failure is sudden failure of a previously healthy liver — rare, lethal, and time-critical. Focal lesions are the incidental spots found on imaging.

Must know
  • ALF = INR ≥1.5 with any encephalopathy, <26 weeks, no pre-existing liver disease.
  • Call the transplant centre early, and give NAC in acetaminophen and non-acetaminophen ALF.
  • HCC needs no biopsy if a cirrhotic liver shows arterial hyperenhancement with washout.

AbbreviationsALF acute liver failure · HCC hepatocellular carcinoma · INR international normalised ratio · LI-RADS Liver Imaging Reporting and Data System · NAC N-acetylcysteine

Full detail
Acute liver failure
  • Definition: INR ≥1.5 with any degree of hepatic encephalopathy, illness <26 weeks, in a patient without pre-existing liver disease.
  • Contact a transplant center early — before the patient meets criteria, not after.
  • Acetaminophen is the leading US cause. Give N-acetylcysteine — in acetaminophen and in non-acetaminophen ALF.
  • King's College criteria for transplantation: acetaminophen — arterial pH <7.3, or the triad of INR >6.5, creatinine >3.4 mg/dL, and grade III–IV encephalopathy. Non-acetaminophen — INR >6.5, or any three of five adverse factors.
  • Cerebral edema is the leading cause of death: elevate the head of bed, avoid hypotonic fluids, treat with hypertonic saline or mannitol, and consider hypothermia. Avoid over-correcting coagulopathy — INR is your monitoring parameter.
Focal liver lesions
  • Hemangioma — the most common benign lesion; peripheral nodular discontinuous enhancement with centripetal fill-in. No follow-up needed once characterized.
  • Focal nodular hyperplasia — central scar, homogeneous arterial enhancement; a benign hyperplastic response, not neoplastic. No resection, no surveillance, oral contraceptives may be continued.
  • Hepatic adenoma — associated with estrogen exposure and anabolic steroids. Stop the OCP. Risk of hemorrhage and malignant transformation rises above 5 cm; resect lesions >5 cm, any adenoma in a man, and the β-catenin-activated subtype.
  • HCC — in a cirrhotic liver, arterial phase hyperenhancement with washout on multiphase CT or MRI is diagnostic (LI-RADS 5). Biopsy is not required — an important point, since biopsy carries a small seeding risk.

Liver disease in pregnancy — the trimester narrows the diagnosis, and delivery treats the dangerous ones

ACG Clinical Guideline: Liver Disease and Pregnancy, Tran TT, Ahn J, Reau NS, Am J Gastroenterol 2016;111:176–194 · AASLD Practice Guidance: Reproductive Health and Liver Disease, Sarkar M, et al., Hepatology 2021;73:318–365 · EASL Clinical Practice Guidelines on the management of liver diseases in pregnancy, J Hepatol 2023;79:768–828 · SMFM Consult Series #53, Lee RH, et al., Am J Obstet Gynecol 2021;224:B2–B9 · RCOG Green-top Guideline No. 43, Girling J, et al., BJOG 2022;129:e95–e114 · Swansea criteria, Ch'ng CL, et al., Gut 2002;51:876–880 · Ovadia C, et al., Lancet 2019;393:899–909 · PITCHES, Chappell LC, et al., Lancet 2019;394:849–860 · Ovadia C, et al., Lancet Gastroenterol Hepatol 2021;6:547–558 · AASLD–IDSA HCV Guidance, HCV in pregnancy (hcvguidelines.org) · ASGE Guideline: endoscopy in pregnant and lactating women, Shergill AK, et al., Gastrointest Endosc 2012;76:18–24

InsideWhat is normal in pregnancyThe trimester frameworkHyperemesis and intrahepatic cholestasisHELLP and acute fatty liver — the two that killDiseases that behave differently in pregnancyPre-existing liver diseaseDrugs, endoscopy, imaging and breastfeeding

Abnormal liver tests turn up in around 3% of pregnancies. Most are one of four conditions that belong to pregnancy itself, and each has a trimester, a laboratory signature and — for the two dangerous ones — a treatment that is delivery. The rest are ordinary liver diseases that behave differently, sometimes far more dangerously, because the patient is pregnant.

Must know
  • Alkaline phosphatase rises and albumin falls in normal pregnancy. AST, ALT, bilirubin, GGT and bile acids do not — any rise is disease and gets the usual workup.
  • Intrahepatic cholestasis: pruritus plus raised bile acids. Ursodeoxycholic acid 10–15 mg/kg/day treats the itch; bile acids ≥100 μmol/L carry the stillbirth risk that brings delivery forward to about 36 weeks.
  • HELLP and acute fatty liver are third-trimester emergencies and delivery is the treatment. HELLP is haemolysis, AST ≥70 and platelets below 100; AFLP is Swansea ≥6 with hypoglycaemia, coagulopathy, raised ammonia and renal failure.
  • Pregnancy changes the rules: hepatitis E kills mothers, HSV hepatitis is anicteric with ALT in the thousands and gets empirical acyclovir, mycophenolate and ribavirin are contraindicated, and azathioprine, steroids, tenofovir, UDCA and chelators continue.

AbbreviationsAFLP acute fatty liver of pregnancy · AIH autoimmune hepatitis · ALP alkaline phosphatase · ALT alanine aminotransferase · AST aspartate aminotransferase · DAA direct-acting antiviral · DIC disseminated intravascular coagulation · EGD oesophagogastroduodenoscopy · ERCP endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography · EUS endoscopic ultrasound · FFP fresh frozen plasma · FNH focal nodular hyperplasia · GGT gamma-glutamyl transferase · HBIG hepatitis B immune globulin · HBV hepatitis B virus · HCV hepatitis C virus · HELLP haemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, low platelets · HEV hepatitis E virus · HSV herpes simplex virus · ICP intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy · ICU intensive care unit · INR international normalised ratio · LCHAD long-chain 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase · LDH lactate dehydrogenase · LMWH low-molecular-weight heparin · MELD Model for End-Stage Liver Disease · MRCP magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography · NSAID non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug · NSBB non-selective beta-blocker · PBC primary biliary cholangitis · PCR polymerase chain reaction · PPI proton pump inhibitor · PSC primary sclerosing cholangitis · PT prothrombin time · TDF tenofovir disoproxil fumarate · TIPS transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt · UDCA ursodeoxycholic acid

Full detail
What is normal in pregnancy

Plasma volume expands by roughly half, so albumin and haemoglobin fall by dilution. ALP rises from mid-pregnancy (the placental isoenzyme), so a raised ALP alone means nothing — check the GGT. Clotting factors rise, so a prolonged INR is never physiological. AST, ALT, bilirubin, GGT and fasting bile acids stay in the non-pregnant range: any rise is disease and gets the usual workup plus blood pressure, urine protein, platelets, film, LDH, glucose, INR, creatinine, urate and bile acids.

The trimester framework

Gestational age is the most useful piece of history: hyperemesis in the first trimester, cholestasis in the second half, HELLP and AFLP in the third trimester and the first week after delivery.

ConditionWhenLaboratory cluesTreatment
Hyperemesis gravidarumFirst trimester; settles by 20 weeksALT above AST, usually low hundreds; mild bilirubin rise; ketonuriaFluids, thiamine before glucose, antiemetics
Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancySecond half, mostly after 30 weeksFasting bile acids >10 μmol/L (RCOG: non-fasting ≥19); ≥40 "severe", ≥100 stillbirth risk; ALT raised, occasionally >1,000 U/L; GGT usually normal; no primary rashUDCA 10–15 mg/kg/day; vitamin K if the PT is prolonged; delivery at about 36 weeks if bile acids ≥100, otherwise 36–39 weeks (SMFM)
Pre-eclampsia and HELLPThird trimester, mostly 27–37 weeks; about 30% within a week of deliveryHypertension and proteinuria (absent in up to 15–20%); schistocytes, LDH ≥600 U/L, AST ≥70 U/L, platelets <100 × 10⁹/L (Tennessee); INR normal unless DICDeliver at 34 weeks or beyond, or at any gestation with deterioration; before 34 weeks and stable, 24–48 hours of corticosteroids first; magnesium sulfate; treat blood pressure
Acute fatty liver of pregnancyThird trimester, mostly after 30 weeks, or just postpartumSwansea ≥6 of 14: vomiting, abdominal pain, polydipsia or polyuria, encephalopathy, hypoglycaemia, raised ammonia, bilirubin, urate and creatinine, leucocytosis, prolonged PT, raised transaminases (criterion only >42 U/L; typically hundreds), bright liver or ascites on ultrasound, microvesicular steatosisCorrect glucose and clotting, deliver once stable, ICU; test mother and infant for LCHAD deficiency
Hyperemesis and intrahepatic cholestasis
  • Hyperemesis affects 0.3–2% of pregnancies; about half of those admitted have abnormal liver tests. The liver is a bystander to starvation — if the tests do not settle with the vomiting, look for another cause.
  • ICP is itch of the palms and soles, worse at night, with raised bile acids. Itch can precede the rise, so repeat a normal first level, and SMFM recommends against early delivery for itch without laboratory confirmation. In the individual-participant meta-analysis that changed practice, stillbirth was concentrated at bile acids of 100 μmol/L or more (about 3.4%, against 0.1–0.3% below), which is why the level is repeated as pregnancy advances and delivery is planned at about 36 weeks once it is crossed.TrialOvadia C, et al. Lancet 2019;393:899–909 — stillbirth rises above 100 μmol/L
  • UDCA 10–15 mg/kg/day relieves the itch and improves the liver tests. In PITCHES it did not reduce the composite of perinatal death, preterm birth or neonatal unit admission, so in US practice it is a symptom drug and bile acids and gestation drive delivery.TrialPITCHES — Chappell LC, et al. Lancet 2019;394:849–860 — UDCA did not improve the composite perinatal outcome The 2021 individual-participant meta-analysis (Ovadia, Lancet Gastroenterol Hepatol 2021;6:547–558) found no change in stillbirth but fewer stillbirths-plus-preterm births in the randomised trials (adjusted odds ratio 0.60), so EASL 2023 offers it at bile acids ≥40 μmol/L. Cholestyramine worsens vitamin K deficiency — check the PT and give vitamin K if prolonged, because postpartum haemorrhage is the risk.
  • Itch and liver tests settle within weeks — check them at six weeks; persistent cholestasis means PBC, PSC or ABCB4 (MDR3) disease. Test for hepatitis C, advise non-oestrogen contraception, warn her that it recurs in 40–90%, and consider genetic testing (ABCB4, ABCB11, ATP8B1) after severe, early or recurrent disease.
HELLP and acute fatty liver — the two that kill

HELLP is severe pre-eclampsia with a microangiopathy in the liver; the Tennessee criteria are in the table. Up to 15–20% have neither hypertension nor proteinuria at first, and about 30% present after delivery. Dexamethasone raises the platelet count but improves no maternal or perinatal outcome; transfuse platelets to above 40–50 before a caesarean. Severe pain, shoulder-tip pain or unexplained hypotension means a subcapsular haematoma — CT or MRI at once. Contained, it is watched closely without abdominal manipulation and embolised if it enlarges; ruptured, it is haemorrhagic shock needing packing, angioembolisation or resection. Platelets and liver tests usually turn within 48 hours of delivery, and if they do not, think of AFLP, thrombotic microangiopathy or lupus.

AFLP is a failure of mitochondrial fatty-acid oxidation: a fetus homozygous for LCHAD deficiency (classically G1528C in HADHA) floods a heterozygous mother with metabolites she cannot clear, so both are tested afterwards. Pre-eclampsia coexists in about half of cases. What separates it from HELLP is hypoglycaemia, coagulopathy with a low fibrinogen, raised ammonia, encephalopathy, high bilirubin and renal failure. Biopsy is rarely needed or safe; do image the liver, because rupture is rare but lethal. Correct glucose and coagulopathy, deliver, then ICU support with dextrose, FFP and cryoprecipitate, watching for pancreatitis and bleeding. Most recover within two weeks; maternal mortality is now under 10%, and the mother still deteriorating after delivery belongs in a transplant centre.

Diseases that behave differently in pregnancy
  • Hepatitis E (genotype 1, South Asia and Africa) turns fulminant in the third trimester, with maternal mortality of roughly one in five. ACG says send HEV IgM and RNA in every pregnant woman with acute hepatitis, not only travellers — genotype 3 is home-grown in Europe and the US. Supportive care; ribavirin is teratogenic.
  • HSV hepatitis: fever, a bilirubin that is normal or barely raised while the ALT is in the thousands, leucopenia, low platelets, coagulopathy, and mucocutaneous lesions in fewer than half. Untreated it is often fatal. Send HSV PCR and start IV acyclovir 10 mg/kg every 8 hours empirically.
  • Gallstones: ACG recommends early laparoscopic cholecystectomy for symptomatic disease, because waiting means recurrence and a later emergency; it is safest in the second trimester, and AASLD prefers non-operative management in the third when it can wait. MRCP without gadolinium or EUS confirms a duct stone; ERCP with shielding and minimal fluoroscopy removes it.
  • Budd-Chiari syndrome: LMWH — warfarin is contraindicated throughout pregnancy (teratogenic early, fetal haemorrhage later), though fine while breastfeeding; a new thrombosis still gets the JAK2 and thrombophilia workup.
  • Hepatic adenoma is oestrogen-driven and can grow and bleed in pregnancy. Above 5 cm, embolise or resect before conception; below it, ultrasound each trimester and once postpartum. FNH and haemangioma need no monitoring.
Pre-existing liver disease
  • Cirrhosis: portal pressure rises with blood volume and the second stage of labour is a Valsalva, so variceal bleeding clusters in the second trimester and at delivery. AASLD 2021 wants a screening EGD within the year before conception (failing that, ACG's second-trimester EGD), banding for large varices, and propranolol as the NSBB — carvedilol, the module's default elsewhere, has almost no pregnancy data — watching fetal growth and neonatal bradycardia. A bleed gets banding, octreotide, a cephalosporin and a PPI, with TIPS as rescue; terlipressin and vasopressin are avoided because they contract the uterus and cut uterine blood flow. Mode of delivery is an obstetric decision; an assisted, short second stage limits straining. A MELD of 10 or more at conception predicts liver-related complications, and a known splenic artery aneurysm is treated beforehand because rupture in pregnancy is often fatal.
  • After transplant: wait at least a year with a stable graft and stable immunosuppression. Tacrolimus, ciclosporin, azathioprine and prednisone continue; mycophenolate is stopped at least six weeks before conception (the US label; EASL 2023 says twelve) — first-trimester loss and malformations.
  • AIH: continue prednisone and azathioprine — untreated disease costs more pregnancies than the drugs do. Flares cluster in the three months after delivery, so restore pre-pregnancy doses at delivery and check liver tests for six months postpartum. Mycophenolate is contraindicated.
  • Wilson disease: never stop chelation — stopping causes haemolysis and acute liver failure. Penicillamine or trientine continue at a reduced dose through pregnancy (typically 25–50% below the pre-pregnancy dose, by the third trimester at the latest) to leave copper for the fetus and allow wound healing; zinc continues at full dose. Neither is generally recommended while breastfeeding.
  • Hepatitis B: TDF from 28–32 weeks (EASL: 24–28) when HBV DNA is above 200,000 IU/mL, HBIG and vaccine within 12 hours of birth, breastfeeding allowed — details in the hepatitis B and C topic. Stop TDF at delivery or by three months postpartum and check ALT and HBV DNA every three months for six months, because that is when the flare comes.
  • Hepatitis C: screen every pregnancy. Vertical transmission is about 6% (double with HIV); caesarean does not prevent it, but avoid invasive fetal monitoring, episiotomy and prolonged rupture of membranes; breastfeeding is fine unless the nipples are cracked and bleeding. DAAs are not routine in pregnancy — treat before conception or after delivery — though AASLD–IDSA guidance now allows a case-by-case decision after a risk–benefit discussion; ribavirin is contraindicated. Test the infant with HCV RNA at 2–6 months or antibody from 18 months.
Drugs, endoscopy, imaging and breastfeeding
  • Endoscopy (ASGE 2012): a strong indication, deferred to the second trimester when it can wait, obstetrics involved, fetal heart tones documented before sedation and after. From the second trimester she does not lie flat — left lateral or left pelvic tilt keeps the uterus off the vena cava. Least sedation that works: meperidine and propofol are the ASGE and ACG choices (propofol by an anaesthesia provider); low-dose fentanyl appears safe; midazolam is avoided in the first trimester; bipolar cautery where possible.
  • Imaging: ultrasound, then MRI without gadolinium. CT when it changes management — one abdominopelvic study gives the fetus up to about 35 mGy, below the 50 mGy cumulative level at which harm is considered — and fear of radiation must not delay a diagnosis of hepatic rupture.
  • Also avoid methotrexate, spironolactone and NSAIDs from 20 weeks; lactulose, PPIs, ondansetron and metoclopramide are fine; entecavir is swapped for tenofovir. Breastfeeding: tenofovir, azathioprine, prednisone, tacrolimus, UDCA, LMWH and warfarin are compatible; mycophenolate is not.
Numbers to know
  • ICP bile acids: >10 μmol/L fasting (RCOG ≥19 non-fasting) · ≥100 stillbirth about 3.4% → deliver at about 36 weeks · recurrence 40–90% · PITCHES composite 23% vs 27%
  • HELLP: up to 15–20% without hypertension · 30% postpartum · platelets >40–50 before caesarean · AFLP about 1 in 10,000–20,000, mortality now <10%
  • Acyclovir 10 mg/kg IV every 8 h · HCV vertical transmission ~6% · mycophenolate stopped ≥6 weeks before conception (EASL ≥12) · adenoma >5 cm · fetal radiation threshold 50 mGy
PitfallThird-trimester nausea and right upper quadrant pain is not "reflux of pregnancy" until you have seen the blood pressure, platelets, glucose and INR — and a normal blood pressure does not exclude HELLP, because up to a fifth present without it and 30% present after delivery. The quieter error is the febrile woman with a normal bilirubin and an ALT of 4,000 whose acyclovir is waiting for the HSV PCR.
On rounds, sayShe's 34 weeks with itchy palms and soles at night, no rash, an ALT of 110 and bile acids of 112, so this is cholestasis of pregnancy — and above 100 is where the stillbirth risk climbs to about 3%. I'd start ursodeoxycholic acid at 10 to 15 milligrams per kilo for the itch, knowing PITCHES showed no clear perinatal benefit, check her PT and give vitamin K if it's long, repeat the bile acids weekly, and ask obstetrics to plan delivery at 36 weeks. Her platelets, LDH and film are normal and so is her blood pressure, so this isn't HELLP, and she needs a hepatitis C test now and liver tests at six weeks postpartum.

11Nutrition

The consult service's quietest responsibility — ACG, ASPEN and SCCM guidance

3 topics in this chapter
  1. 01Nutrition therapy in the hospitalized adult
  2. 02Enteral access — and when not to place it
  3. 03Malabsorption, short bowel, and bariatric deficiencies

Nutrition therapy in the hospitalized adult

ACG Clinical Guideline, McClave et al., Am J Gastroenterol 2016;111:315–334 · ASPEN/SCCM

InsideScreen everyone on admissionStart EN within 24–48 hoursParenteral nutrition

Malnutrition is common in hospital, poorly recognised, and independently predicts death, length of stay and readmission.

Must know
  • Screen everyone on admission.
  • Enteral over parenteral, started within 24–48 hours — do not wait for bowel sounds.
  • Thiamine before glucose; hypophosphatemia is the hallmark of refeeding.

AbbreviationsBMI body mass index · EN enteral nutrition · NRS-2002 Nutritional Risk Screening 2002 · PN parenteral nutrition

Full detail
  • Screen everyone on admission — NRS-2002 or the NUTRIC score in critical illness. Malnutrition is under-diagnosed and independently predicts mortality, length of stay, and readmission.
  • Enteral nutrition is preferred over parenteral whenever the gut works. "If the gut works, use it." EN maintains mucosal integrity, reduces infectious complications, and costs far less.
  • Start EN within 24–48 hours in a critically ill patient who can't take oral intake. Do not wait for bowel sounds or flatus — they are not required for feeding.
  • Gastric feeding is appropriate for most patients. Reserve post-pyloric access for documented intolerance, high aspiration risk, or severe pancreatitis with gastric outlet issues.
  • Gastric residual volumes should not be used routinely to hold feeds; if used at all, the threshold is 500 mL, not 200.
  • Parenteral nutrition when the gut is unusable or EN fails to meet needs after 7–10 days in a previously well-nourished patient — sooner in severe malnutrition. PN carries real line-infection, hepatobiliary, and metabolic risk.
  • Targets: roughly 25–30 kcal/kg/day and 1.2–2.0 g/kg/day protein; higher protein in critical illness, burns, and liver disease.
Refeeding syndrome
  • At-risk: prolonged starvation, alcohol use disorder, anorexia nervosa, very low BMI, significant unintentional weight loss, post-bariatric surgery.
  • Check and replete phosphate, potassium, and magnesium before and during initiation. Give thiamine before any glucose load.
  • Start at roughly 25% of the goal rate and advance over 3–5 days with daily electrolyte monitoring. Hypophosphatemia is the hallmark.

Enteral access — and when not to place it

ACG · DiBaise & Decker, J Clin Gastroenterol 2007 · ASGE guidance

InsideNasoenteric tubesPEG placement requiresPEG contraindications

How to feed someone who cannot safely swallow — and, just as importantly, when a feeding tube will not help.

Must know
  • Nasoenteric under 4 weeks; PEG beyond that.
  • PEG in advanced dementia does not prolong survival or prevent aspiration.
  • Tube dislodgement before the tract matures at ~4 weeks is an emergency.

AbbreviationsASGE American Society for Gastrointestinal Endoscopy · PEG percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy

Full detail
  • Nasoenteric tubes for expected duration <4 weeks. PEG or PEG-J beyond that.
  • PEG placement requires: transillumination and finger indentation, adequate coagulation status, and antibiotic prophylaxis (a single dose of a first-generation cephalosporin).
  • PEG contraindications: uncorrectable coagulopathy, hemodynamic instability, peritonitis, obstruction distal to the intended site, and inability to safely appose the stomach to the abdominal wall (massive ascites, prior surgery, interposed colon).
  • PEG in advanced dementia does not prolong survival, prevent aspiration, improve pressure ulcers, or improve quality of life. This is a firm evidence base. Handle the conversation with families gently, but do not place the tube because it feels easier than the discussion. Careful hand feeding is the alternative.
  • Buried bumper syndrome, peristomal leak, and inadvertent early tube removal (before the tract matures at ~4 weeks — treat as an emergency) are the complications to know.

Malabsorption, short bowel, and bariatric deficiencies

Jeejeebhoy & Duerksen, Gastroenterol Clin North Am 2018 · Lupoli, World J Diabetes 2017 · Kirby, JPEN 2012

InsideShort bowel syndromePost-bariatric surgeryMalnutrition in liver disease

What happens when the gut cannot absorb what passes through it, whether from disease, surgical resection, or a bariatric operation.

Must know
  • Terminal ileal resection → B12 deficiency and bile acid malabsorption.
  • Lifelong micronutrient monitoring after bariatric surgery.
  • Thiamine deficiency after protracted vomiting is a medical emergency.

AbbreviationsPPI proton pump inhibitor

Full detail
Short bowel syndrome
  • Outcome depends on remnant length, presence of the ileocecal valve, and whether the colon is in continuity. Ileum adapts; jejunum does not.
  • Terminal ileal resection → B12 deficiency and bile acid malabsorption. <100 cm resected → bile acid diarrhea (sequestrant helps); >100 cm → steatorrhea (sequestrant makes it worse).
  • Management: small frequent meals, oral rehydration solution, antimotility agents, PPI for gastric hypersecretion, teduglutide (GLP-2 analogue) to reduce parenteral dependenceTrialJeppesen PB, et al. Gastroenterology 2012;143:1473–1481.
  • Oxalate nephrolithiasis with an intact colon — restrict oxalate, supplement calcium with meals.
Post-bariatric surgery
  • Routine lifelong supplementation and monitoring: iron, vitamin B12, folate, calcium, vitamin D, thiamine, zinc, copper, and fat-soluble vitamins.
  • Thiamine deficiency after protracted vomiting is a medical emergency — Wernicke encephalopathy has been reported within weeks of surgery.
  • Copper deficiency causes a myeloneuropathy that mimics B12 deficiency and is easily missed.
  • Roux-en-Y produces more deficiency than sleeve gastrectomy; both need monitoring.
  • Also watch for dumping syndrome, marginal ulcer (smoking and NSAIDs are the drivers), internal hernia, and post-bypass hypoglycemia.
Malnutrition in liver disease
  • ACG 2025 guideline on malnutrition in liver disease: sarcopenia is common, under-recognized, and independently predicts mortality and post-transplant outcomes.
  • Target 1.2–1.5 g/kg/day protein; do not restrict protein even with encephalopathy.
  • Late-night snack to shorten the overnight fasting interval — cirrhotic patients enter a starvation-like catabolic state after a few hours without food.
  • Screen for and supplement fat-soluble vitamins in cholestatic disease; check zinc.
