The endoscopy suite — how to be useful, not decorative

Practice synthesis

InsideBefore each case, know the indicationLearn the anatomy call-outsLearn the Paris classificationKnow what the tools do

How to be genuinely useful in the procedure room rather than an ornament at the back of it.

Must know
  • Know the indication for every case in one sentence.
  • Learn the landmarks so you can follow the exam.
  • Offer to write the notes — and get the surveillance interval right.

AbbreviationsAPC argon plasma coagulation · BLI blue light imaging · NBI narrow-band imaging

Full detail
  • Before each case, know the indication. "Why are we scoping this patient?" is the most common question asked of an observer, and the answer should be one sentence.
  • Learn the anatomy call-outs so you can follow: for colonoscopy — appendiceal orifice, ileocecal valve, triangular transverse folds, the blue liver shadow at the hepatic flexure, the spleen at the splenic flexure, retroflexion in the rectum. For EGD — the Z-line, the diaphragmatic pinch, the incisura, retroflexion to see the cardia and fundus, the pylorus, the bulb, the second portion and the ampulla.
  • Learn the Paris classification so you can describe a lesion the way the endoscopist does, and know that photodocumentation of cecal landmarks is a quality requirement, not a formality.
  • Know what the tools do: cold snare, hot snare, injection needle, hemostatic clip, over-the-scope clip, APC probe, band ligator, balloon dilator, Savary dilators, biopsy forceps, and the roles of NBI/BLI virtual chromoendoscopy.
  • Offer to write the procedure notes and the follow-up recommendations. Getting the surveillance interval right on a note is genuinely useful and it is exactly what quality metrics measure.

Sedation and periprocedural safety

ASGE guidance · practice synthesis

InsideModerate sedationFasting

Making the procedure itself safe. Sedation-related events are the commonest category of endoscopic complication — commoner than perforation or bleeding.

Must know
  • Fasting: 2 hours clear liquids, 6 light meal, 8 full meal.
  • GLP-1 agonists delay gastric emptying — hold before elective endoscopy.
  • No endocarditis prophylaxis for any GI endoscopic procedure.

AbbreviationsASA American Society of Anesthesiologists · ASGE American Society for Gastrointestinal Endoscopy · ERCP endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography · GLP-1 glucagon-like peptide-1 · PEG polyethylene glycol · PSC primary sclerosing cholangitis

Full detail
  • Moderate sedation (midazolam + fentanyl) versus monitored anesthesia care with propofol. Propofol has faster onset and recovery and no reversal agent — so airway skills matter.
  • Higher-risk airways: obesity, obstructive sleep apnea, ASA class III–IV, difficult airway anatomy, high opioid or benzodiazepine tolerance. These push toward anesthesia support.
  • Fasting: 2 hours clear liquids, 6 hours light meal, 8 hours full meal. GLP-1 receptor agonists delay gastric emptying, but the 2024 multi-society guidance (ASA, AGA, ASMBS, SAGES and others) moved away from routinely holding them: most patients continue the drug; those at higher risk of retained food (dose-escalation phase, higher doses, weekly dosing, GI symptoms) take a liquid diet for the 24 hours before the procedure; and anyone with nausea, vomiting, bloating or abdominal pain on the day is delayed or managed as a full stomach (point-of-care gastric ultrasound, rapid-sequence induction). Retained food at endoscopy is common enough that it is worth mentioning at the pre-procedure huddle.
  • Antibiotic prophylaxis is not indicated to prevent endocarditis for any GI endoscopic procedure. It is indicated for PEG placement, for ERCP where complete biliary drainage is unlikely (PSC, hilar obstruction), and for cirrhotic patients with GI bleeding.

Adverse events worth being able to recite

ASGE adverse events guidance · ACG guidelines

InsidePerforationPost-polypectomy bleedingPost-ERCP pancreatitisSedation eventsElectrocoagulation syndrome

The complications of endoscopy and roughly how often each one happens — the numbers you need for a consent conversation.

Must know
  • Post-polypectomy bleeding can occur up to 2 weeks later.
  • Post-polypectomy electrocoagulation syndrome has no free air — manage medically.
  • Sedation-related events are the commonest category overall.

AbbreviationsASGE American Society for Gastrointestinal Endoscopy · EMR endoscopic mucosal resection · EoE eosinophilic oesophagitis · NSAID non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug

Full detail
EventApproximate rateNote
Colonoscopy perforation~0.05% diagnostic; higher with polypectomySigmoid most common; consider clip closure and surgery consult
Post-polypectomy bleeding~1–2%, up to ~6–7% after large EMRCan occur up to 2 weeks later
Post-ERCP pancreatitis~3–10% overall; higher in high-risk patientsRectal NSAID + aggressive LR + PD stent for prophylaxis
EGD perforation<0.05% diagnosticHigher with dilation, especially in EoE and caustic strictures
Sedation-related eventsMost common category overallHypoxia, hypotension, aspiration
Post-polypectomy electrocoagulation syndrome<1%Pain, fever, leukocytosis, no free air — manage medically, not surgically

Bowel preparation — the biggest lever on colonoscopy quality

USMSTF Consensus Recommendations, Jacobson et al., Am J Gastroenterol 2025 · ASGE-ACG Quality Indicators 2024

InsideSplit-dose preparation is the standardPredictors of inadequate prepInadequate prep → repeat within 1 year

How clean the colon is remains the single biggest determinant of whether a colonoscopy finds anything.

Must know
  • Split dosing, finishing 2+ hours before the procedure.
  • Adequate = Boston score ≥2 in each of the three segments, not a total.
  • Inadequate prep → repeat within a year, not the standard interval.

AbbreviationsUSMSTF US Multi-Society Task Force on Colorectal Cancer

Full detail
  • Split-dose preparation is the standard — half the evening before, half beginning 4–6 hours before the procedure, finishing at least 2 hours before. Same-day dosing is acceptable for afternoon procedures.
  • Score every prep with the Boston Bowel Preparation Scale. Adequate = ≥2 in each of the three colon segments. A total score is not enough — one segment scoring 1 makes the prep inadequate.
  • Unit target: adequate preparation in ≥90% of exams (raised from ≥85% in 2024).
  • Predictors of inadequate prep: constipation, opioids, diabetes, prior inadequate prep, immobility, inpatient status, cirrhosis, tricyclics, and non-adherence to split dosing. Intensify the regimen prospectively in these patients rather than repeating the exam later.
  • Inadequate prep → repeat within 1 year, and sooner if the prep was poor or the indication is high-risk. Do not apply the standard surveillance interval to an inadequately prepped exam.
  • Clear-liquid diet the day before is standard; low-residue diets are an acceptable, better-tolerated alternative in selected patients.

Quality indicators across the other procedures

ACG Competencies in Endoscopy series: Common to All Procedures (2024) · Upper GI Endoscopy (Feb 2025) · EUS (Apr 2025) · ERCP (Jan 2026)

InsideCommon to all proceduresUpper GI endoscopyERCP (new January 2026, AJG 121:80–95)EUSComputer-aided detection (CADe)

The quality measures for the procedures other than colonoscopy — upper endoscopy, endoscopic ultrasound, and ERCP.

Must know
  • Five priority colonoscopy indicators: ADR, SSLDR, prep adequacy, interval adherence, cecal intubation.
  • ERCP: deep cannulation of a native papilla is the priority indicator, with universal rectal NSAIDs.

AbbreviationsADR adenoma detection rate · ASGE American Society for Gastrointestinal Endoscopy · CADe computer-aided detection · ERCP endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography · EUS endoscopic ultrasound · FNA fine needle aspiration · FNB fine needle biopsy · SSLDR sessile serrated lesion detection rate

Full detail
  • Common to all procedures: appropriate indication documented, informed consent, correct antibiotic prophylaxis, sedation plan, complete procedure documentation, adverse event tracking, and adherence to reprocessing standards.
  • Upper GI endoscopy: photodocumentation of key landmarks, adequate biopsy protocols for Barrett's (Seattle) and for gastric intestinal metaplasia (Sydney), and inspection time — a minimum inspection time improves neoplasia detection just as withdrawal time does in the colon.
  • ERCP (new January 2026, AJG 121:80–95): 13 indicators across pre-, intra-, and post-procedure care. Deep cannulation of the duct of interest in a native papilla with standard anatomy is a priority indicator (≈90% is the conventional benchmark, though the document explicitly cautions that rigidly chasing cannulation or stent targets can push operators toward aggressive maneuvers). Other headline items: universal rectal NSAIDs in patients with an intact papilla, a deliberately more restrictive approach to indications reinforcing ERCP as a therapeutic rather than diagnostic procedure, and unplanned hospitalization and biliary reintervention as pragmatic outcome measures.
  • EUS: appropriate indication, complete staging documentation, diagnostic yield of FNA/FNB with rapid on-site or macroscopic evaluation.
  • Computer-aided detection (CADe) in colonoscopy raises adenoma detection in trials; ASGE guidance on its role is evolving. It's a good topic to have an opinion on if you're interested in endoscopy quality research.
On rounds, sayIf we're tracking quality here, the five priority colonoscopy indicators in the 2024 document are adenoma detection rate, sessile serrated lesion detection rate, bowel prep adequacy, cecal intubation rate, and adherence to recommended intervals — and I'd be curious whether the unit has moved to the expanded all-outpatient ADR denominator yet.

13Presenting on Service

A full worked consult, and the same case presented badly

A worked GI consult — presented the way a fellow presents it

Practice synthesis

InsideThe 30-second openerThe focused historyOnly the numbers that matterWhat you have already doneAssessment and planThe same case done badlyA clinic version

Presenting to a gastroenterologist is not the same as presenting on a medicine round. They want the consult question answered first, the GI-relevant history only, and a plan with a timeline attached. Below is one case presented in full, then the same case presented badly, so the difference is visible.

Must know
  • Open with one sentence and the consult question restated. Never begin with the chief complaint and work forwards.
  • Give GI-relevant history only — prior scopes, prior bleeds, NSAIDs, anticoagulants, alcohol, family history. Not the full medicine history.
  • Quote only the numbers that drive the decision, and give them as a trend rather than a single value.
  • Commit to a plan with a timeline. “I'd scope within 24 hours” beats “we could consider endoscopy” every time.
Full detail
The 30-second opener
Say this“This is a 58-year-old man with alcohol-associated cirrhosis, Child-Pugh B, admitted overnight with haematemesis and melaena. Medicine is asking whether he needs urgent endoscopy and whether his beta-blocker should continue.”

Three things happened in that sentence: the attending knows who the patient is, what the underlying liver disease is, and what they are being asked to decide. Everything after this is supporting evidence.

The focused history — GI relevant only
Say this“He has known cirrhosis diagnosed two years ago, with one previous variceal bleed eighteen months ago treated with banding — he had three sessions and then stopped attending. He has been on carvedilol 6.25 mg twice daily. He drinks around a bottle of wine most days and last drank two days ago. No NSAIDs, no anticoagulants. His last endoscopy was fourteen months ago and showed grade 2 varices with red signs. No prior H. pylori testing.”

Notice what is not there: his hypertension, his knee replacement, his allergy list. If the attending wants those, they will ask.

Only the numbers that drive the decision
Say this“Haemoglobin 7.4, down from 11.2 a month ago. Platelets 68. INR 1.6, bilirubin 3.1, albumin 2.9 — so Child-Pugh B, 8 points. Creatinine 1.1, sodium 133, MELD around 18. Blatchford is 14. He's tachycardic at 108 with a systolic of 96.”
  • Give haemoglobin as a trend, not a value. A haemoglobin of 7.4 means something entirely different if it was 7.6 last week.
  • Quote the score, and quote what it implies. Not “Blatchford is 14” but, when asked, “14, so nowhere near dischargeable.”
  • Say the Child-Pugh class and the points. It shows you calculated it rather than repeating the chart.
What you have already done
Say this“I've started octreotide and IV ceftriaxone 1 gram, held the carvedilol because he's hypotensive, sent a group and save, and kept him nil by mouth from midnight. He's got two large-bore cannulas and the unit knows he may need a bed.”

This is the part junior presenters most often leave out, and the part that most changes how the attending sees you. It also demonstrates you know that antibiotics in variceal bleeding reduce mortality rather than just infection.

Assessment and plan — commit
Say this“I think this is a recurrent variceal bleed in someone who dropped out of a banding programme. I'd transfuse to a target of 7 rather than higher, because over-transfusing raises portal pressure. I'd scope him within 12 hours given the variceal history, band anything that's bleeding, and if he turns out to be Child-Pugh C at endoscopy or is still bleeding, I'd raise pre-emptive TIPS with the interventional team within 72 hours. Once he's stable he needs carvedilol restarted, a proper banding programme to eradication, and alcohol treatment referral before discharge.”

That answers the consult question, gives a timeline, names the threshold that would change the plan, and thinks past the admission. An attending can disagree with all of it and still think you are worth teaching.

The same case, presented badly
Don't say this“So this is a 58-year-old gentleman with a past medical history of hypertension, type 2 diabetes, osteoarthritis and cirrhosis, who presented to the emergency department at about 2 a.m. complaining of feeling unwell. He'd been at home and had noticed some dark stools since Tuesday, and then vomited what his wife described as coffee grounds. Systems review was otherwise unremarkable except for some mild ankle swelling. On examination he was alert, chest was clear, heart sounds one and two, abdomen was soft with no organomegaly… His sodium is 133, potassium 4.1, urea 14, creatinine 1.1, bilirubin 3.1, ALT 44, AST 88, ALP 121, albumin 2.9, white count 9.6, haemoglobin 7.4, platelets 68, INR 1.6… so we were wondering what you thought.”
  • Two minutes in, the attending still does not know the question.
  • The cirrhosis — the entire point — arrived fourth in a list.
  • Every laboratory value was read out, so none of them landed.
  • It ends with no assessment and no plan, which puts all the work back on the person you are asking for help.
The clinic version

Outpatient presentations use the same spine but a different emphasis, because the question is usually diagnostic rather than temporal:

Say this“This is a 34-year-old woman referred with three months of non-bloody diarrhoea and 6 kg of weight loss. Calprotectin is 480, CRP 22, haemoglobin 10.8 with ferritin 9. Coeliac serology negative on a gluten-containing diet. No travel, no antibiotics, no NSAIDs, and her brother has Crohn's. I think this is inflammatory rather than functional, and I'd like to do an ileocolonoscopy with biopsies and MR enterography, and check TB and hepatitis B serology now in case she needs a biologic.”
  • Note the pre-emptive TB and hepatitis B testing — ordering it before it is needed is the kind of detail that reads as experience.
  • Note also that the negative coeliac serology is qualified with “on a gluten-containing diet”, which tells the attending you know the test is otherwise uninterpretable.
PitfallThe two commonest failures are presenting a complete internal medicine clerking, and having no opinion. Attendings forgive a wrong plan far more readily than an absent one — a wrong plan gives them something to teach against.
If you take one thingStructure every GI presentation as: one line and the question · GI-relevant history only · the numbers that decide · what you have already done · your plan, with a time attached.

14Presentation Flashcards

One card per common consult — what to ask, the scores and criteria to use, the labs to order, and what not to miss

Presenting a consult — ask, score, order, don't miss

Practice synthesis, cross-referenced to the chapters above

One card per common consult. Each gives the questions to ask the patient, the scores and criteria that decide management, the labs to have sent before you present, and the things you must not miss.

How to use a card
  • Ask — the history that splits the differential and changes what happens next.
  • Scores & criteria — quote the number with the threshold it sits against.
  • Labs — send them before you call. The missing one is the first question you get.
  • Don't miss — name the dangerous possibility out loud, even if only to rule it out.

Upper GI bleeding

Chapter 3 · non-variceal and variceal

Ask
  • Prior bleeds, ulcers and scopes
  • Antithrombotics and NSAIDs — indication and last dose
  • Alcohol and known liver disease
  • Retching before the haematemesis
  • Dysphagia or weight loss
  • Aortic graft
  • Syncope
Scores & criteria
  • Glasgow-Blatchford ≤1 can go home
  • AIMS65 predicts mortality
  • Forrest class Ia–IIa need endoscopic therapy
  • Child-Pugh and MELD 3.0 if cirrhotic
  • BUN:creatinine >30 favours an upper source
Labs to order
  • CBC
  • Group and save
  • INR
  • BUN and creatinine
  • Lactate
Don't miss
  • Varices in known or suspected cirrhosis
  • Aortoenteric fistula after aortic surgery
  • Swallowed blood from the nose or lungs
  • Antithrombotic held without a written restart plan

Lower GI bleeding

Chapter 3

Ask
  • Colour and volume of blood
  • Painful or painless
  • Polypectomy in the last 2 weeks
  • Known diverticulosis or IBD
  • NSAIDs and antithrombotics
  • Pelvic radiation
  • Aortic stenosis, CKD or LVAD
Scores & criteria
  • Oakland ≤8 for outpatient management
  • Shock index unstable → CT angiography first
  • BUN:creatinine a high ratio points to an upper source
  • Transfusion threshold 7 g/dL, higher with cardiovascular disease
Labs to order
  • Rectal examination
  • CBC
  • Group and save
  • BUN and creatinine
  • CT angiography if unstable
Don't miss
  • Brisk upper source in 10–15% — consider EGD first
  • Ischaemic colitis when pain is prominent
  • Malignancy with weight loss or habit change
  • Meckel's diverticulum in the young

Cirrhosis with decompensation

Chapter 10 · ascites, SBP, encephalopathy, AKI

Ask
  • Aetiology and whether controlled — last drink
  • Prior decompensations and prior SBP
  • Last endoscopy, varices and beta-blocker dose
  • Diuretic doses and adherence
  • Lactulose stool count
  • Infection, bleeding, constipation or dehydration
  • NSAIDs, sedatives or opioids
Scores & criteria
  • Child-Pugh and MELD 3.0 with sodium, creatinine and bilirubin trends
  • Ascitic PMN ≥250 = SBP
  • SAAG ≥1.1, with ascitic protein
  • ICA criteria stage the AKI
  • West Haven grade the encephalopathy
Labs to order
  • Diagnostic paracentesis
  • Ascitic cell count
  • Ascitic culture bottles
  • Blood cultures
  • Urine culture
  • Sodium
  • Creatinine
  • Bilirubin
  • INR
  • Albumin
  • Glucose
Don't miss
  • SBP — tap every admission with ascites
  • GI bleeding as the precipitant
  • HCC or portal vein thrombosis
  • NSAIDs or nephrotoxins still charted

Alcohol-associated hepatitis

Chapter 10

Ask
  • Quantity, pattern and last drink
  • Prior episodes
  • Fever, cough, dysuria or abdominal pain
  • Melaena or haematemesis
  • Paracetamol and other hepatotoxins
  • Hepatitis B and C status
  • Readiness to stop drinking
Scores & criteria
  • Clinical diagnosis jaundice within 8 weeks, AST:ALT >1.5, AST <400, bilirubin >3
  • Maddrey ≥32 = severe
  • MELD >20 = severe
  • Lille day 7 >0.45 = stop steroids
  • AUDIT-C and PEth document alcohol use
Labs to order
  • Bilirubin
  • INR
  • Creatinine
  • Blood cultures
  • Urine culture
  • Chest X-ray
  • Hepatitis B and C serology
  • Ultrasound with Doppler
  • Ascitic PMN if ascites
  • Phosphatidylethanol
Don't miss
  • Infection before steroids start
  • Steroid contraindications — GI bleed, AKI, hepatorenal syndrome
  • Paracetamol or drug-induced injury
  • Biliary obstruction or cholangitis

Abnormal liver tests / acute hepatitis

Chapter 10

Ask
  • Alcohol
  • Every drug, herbal and supplement — start dates
  • Paracetamol dose
  • Viral risk — injecting, sexual history, endemic birthplace
  • Diabetes and weight
  • Pregnancy
  • Hypotension or heart failure
Scores & criteria
  • R value ≥5 hepatocellular, ≤2 cholestatic
  • Hy's law ALT >3× with bilirubin >2× ULN
  • Acute liver failure INR ≥1.5 plus any encephalopathy, <26 weeks
  • FIB-4 for chronic disease
Labs to order
  • INR
  • CBC and CK
  • GGT
  • Paracetamol level
  • HAV IgM
  • HBsAg and anti-HBc
  • HCV antibody, reflex RNA
  • ANA, SMA and IgG
  • Ferritin and transferrin saturation
  • Ceruloplasmin if under 40
  • Pregnancy test
  • RUQ ultrasound with Doppler
Don't miss
  • Rising INR or any confusion — call the transplant centre
  • Paracetamol toxicity — send a level
  • Ischaemic hepatitis after hypotension
  • Cholestasis of pregnancy

Acute pancreatitis

Chapter 9

Ask
  • Alcohol quantity and timing
  • Gallstones or biliary colic
  • Triglycerides, diabetes, oestrogens
  • New drugs — azathioprine, valproate, thiazides, GLP-1 agonists
  • Recent ERCP
  • Prior episodes and their work-up
  • Weight loss or jaundice
Scores & criteria
  • Diagnosis 2 of 3 — pain, lipase >3× ULN, imaging
  • Revised Atlanta severe = organ failure beyond 48 hours
  • BISAP ≥3
  • BUN rise at 24 hours is the best single predictor
  • ALT >150 points to gallstones
Labs to order
  • Lipase
  • CBC and haematocrit
  • BUN and creatinine
  • LFTs
  • Triglycerides
  • Calcium
  • RUQ ultrasound
Don't miss
  • Cholangitis — the indication for ERCP
  • Perforated ulcer or mesenteric ischaemia
  • Inferior MI or ruptured aortic aneurysm
  • Tumour with weight loss or jaundice

Acute severe ulcerative colitis

Chapter 5 · and the UC flare

Ask
  • Stool count, night stools and blood
  • Antibiotics, NSAIDs or travel
  • Every prior biologic and why it stopped
  • Steroid courses and dependence
  • TB, hepatitis B, HIV and VZV status
  • Recent smoking cessation
  • Pregnancy
Scores & criteria
  • Truelove and Witts ≥6 bloody stools plus fever, pulse >90, Hb <10.5 or ESR >30
  • Oxford day-3 index >8 stools, or 3–8 with CRP >45 → ~85% colectomy
  • Toxic megacolon transverse colon >6 cm with toxicity
  • Mayo endoscopic subscore at sigmoidoscopy
  • Montreal extent E1–E3
Labs to order
  • CBC
  • CRP
  • ESR
  • Stool studies incl. C. difficile
  • Iron studies
  • TB screen
  • Hepatitis B serology
  • TPMT and NUDT15
  • Abdominal X-ray
  • Sigmoidoscopy with CMV biopsies
Don't miss
  • C. difficile and CMV before escalating
  • Toxic megacolon on the abdominal film
  • Surgery not informed on day 1
  • Opioids, anticholinergics or NSAIDs still charted

Crohn's disease

Chapter 5

Ask
  • Post-prandial pain, vomiting, distension
  • Fever, perianal pain or drainage
  • Weight and nutrition
  • Prior surgery and length resected
  • Smoking
  • Prior biologics, why stopped, drug levels
  • TB, hepatitis B, HIV and vaccines
Scores & criteria
  • Montreal age, location, behaviour ± perianal
  • Rutgeerts i2b or above after resection → escalate
  • Harvey-Bradshaw or CDAI clinical activity
  • SES-CD endoscopic activity
  • Calprotectin and CRP treat-to-target markers
Labs to order
  • CBC
  • CRP
  • Faecal calprotectin
  • B12
  • TB screen
  • Hepatitis B serology
  • TPMT and NUDT15
  • CT or MR enterography
  • MRI pelvis if perianal
Don't miss
  • Abscess — drain before any immunosuppression
  • Fibrotic stricture versus active inflammation
  • Infectious ileitis — Yersinia, tuberculosis
  • Bile acid diarrhoea or SIBO after resection

Gastroparesis, nausea and vomiting

Chapter 2

Ask
  • Vomit timing and undigested food
  • Early satiety, bloating, weight loss
  • Diabetes control
  • GLP-1 agonists, opioids, anticholinergics
  • Cannabis and relief with hot showers
  • Stereotyped attacks with well periods
  • Effortless regurgitation within minutes of eating
Scores & criteria
  • Delayed emptying >60% at 2 h or >10% at 4 h
  • Valid study glucose <275 mg/dL, drugs held 48–72 h
  • Rome IV cyclic vomiting and rumination
  • Gastroparesis Cardinal Symptom Index to track symptoms
Labs to order
  • Potassium
  • Magnesium
  • Bicarbonate
  • Glucose and HbA1c
  • Thiamine
  • Calcium
  • Urea and creatinine
  • Pregnancy test
  • EGD
  • 4-hour gastric emptying study
Don't miss
  • Mechanical obstruction — EGD first
  • Cannabinoid hyperemesis
  • Emptying study done on opioids or GLP-1
  • Raised intracranial pressure

Dysphagia

Chapter 1

Ask
  • Coughing, choking or nasal regurgitation
  • Solids only, or solids and liquids
  • Progressive or intermittent
  • Food impactions
  • Weight loss
  • Asthma, eczema or food allergy
  • Regurgitation of undigested food
Scores & criteria
  • Eckardt ≤3 = treatment success
  • Chicago v4.0 raised IRP in both positions
  • EoE histology ≥15 eosinophils per high-power field
  • EREFS endoscopic score for EoE
  • Pseudoachalasia flags over 60, under 6 months, marked weight loss
Labs to order
  • EGD, ≥6 biopsies from 2 levels
  • High-resolution manometry
  • Timed barium swallow
  • FLIP if outflow obstruction
  • Videofluoroscopy if oropharyngeal
Don't miss
  • Malignancy — progressive dysphagia with weight loss
  • Pseudoachalasia before any achalasia treatment
  • EoE — biopsy even if the oesophagus looks normal
  • Oropharyngeal cause — stroke, Parkinson's, myasthenia

GERD and hiatal hernia

Chapter 1

Ask
  • PPI timing relative to meals
  • Heartburn, regurgitation or chest pain
  • Nocturnal symptoms
  • How well the PPI worked
  • Dysphagia, weight loss or bleeding
  • Prior endoscopy and pH testing
  • Family history of Barrett's or oesophageal cancer
Scores & criteria
  • LA grade B, C and D conclusive under Lyon 2.0
  • Acid exposure time >6% conclusive, <4% physiological
  • Hill grade with hernia length in cm
  • Prague C&M for Barrett's
Labs to order
  • EGD off PPI 2–4 weeks
  • pH-impedance off therapy
  • Manometry before antireflux surgery
  • Cardiac work-up if chest pain
Don't miss
  • Alarm features — dysphagia, weight loss, bleeding
  • Cardiac chest pain
  • Paraoesophageal hernia with obstructive symptoms
  • EoE or achalasia posing as reflux

Acute diarrhoea and C. difficile

Chapter 4

Ask
  • Duration and stools per day
  • Blood, mucus or fever
  • Antibiotics in the last 3 months
  • PPI use or recent hospital stay
  • Travel, food, sick contacts
  • Immunosuppression, HIV or IBD
  • Laxatives or tube feeds
Scores & criteria
  • Test only if ≥3 unformed stools in 24 hours
  • C. difficile severe WBC ≥15,000 or creatinine >1.5
  • C. difficile fulminant hypotension or shock, ileus, megacolon
  • Two-step testing GDH and toxin, PCR to arbitrate
Labs to order
  • C. difficile GDH and toxin
  • CBC
  • Creatinine
  • Lactate
  • Shiga toxin if bloody
Don't miss
  • Fulminant C. difficile — ileus or megacolon
  • Shiga toxin E. coli before any antibiotic
  • Antimotility drugs in dysentery
  • Laxatives or tube feeds giving a false positive

Chronic diarrhoea and IBS

Chapter 4

Ask
  • Nocturnal stools, persistence with fasting
  • Greasy, floating stool
  • Weight loss or blood
  • Metformin, PPIs, SSRIs, magnesium, laxatives
  • Cholecystectomy, ileal or bariatric surgery
  • Family history of coeliac, IBD, colorectal cancer
  • Urgency and incontinence
Scores & criteria
  • Rome IV pain ≥1 day a week for 3 months
  • Faecal calprotectin separates IBS from IBD
  • Faecal elastase <100 µg/g
  • Stool osmotic gap >125 osmotic, <50 secretory
  • Bristol stool form record the type
Labs to order
  • CBC
  • Chemistry
  • CRP
  • TSH
  • tTG-IgA with total IgA
  • Faecal calprotectin
  • Stool C. difficile
  • Giardia antigen
  • Faecal elastase
Don't miss
  • Coeliac serology is only valid on gluten
  • Microscopic colitis — random colonic biopsies
  • Weight loss, blood or nocturnal symptoms
  • Laxative misuse

Iron-deficiency anaemia and occult GI bleeding

Chapters 3 and 4

Ask
  • Overt bleeding or melaena
  • NSAIDs, aspirin or anticoagulants
  • Menstrual losses
  • Diet — vegetarian or restricted
  • Gastric or bariatric surgery
  • Family history of colorectal cancer
  • CKD, aortic stenosis or LVAD
Scores & criteria
  • Ferritin <30 ng/mL diagnostic, up to ~100 with inflammation or CKD
  • Transferrin saturation <20%
  • Positive FIT never explained by haemorrhoids
Labs to order
  • CBC with MCV
  • Ferritin
  • Transferrin saturation
  • B12 and folate
  • Reticulocytes
  • Urinalysis
  • Coeliac serology
  • EGD and colonoscopy, same sitting
Don't miss
  • Man or postmenopausal woman — GI lesion until proven otherwise
  • Menstruation used as the default explanation
  • Duodenal and gastric biopsies at EGD
  • Coeliac disease

Cholangitis, stones and biliary obstruction

Chapter 9

Ask
  • Gallstones, cholecystectomy, ERCP or stents
  • PSC or IBD
  • Painless jaundice and weight loss
  • Anticoagulants
  • Contrast allergy
  • Roux-en-Y or prior biliary surgery
  • Recent instrumentation
Scores & criteria
  • Tokyo 2018 grade III drain within 24 h, grade II 24–48 h
  • ASGE high probability stone seen, cholangitis, or bilirubin >4 + dilated duct → ERCP
  • ASGE intermediate abnormal LFTs, age >55 or dilated duct → EUS or MRCP
  • Charcot's triad pain, jaundice, fever
  • Reynolds' pentad adds hypotension and confusion
Labs to order
  • Blood cultures
  • CBC
  • Bilirubin and ALP
  • ALT
  • INR and platelets
  • RUQ ultrasound
  • MRCP or EUS if intermediate
Don't miss
  • Tokyo grade III — drain within 24 hours
  • Malignant obstruction — painless jaundice
  • Liver abscess
  • Stenting a hilar tumour before cross-sectional imaging

Diverticulitis

Chapter 8

Ask
  • Prior episodes and complications
  • Prior colonoscopy
  • Immunosuppression or steroids
  • NSAIDs and opioids
  • Bleeding, weight loss or habit change
  • Pneumaturia or faecaluria
  • Frailty and support at home
Scores & criteria
  • Modified Hinchey Ia phlegmon · Ib–II abscess · III purulent · IV faeculent
  • Abscess size drain from about 3–4 cm
  • No antibiotics only if all immunocompetent, stable outpatient, eating, no SIRS, not frail, reliable follow-up
Labs to order
  • CBC
  • CRP
  • CT abdomen and pelvis
  • Urinalysis
  • Pregnancy test
Don't miss
  • Colorectal cancer — colonoscopy 6–8 weeks after complicated disease
  • Free air or peritonitis — surgery now
  • Fistula — pneumaturia or faecaluria
  • Gynaecological cause — torsion, ectopic pregnancy

Chronic constipation

Chapter 7

Ask
  • New onset over 45
  • Blockage, digitation or splinting
  • Every laxative tried and the dose
  • Opioids and other constipating drugs
  • Bleeding, weight loss or anaemia
  • Family history of colorectal cancer
  • Thyroid disease, diabetes, neurological disease
Scores & criteria
  • Rome IV functional constipation
  • Bristol stool form types 1–2
  • Anorectal manometry + balloon expulsion dyssynergia in up to half of refractory cases
  • Alarm features → colonoscopy
Labs to order
  • Digital rectal examination
  • TSH
  • Calcium
  • Glucose
  • CBC
  • Colonoscopy if alarm features
Don't miss
  • Colorectal cancer — alarm features or never screened
  • Faecal impaction with overflow
  • Dyssynergic defecation — do the rectal exam
  • Opioid or other drug cause
If you take one thingKnow the score and its threshold, and have the labs back before you present.

15Score Calculators

Tap a score to open it. Enter the values and it works itself out.

2 topics in this chapter
  1. 01Calculators

Calculators

Enter values and the score and its interpretation update as you type

InsideBleeding — Blatchford, Rockall, AIMS65, OaklandLiver — Child-Pugh, MELD 3.0, Maddrey, FIB-4, R valueActivity — BISAP, Truelove & Witts, Oxford, Eckardt, Boston

Must know
  • Blatchford ≤1 is the only score that safely sends an upper GI bleed home.
  • Child-Pugh is five variables scored 1–3; A 5–6, B 7–9, C 10–15.
  • Maddrey ≥32 or MELD >20 triggers steroids in alcohol-associated hepatitis.
  • FIB-4 <1.3 low, >2.67 high — the one score you can do from a routine blood panel.

Every score used anywhere in this module, as a working calculator rather than a table you have to do arithmetic against. One opens at a time so the page stays short.

MELD 3.0 is implemented from the published formula with the standard bounds applied (bilirubin and INR floored at 1, creatinine capped at 3, sodium clamped to 125–137, albumin to 1.5–3.5). Use it to learn what drives the number — for an actual listing decision use the official OPTN calculator.

Classifications that are described rather than calculated

Forrest · Mayo · Prague · Hill · Rutgeerts · Montreal · Rome IV · Marsh · Atlanta · Hinchey · Tokyo · King's College · Lille

InsideEndoscopicIBDFunctional and histologicalSeverity

These are descriptive systems, not sums — you assign a category by what you see rather than adding points. Kept short deliberately.

Must know
  • Forrest Ia, Ib and IIa get endoscopic therapy; IIc and III do not.
  • Rutgeerts i2b or above after ileocolonic resection means escalate.
  • Mayo 0 or 1 is mucosal healing; most trials now demand 0.
  • Revised Atlanta severity turns on organ failure persisting beyond 48 hours.
Full detail
Endoscopic
  • Forrest — Ia spurting · Ib oozing · IIa visible vessel · IIb adherent clot · IIc flat spot · III clean base.
  • Mayo endoscopic subscore — 0 normal · 1 erythema with reduced vascular pattern · 2 vascular pattern absent, friable, erosions · 3 spontaneous bleeding and ulceration.
  • Prague C&M — C is the circumferential extent in cm above the top of the gastric folds, M the maximal extent to the tip of the longest tongue; islands are not counted. Written C2M5. M is the segment length that sets the surveillance interval (<3 cm 5-yearly, ≥3 cm 3-yearly).
  • Hill flap valve (on retroflexion) — I prominent fold hugging the scope, 3–4 cm along the lesser curve · II fold present but opens and closes with respiration · III fold barely present, scope not gripped, hiatus often open · IV no fold, hiatus gapes, squamous epithelium visible from below — hernia always present. III–IV means a defective valve.
Inflammatory bowel disease
  • Rutgeerts — i0 none · i1 ≤5 aphthous ulcers · i2a anastomosis only · i2b >5 aphthous ulcers with normal mucosa between · i3 diffuse aphthous ileitis · i4 large ulcers, nodules or narrowing.
  • Montreal, Crohn's — age A1 ≤16, A2 17–40, A3 >40 · location L1 ileal, L2 colonic, L3 ileocolonic, L4 upper GI modifier · behaviour B1 inflammatory, B2 stricturing, B3 penetrating, with p for perianal.
  • Montreal, ulcerative colitis — E1 proctitis · E2 left-sided · E3 extensive beyond the splenic flexure.
Functional and histological
  • Rome IV for IBS — abdominal pain ≥1 day per week over 3 months, onset ≥6 months ago, with two or more of: related to defecation, change in stool frequency, change in stool form.
  • Bristol — 1 hard lumps to 7 entirely liquid; 1–2 constipation, 6–7 diarrhoea.
  • Marsh — 0 normal · 1 raised intraepithelial lymphocytes · 2 crypt hyperplasia · 3a partial, 3b subtotal, 3c total villous atrophy.
Severity and prognosis
  • Revised Atlanta — mild (no organ failure or local complications) · moderately severe (transient organ failure under 48 hours, or local complications) · severe (organ failure persisting beyond 48 hours).
  • Hinchey — I pericolic abscess · II pelvic or distant abscess · III purulent peritonitis · IV faeculent peritonitis.
  • Tokyo cholangitis — grade III (organ dysfunction) needs biliary drainage within 24 hours, sooner if shocked.
  • King's College — paracetamol: pH <7.3, or all of INR >6.5, creatinine >3.4 mg/dL and grade III–IV encephalopathy. Non-paracetamol: INR >6.5 alone, or any three adverse factors.
  • Lille — computed from age, albumin, creatinine, prothrombin time and bilirubin on days 0 and 7. Above 0.45 at day 7 means stop the steroid. Deliberately not implemented here: it is unit-sensitive and easy to get wrong, so use a validated calculator.

16The Trials

All 58, gathered in one place — snapshot and paper link on each

The evidence base, in one list

Grouped by area · every entry carries a snapshot and a link to the paper

InsideOesophagus and stomachGI bleedingLuminal and functionalInflammatory bowel diseaseColorectalPancreas and biliaryLiverNutrition

The same trials are attached to the recommendations they support throughout the module. This chapter gathers them so you can revise the evidence base as a block, or find a trial when you remember the finding but not the topic.

Must know
  • Six trials reversed prior practice — WATERFALL (fluids), Lau (endoscopy timing), Villanueva (transfusion), the diverticulitis antibiotic trials, PYTHON (feeding), and Lindor (high-dose UDCA causes harm).
  • Three define a stop rule or a decision point — Lille at day 7, Travis at day 3, Corley for adenoma detection.
  • Know one trial properly for each area you are asked about; naming three badly is worse than naming one well.

17Where to Get the Pictures

Sources whose licence actually permits reuse — and how to credit them

Verified free-licence sources for GI images

Licence terms as published by each repository — confirm on the individual file page before you rely on it

InsideRepositories worth your timeLicence types in plain termsAdding an image to this file

Where to find pictures you are actually allowed to use, and how to credit them.

Must know
  • “Personal use” is not a copyright exemption. What makes an image safe to reuse is its licence, not your intention — so work from repositories that state one.
  • Kvasir and NIDDK are the two highest-yield sources for this module — one for endoscopic photographs, one for illustrations.
  • Almost every free licence still requires attribution. Paste the credit line into the slot when you add the image.
  • Your own unit's de-identified images are the best source of all — no licence question, and they show the equipment you will actually be standing next to.
Full detail
Repositories worth your time
SourceWhat's thereLicence
Kvasir / Kvasir-CapsuleThousands of annotated GI endoscopy images sorted into classes — Z-line, pylorus, caecum, oesophagitis, ulcerative colitis, polyps, dyed and lifted polyps, resection marginsCC BY 4.0 — reuse with attribution. The single best match for what this module needs.
NIDDK Media Library (NIH)Digestive and liver illustrations and diagramsFree of copyright, credit required: “National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases, National Institutes of Health.”
Wikimedia CommonsEndoscopic photographs, barium studies, histology, anatomical diagramsFree content only by policy, but the specific licence varies file by file — public domain, CC0, CC BY, CC BY-SA. Open the file page and read it.
Open-i (US National Library of Medicine)Figures pulled from open-access biomedical literature; filterable by licenceVaries by article — the interface tells you. Prefer CC BY.
PubMed Central open-access subsetFigures from CC BY papers, including endoscopy and guideline reviewsCC BY figures are reusable with citation. Check the article's own licence statement, not just that it is free to read.
Wellcome CollectionHistorical and contemporary medical imageryMuch of it CC BY or public domain; stated per item.
RadiopaediaCase-based radiology — barium swallows, CT for diverticulitis and pancreatitisUsually CC BY-NC-SA. Non-commercial, so fine for private study, not for a published talk.
Worth knowingTwo things that look free and are not: figures in subscription journal articles (free to read at your institution is not free to reuse), and anything reached through Google Images or ResearchGate, which are indexes rather than licensors. If you cannot find a licence statement, treat the image as all rights reserved.
If you are putting a talk together
  • CC BY — use anywhere, credit the author. The most permissive practical licence.
  • CC BY-SA — same, but a derivative work must carry the same licence.
  • CC BY-NC — no commercial use. Teaching at your programme is normally fine; a sponsored talk is not.
  • Public domain / CC0 — no restrictions, though crediting is still good manners.
  • A workable credit line: Author, title, source, licence — for example, “Kvasir dataset, Simula, CC BY 4.0”.
Adding an image to this file
  1. Press Add images in the toolbar. The empty slots appear — until you do, they are completely hidden, so an unfilled slot never shows as a gap.
  2. Drag an image file onto a slot, or press Choose image. It is resized automatically and appears straight away.
  3. Type the credit line in the field beneath it.
  4. Press Save copy with images. You get a new self-contained file with every image permanently embedded, which works offline and needs no folder of pictures beside it.

If you would rather edit the file directly, the same slots are listed in a block marked YOUR IMAGES near the bottom of the source — set src to a URL or to a filename sitting in the same folder.

Seven slots sit in the chapters where a photograph shows something a schematic cannot — Barrett's mucosa, intestinal metaplasia on narrow-band imaging, cobblestoning, a non-bleeding visible vessel, achalasia on barium, polyp morphology, and the endoscopic landmarks. They stay hidden until you want them. Press Add images in the top bar to reveal them, drop a picture onto one, then press Save copy with images for a permanent file. The other five findings that were originally slots — LA grades, the Mayo subscore, EREFS, bowel-preparation scoring and varix grading — are now drawn diagrams, because those are classification systems rather than things you need a photograph of.

The best source of allAsk whether your unit keeps a teaching image library, and whether you may use de-identified images from cases you have been involved in. No licence question arises, and images from a scope you stood beside stay with you far better than anything downloaded.
